questions.stem: Pauling electronegativity values are H = 2.2 and Cl = 3.16. Which statement best describes the bonding electrons in a molecule of HCl?

options.text: They are transferred completely from hydrogen to chlorine, producing full ionic charges.
They are shared equally, because a bond between two nonmetal atoms is always nonpolar.
They are shared unequally and held closer to chlorine, giving chlorine a partial negative charge.
They are held closer to hydrogen, because the smaller hydrogen nucleus attracts them more strongly.

rationales.whyCorrect: The electronegativity difference is 3.16 - 2.2 = 0.96, which falls in the polar covalent range (roughly 0.4 to 1.7 on the Pauling scale; differences above about 1.7 to 2.0 are treated as ionic). The pair remains shared, but chlorine's greater effective nuclear attraction for bonding electrons shifts electron density toward it, creating a partial negative charge on Cl and a partial positive charge on H. This permanent bond dipole (HCl has a measured dipole moment near 1.08 D) is the foundation for predicting molecular polarity and intermolecular forces.
rationales.eli10: Both atoms keep hold of the shared electrons, but chlorine pulls harder, so the electron cloud sits lopsided toward the chlorine side. Lopsided electron density means chlorine ends up slightly negative and hydrogen slightly positive, written as delta-minus and delta-plus. That is what 'polar covalent' means: still sharing, just not fairly. Complete transfer would be ionic, and that takes a much larger electronegativity gap than 0.96.

questions.stem: Which intermolecular force acts between every pair of neighboring molecules, whether those molecules are polar or nonpolar?

rationales.whyCorrect: London dispersion forces arise from instantaneous fluctuations in an electron cloud that induce a matching temporary dipole in a neighboring particle. Because every atom and molecule contains electrons, dispersion is universal, while hydrogen bonding requires an H bonded to N, O, or F, dipole-dipole requires a permanent dipole, and ion-dipole requires an ion. Methane, with only 10 electrons and no permanent dipole, still condenses at about -161 degrees Celsius solely because of dispersion.
rationales.eli10: Electrons are constantly moving, so at any instant they can be bunched slightly to one side of a molecule. That momentary imbalance repels or attracts electrons in the molecule next door, creating a matching imbalance, and the two lopsided clouds attract. Since electrons exist in every molecule, this attraction never switches off, even in molecules with no permanent plus or minus end. The other three forces each need a special ingredient that many substances simply do not have.

questions.stem: A true hydrogen bond requires a hydrogen atom to be covalently bonded directly to which set of atoms?

options.text: Any element more electronegative than hydrogen

rationales.whyCorrect: N, O, and F combine high electronegativity with small atomic radius, so they strip enough electron density from hydrogen to leave a highly concentrated partial positive charge on a very small, unshielded nucleus. That exposed proton can approach a lone pair on a nearby N, O, or F closely enough to give an unusually strong dipole-dipole interaction, typically 4 to 40 kJ/mol. The weakest qualifying case, N-H, still has an electronegativity difference of 3.04 - 2.2 = 0.84, whereas larger atoms such as S and Cl are too diffuse to produce the same effect despite reasonable electronegativity.
rationales.eli10: Hydrogen has only one electron, so when a very electronegative partner pulls that electron away, almost nothing is left shielding the proton. Size matters as much as pull: the partner has to be small enough that the stripped hydrogen sits close to it and stays exposed. Nitrogen, oxygen, and fluorine are the only common atoms that are both small and greedy enough. Chlorine is electronegative but large, so its electron cloud spreads out and the effect fades.

questions.stem: A beaker of liquid water is heated until it boils completely away at 100 degrees Celsius. Which forces are overcome during this process?

options.text: Only London dispersion forces, because hydrogen bonds persist unchanged in steam
The O-H covalent bonds inside each molecule, releasing hydrogen and oxygen atoms
Both the O-H covalent bonds and the hydrogen bonds, in roughly equal proportion
Attractions between molecules, mainly hydrogen bonds, while O-H covalent bonds stay intact

rationales.whyCorrect: Boiling is a physical change that separates intact molecules from one another, so only intermolecular attractions are disrupted. The energy scale confirms this: the average O-H covalent bond enthalpy is about 463 kJ/mol, while a single hydrogen bond in water is roughly 21 kJ/mol, a gap of 442 kJ/mol, and water's enthalpy of vaporization is only 40.7 kJ/mol. Steam is still H2O; if covalent bonds were broken, boiling water would generate hydrogen and oxygen gas, which it does not.
rationales.eli10: Water molecules in the liquid are stuck to each other by hydrogen bonds, like magnets on a fridge. Boiling pulls the magnets apart, but each molecule stays a molecule, which is why steam is still water. Splitting the O-H bonds inside a molecule is a chemical change that costs more than ten times as much energy per bond and would give you hydrogen and oxygen gas instead of steam. Any time you see melting, boiling, or evaporating, think intermolecular, not intramolecular.

computation.unit: kJ/mol difference between an O-H bond and a hydrogen bond

questions.stem: Carbon dioxide contains two strongly polar C=O bonds, yet the whole molecule is nonpolar. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: The molecule is linear, so two equal bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel.
The individual C=O bond dipoles are too small to give the molecule measurable polarity.
Double bonds share four electrons, and that larger shared count cancels bond polarity.
Lone pairs on the central carbon atom offset the partial charges on the two oxygens.

rationales.whyCorrect: Molecular polarity is the vector sum of bond dipoles, so geometry matters as much as electronegativity. Each C=O bond is genuinely polar, with an electronegativity difference of 3.44 - 2.55 = 0.89, but the central carbon has no lone pairs, giving a linear 180-degree arrangement in which two identical dipoles point directly away from each other and sum to zero. Water contains comparably polar O-H bonds but is bent at about 104.5 degrees, so its bond dipoles cannot cancel and the molecule has a net dipole of 1.85 D.
rationales.eli10: Think of the two oxygens as equally strong pulls on the electrons, aimed in exactly opposite directions along a straight line. Real forces exist on each bond, but they add up to nothing overall, so the molecule has no plus end or minus end for a neighbor to grab. The key skill is checking geometry before declaring a molecule polar: identical polar bonds arranged symmetrically cancel, and the same bonds arranged asymmetrically, as in bent water, do not.

computation.unit: Pauling electronegativity difference per C=O bond

questions.stem: Fluorine (F2) is a gas at room temperature while iodine (I2) is a solid, even though both are nonpolar diatomic molecules. Which comparison is accurate?

options.text: Iodine molecules are polar and fluorine molecules are not, so iodine has dipole-dipole forces.
Iodine molecules hydrogen bond to one another, which fluorine molecules cannot do.
Iodine has far more electrons in a larger, more polarizable cloud, so dispersion is stronger.
Fluorine is more electronegative, so fluorine molecules attract one another more strongly.

rationales.whyCorrect: Both molecules are homonuclear, so neither has a permanent dipole and dispersion is the only force available to either. Dispersion strength tracks polarizability, which rises with the number of electrons and how loosely the outer ones are held: I2 carries 106 electrons versus 18 for F2, a difference of 88. Iodine's large, easily distorted cloud produces attractions strong enough to hold a crystalline solid melting at 113.7 degrees Celsius, while F2 boils at -188 degrees Celsius. Note that electronegativity describes electron pull within a bond, not attraction between separate molecules.
rationales.eli10: Dispersion depends on how easily an electron cloud can be pushed out of shape, and big loose clouds distort far more than small tight ones. Fluorine's eighteen electrons are held close to two small nuclei, so its momentary dipoles are tiny and the molecules barely stick. Iodine's one hundred six electrons sit in large outer shells that shift easily, producing much stronger momentary dipoles. More electrons and greater volume mean stronger dispersion, which is the usual reason substances get less volatile as you move down a group.

computation.unit: more electrons in I2 than in F2

questions.stem: When solid sodium chloride dissolves in water, which interaction primarily stabilizes the separated sodium and chloride ions in solution?

options.text: Ion-dipole attractions between each ion and the oppositely charged end of nearby water molecules
Hydrogen bonds formed directly between sodium ions and the oxygen atoms of water molecules
London dispersion forces between the ions and the electron clouds of water molecules
New covalent bonds formed between the sodium ions and the oxygen atoms of water

rationales.whyCorrect: Water is polar, with partial negative charge on oxygen and partial positive charge on the hydrogens, so oxygen ends orient toward Na+ and hydrogen ends orient toward Cl-. These ion-dipole attractions are the strongest of the intermolecular interactions and build hydration shells whose released hydration energy roughly offsets the 787 kJ/mol lattice energy of NaCl. Because each formula unit releases two ions, dissolving 0.15 mol NaCl yields 0.3 mol of solute particles, which is why saline solutions conduct current and exert osmotic pressure roughly double that of an equimolar nonelectrolyte.
rationales.eli10: An ion carries a full charge and water carries partial charges, so the two line up: oxygen ends crowd around the sodium ion and hydrogen ends crowd around the chloride ion. Each ion ends up wrapped in a shell of oriented water molecules that keeps it separated from its former partner. This is not a hydrogen bond, because no hydrogen is being shared with a lone pair on N, O, or F, and it is not covalent, because no electrons are shared. Full charge meeting partial charge is called ion-dipole.

computation.unit: mol of dissolved ions from 0.15 mol NaCl

questions.stem: In a hypothetical lab exercise, Solid X dissolves in water to 36 g per 100 mL, while Solid Y dissolves to only 0.003 g per 100 mL. Which conclusion is best supported by these data?

options.text: Solid Y is the more polar substance, because polar solids resist dissolving in polar solvents.
Solid X is likely ionic or polar and solvates well, while Solid Y is likely nonpolar.
Solid X is nonpolar and Solid Y is polar, because nonpolar solids mix freely with water.
Both solids are nonpolar, and the gap reflects only the particle size of each solid.

rationales.whyCorrect: The rule that like dissolves like is an energetic statement: dissolving proceeds readily when new solute-solvent attractions repay the energy spent separating solvent molecules from each other and solute particles from each other. Solid X is 36 / 0.003 = 12,000 times more soluble, consistent with ion-dipole or hydrogen-bonding interactions strong enough to pay that cost, while a nonpolar Solid Y offers only weak dispersion forces and cannot compete with water's hydrogen-bond network. The same logic explains why glucose and electrolytes travel freely in plasma while lipids require carrier proteins or lipoproteins.
rationales.eli10: Water molecules already hold each other tightly with hydrogen bonds, so a solute has to offer something comparable to be let in. A charged or polar solid offers strong attractions to water's partial charges, so water rearranges around it and it dissolves. A nonpolar solid offers only weak dispersion, so water prefers its own company and the solid stays undissolved. A twelve-thousand-fold solubility gap is exactly the fingerprint of one solute matching water's polarity and the other not.

questions.stem: Ethanol (CH3CH2OH) boils at 78 degrees Celsius, but dimethyl ether (CH3OCH3), which has the identical molecular formula C2H6O, boils near -24 degrees Celsius. Which statement best explains this difference?

options.text: Ethanol's O-H group can donate and accept hydrogen bonds; the ether oxygen can only accept.
Dimethyl ether is fully nonpolar, so only dispersion forces operate between its molecules.
Ethanol contains an extra carbon-oxygen bond that raises the energy needed to vaporize it.
Ethanol has the greater molar mass, so its London dispersion forces are much stronger.

rationales.whyCorrect: These isomers share the formula C2H6O and a molar mass of about 46 g/mol, so dispersion forces are comparable and cannot account for the 78 - (-24) = 102 degree Celsius gap. Hydrogen bonding requires a hydrogen covalently bound to N, O, or F: ethanol supplies that donor, so its molecules form an extended hydrogen-bonded network. Dimethyl ether's oxygen is flanked by two carbons and has lone pairs but no attached hydrogen, so in the pure liquid no donor exists and only dipole-dipole and dispersion forces remain. Both isomers are polar; polarity alone is not the deciding factor.
rationales.eli10: Hydrogen bonding takes two parts: a donor, meaning an H attached to N, O, or F, and an acceptor, meaning a lone pair. Ethanol has both, so its molecules link into chains that take a lot of heat to pull apart. Dimethyl ether has acceptors only, and an acceptor with no donor nearby has nothing to bond to, so pure ether molecules just brush past each other. Same atoms, different arrangement, and the presence or absence of one donor hydrogen shifts the boiling point by over 100 degrees.

computation.unit: degrees Celsius difference in boiling point

questions.stem: Which change would most likely increase the rate at which a liquid evaporates from an open dish held at constant temperature?

options.text: Replacing the liquid with one whose molecules form an extensive hydrogen-bond network
Dissolving a nonvolatile solute that lowers the liquid's vapor pressure
Replacing the liquid with one whose molecules have weaker intermolecular attractions
Pouring the liquid into a narrow cylinder that exposes less surface area

rationales.whyCorrect: Evaporation occurs when surface molecules acquire enough kinetic energy to escape the attractions of their neighbors, so weakening those attractions increases the fraction of molecules that can escape at any given temperature. Liquids with weak intermolecular forces therefore show high vapor pressure and low enthalpy of vaporization, while water's extensive hydrogen bonding gives it an enthalpy of vaporization of about 40.7 kJ/mol, so 2 mol takes about 81.4 kJ to vaporize. The other options either strengthen the attractions holding molecules in the liquid or reduce the surface area from which escape occurs, both of which slow evaporation.
rationales.eli10: Only molecules at the surface with above-average kinetic energy can break free, so the question is how high the escape barrier sits. Weaker attractions lower that barrier, so a much larger share of surface molecules clears it every second and the dish empties faster. That is why isopropyl alcohol dries on skin within seconds while water lingers: alcohol has fewer hydrogen bonds per molecule. Surface area and added solutes change the rate too, but the options listed move both in the wrong direction.

computation.unit: kJ to vaporize 2 mol of water at 100 degrees Celsius

questions.stem: A phospholipid molecule has one charged phosphate head group and two long hydrocarbon tails. What would happen if a large number of these molecules were placed in water?

options.text: They settle as a disordered solid, since a molecule with long hydrocarbon chains is nonpolar.
They dissolve completely as separate molecules, since the charged head makes each one soluble.
They dissolve because the hydrocarbon tails form hydrogen bonds with surrounding water.
They self-assemble with polar heads facing the water and nonpolar tails clustered away from it.

rationales.whyCorrect: Phospholipids are amphipathic: the charged phosphate head engages in ion-dipole and hydrogen-bonding interactions with water, while the hydrocarbon tails offer only dispersion forces and force surrounding water into an entropically costly ordered cage. The system minimizes free energy by sequestering the tails, and the shape of the aggregate follows the shape of the molecule: two bulky tails under one head make the molecule roughly cylindrical, so it packs into a bilayer that typically closes into a vesicle, whereas single-tailed amphiphiles such as soaps and detergents are cone-shaped and form micelles instead. An aggregate of 500 of these two-tailed phospholipids buries 2 * 500 = 1000 tails in a shielded hydrophobic core. Because the tails are shielded rather than dissolved, the assembly is a stable structure, not a precipitate, which is why cell membranes form and reseal without any energy input.
rationales.eli10: One molecule cannot satisfy both halves at once, since the head wants water contact and the tails want to avoid it. The compromise is collective: thousands of molecules point their heads outward into the water and tuck their tails inward against each other. Two fat tails under one head make this molecule shaped more like a cylinder than a cone, so the sheet it builds is two layers thick and usually curls around to close into a hollow bubble; single-tailed molecules like soap are cone-shaped and ball up into small micelles instead. The driving force is largely the water itself, which regains freedom once it no longer has to cage greasy chains, and this single polarity argument is why every cell membrane exists and why it heals over small punctures.

questions.stem: For a hypothetical polar liquid, the total intermolecular attraction is 21 kJ/mol, of which 17 kJ/mol is attributed to London dispersion and the remainder to dipole-dipole attraction. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The substance behaves as a nonpolar liquid, since dispersion supplies most of the attraction.
Dipole-dipole attraction outweighs dispersion whenever a substance has a permanent dipole.
The substance is capable of hydrogen bonding, since the total attraction exceeds 20 kJ/mol.
Dispersion can dominate in a polar substance, with dipole-dipole supplying under one fifth.

rationales.whyCorrect: Dispersion and dipole-dipole contributions are additive, and dispersion grows steeply with electron count and polarizability, so in many polar molecules of moderate size dispersion supplies the larger share of the total attraction. Here the dipole-dipole term is 21 - 17 = 4 kJ/mol, or (21 - 17) / 21 * 100 = 19.05 percent of the total, which is below one fifth. A nonzero dipole-dipole term establishes that the substance is polar, so it cannot be treated as nonpolar, and a total near 21 kJ/mol says nothing about hydrogen bonding, which requires a hydrogen covalently bonded to N, O, or F rather than a threshold energy.
rationales.eli10: A common misconception is that once a molecule is polar, its permanent dipole becomes the main source of attraction. In reality the dispersion contribution keeps climbing as the electron cloud gets larger, and it routinely overtakes the dipole term in molecules bigger than a few atoms. Here the dipole part is about 19 out of every 100 units of attraction, so polarity is real but minor. Data like these are why chemists compare molecules on total attraction rather than assuming the presence of a dipole settles the ranking.

computation.unit: percent of total attraction from dipole-dipole

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a Brønsted–Lowry acid?

options.text: A substance that accepts a proton from another substance
A substance that donates a proton (H+) to another substance
A substance that accepts a pair of electrons to form a bond
A substance that releases H+ only when dissolved in water

rationales.whyCorrect: In the Brønsted–Lowry framework an acid is defined by proton transfer: it donates H+ to a proton acceptor, which is the base. Option A is the Brønsted–Lowry definition of a base, option C is the Lewis definition of an acid (electron-pair acceptor), and option D is the narrower Arrhenius definition, which is restricted to aqueous solution. The proton-transfer definition is the one used in physiology because it also covers species such as HCO3- and NH3 acting as bases in nonaqueous or biological settings.
rationales.eli10: Acid-base chemistry is bookkeeping for one particle: the proton, H+. In any such reaction one species hands off an H+ and another takes it; the donor is the acid, the acceptor is the base. Defining acids this way is broader than saying 'makes H+ in water,' because it also describes reactions in blood, in gases, and in nonwater solvents. It also means every acid automatically creates a base when it loses its proton.

questions.stem: The pH scale is logarithmic. A solution at pH 4 has a hydronium ion concentration how many times greater than a solution at pH 7?

rationales.whyCorrect: Because pH = -log[H3O+], each whole pH unit corresponds to a tenfold change in hydronium concentration. A difference of 3 pH units is therefore 10 raised to the third power, a 1,000-fold difference in [H3O+]. Option A treats the scale as linear, the most common misconception about pH; option B corresponds to a 2-unit difference and option D to a 4-unit difference.
rationales.eli10: pH counts powers of ten, not equal steps. Moving from pH 7 to pH 6 multiplies the hydronium concentration by 10, from 7 to 5 by 100, and from 7 to 4 by 1,000. Concretely, pH 7 is 0.0000001 mol/L and pH 4 is 0.0001 mol/L. That compression is why a change of even a few tenths of a unit in a patient's blood is chemically large.

questions.stem: Normal arterial blood is maintained in the pH range 7.35 to 7.45. Which description of that range is accurate?

options.text: Strongly acidic, far below the neutral point of water
Slightly alkaline, just above the neutral point of water
Strongly alkaline, near the upper end of the pH scale
Exactly neutral, identical to pure water at 25 °C

rationales.whyCorrect: Pure water at 25 °C is neutral at pH 7, so a range centered near 7.4 lies slightly above neutral and is correctly described as slightly alkaline. It is not strongly alkaline; solutions of strong bases occupy pH values near 12 to 14. Recognizing that blood sits only a few tenths of a unit above neutral explains why deviations of even 0.1 unit are reported as clinically meaningful.
rationales.eli10: On the 0 to 14 scale, 7 marks the point where hydronium and hydroxide are equal. Blood at 7.4 sits just past that point on the basic side, not far out toward the strongly basic end. In concentration terms, 7.4 means about 4 × 10^-8 mol/L hydronium versus 1 × 10^-7 mol/L in neutral water, so blood holds roughly two and a half times less hydronium than plain water. 'Slightly alkaline' is the precise description.

questions.stem: A laboratory solution measured at 25 °C has a pOH of 4.5. What is its pH, and how should the solution be classified?

rationales.whyCorrect: At 25 °C the ion product of water (Kw = 1 × 10^-14) gives pH + pOH = 14, so a pOH of 4.5 corresponds to a pH of 14 - 4.5 = 9.5. Because 9.5 is above 7, hydroxide exceeds hydronium and the solution is basic. Option D comes from adding rather than subtracting, option A from assuming pH equals pOH, and option C from misclassifying a pH above 7.
rationales.eli10: pH and pOH are two readings of the same solution, and at 25 °C they always sum to 14. A pOH of 4.5 is low, which means hydroxide is relatively plentiful, so the solution must be basic and its pH must be the complement, 9.5. A quick check: any pOH below 7 forces a pH above 7. That single relationship lets you convert between the two scales without recalculating concentrations.

questions.stem: Which comparison between a strong acid and a weak acid prepared at the same molar concentration is accurate?

options.text: The strong acid has the higher pH because it holds its protons tightly
Both solutions have the same hydronium concentration because molarity sets pH
The weak acid ionizes completely but neutralizes added base more slowly
The strong acid ionizes essentially completely, so it has the lower pH

rationales.whyCorrect: Acid strength describes the extent of ionization, not the amount of acid dissolved. A strong acid such as HCl dissociates essentially completely, releasing far more hydronium per mole than a weak acid such as acetic acid, which establishes an equilibrium with most molecules still undissociated. More hydronium means a lower pH, so at equal molarity the strong acid gives the more acidic solution.
rationales.eli10: Concentration counts how much acid you added; strength counts what fraction of it actually lets go of its proton. In 0.1 mol/L HCl essentially every molecule releases H+, giving about 0.1 mol/L hydronium and a pH near 1. In 0.1 mol/L acetic acid only about 1 percent releases H+, giving roughly 0.001 mol/L and a pH near 3. Same amount dissolved, about a hundredfold difference in hydronium.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of the bicarbonate buffer system in extracellular fluid?

options.text: To increase the rate at which cells generate carbon dioxide
To excrete metabolic hydrogen ions from the body permanently
To hold extracellular fluid at pH 7, the value of pure water
To resist large shifts in pH when acid or base is added

rationales.whyCorrect: A buffer is a weak acid paired with its conjugate base; added H+ is consumed by the base member and added OH- is consumed by the acid member, so the pH change is blunted rather than eliminated. In extracellular fluid, HCO3- neutralizes added acid while H2CO3 (from dissolved CO2) neutralizes added base. Permanent removal of acid is the job of the lungs and kidneys, not the buffer itself, and buffers hold pH near their working range, which for this system is about 7.4, not 7. Note that this system's apparent pKa is 6.1, which is outside the usual pKa ± 1 window for pH 7.4; it is nonetheless effective in the body because it is an open system, in which the lungs continuously adjust dissolved CO2 (and the kidneys adjust HCO3-) so the acid member is replenished or vented rather than exhausted.
rationales.eli10: A buffer behaves like a shock absorber for pH. When acid enters, bicarbonate captures the H+ and turns it into carbonic acid, a much weaker acid; when base enters, carbonic acid gives up an H+ to neutralize it. The added particles are not destroyed, only converted into a less disruptive form, so pH moves a little instead of a lot. In a sealed beaker this pair would be a mediocre buffer at 7.4, since its pKa of 6.1 is more than a unit away, but the body keeps it open to the air: breathing sets how much CO2 stays dissolved. Actually clearing that acid load requires exhaling CO2 and renal excretion.

questions.stem: Which example correctly illustrates a neutralization reaction?

options.text: Hydrochloric acid reacting with sodium hydroxide to give NaCl and water
Sodium chloride crystals dissolving in water to give Na+ and Cl- ions
Acetic acid partially ionizing in water to give H3O+ and acetate ions
Zinc metal reacting with oxygen gas to form solid zinc oxide

rationales.whyCorrect: Neutralization is the reaction of an acid with a base to yield a salt and water, driven by H+ combining with OH- to form H2O. HCl + NaOH gives NaCl plus water, the standard example. Option B is dissociation of an already formed salt, option C is ionization of a weak acid (which produces hydronium rather than consuming it), and option D is an oxidation-reduction reaction with no proton transfer.
rationales.eli10: To spot a neutralization, look for an acid and a base as the two reactants and for water among the products. The essential step is H+ + OH- forming H2O; the leftover cation and anion simply remain in solution as dissolved salt. Dissolving a salt only separates ions that already existed, ionizing a weak acid releases hydronium instead of removing it, and metal oxidation transfers electrons, not protons.

questions.stem: A hypothetical laboratory solution is reported to have a pH of 3. Which value correctly gives its hydronium ion concentration?

rationales.whyCorrect: Because pH = -log[H3O+], the concentration is recovered as [H3O+] = 10^-pH, so a pH of 3 gives 1 × 10^-3 mol/L. Option B is the hydroxide concentration of this same solution, since pOH = 14 - 3 = 11. Options A and C treat the digit 3 as a coefficient rather than as the exponent, a frequent error when converting between pH and concentration.
rationales.eli10: The pH value is an exponent, so undoing it means raising 10 to the negative of that number. A pH of 3 becomes 10^-3, which is 0.001 mol/L; the leading coefficient is 1, not 3. If the pH had been 3.5, the concentration would fall between 10^-4 and 10^-3, closer to 3 × 10^-4. Whenever a pH is a whole number, the concentration is a 1 sitting in that decimal place: pH 3 gives 0.001 and pH 5 gives 0.00001.

questions.stem: A blood sample's pH is reported as 7.2, compared with a previous value of 7.4 in the same person. Which interpretation of this change is most accurate?

options.text: Hydronium ion concentration rose by about 0.2 mol/L

rationales.whyCorrect: A fall in pH always corresponds to a rise in hydronium concentration, and the magnitude of that rise is 10 raised to the pH difference: 10^(7.4 - 7.2) = 10^0.2, which is about 1.58. So a 0.2-unit drop represents roughly a 58 percent increase in [H3O+]. Option B would require a 2-unit fall, option C reverses the direction of the relationship, and option D misreads a pH difference as a concentration difference in mol/L.
rationales.eli10: Two features of pH have to be applied together here: it runs in reverse, so a lower number means more hydronium, and it is logarithmic, so even a fractional change multiplies the concentration. Raising 10 to the 0.2 power gives about 1.6, meaning roughly 60 percent more hydronium than before. In absolute terms the shift is from about 4 × 10^-8 to about 6 × 10^-8 mol/L, tiny numbers whose ratio is what matters physiologically.

questions.stem: Which change would most likely raise the pH of a bicarbonate-buffered solution that is in contact with a gas phase?

options.text: Bubbling additional carbon dioxide gas through the solution
Adding a measured volume of hydrochloric acid solution
Sweeping dissolved carbon dioxide out of the solution
Adding a neutral salt that does not react with water

rationales.whyCorrect: Dissolved CO2 combines with water to form carbonic acid, the acid member of the bicarbonate buffer pair. Removing CO2 shifts the equilibrium CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3- to the left, lowering H+ and raising the bicarbonate-to-acid ratio, so pH increases. Adding CO2 or a strong acid lowers pH, and an unreactive salt leaves the buffer ratio essentially unchanged.
rationales.eli10: Dissolved carbon dioxide functions as a hidden acid: combine it with water and carbonic acid forms, which then releases H+. Because that whole sequence is an equilibrium, taking CO2 away pulls the reaction backward and consumes H+, so the pH climbs. This is exactly the chemistry behind hyperventilation raising blood pH and hypoventilation lowering it, since ventilation controls how much CO2 stays dissolved.

questions.stem: A hypothetical laboratory buffer must hold a test solution near pH 7.4. Four weak acid/conjugate base pairs are available, with pKa values of 3.75, 4.76, 7.21, and 9.25. Which choice and reasoning are correct?

options.text: The pKa 7.21 pair, because buffering is strongest within about 1 unit of the pKa
The pKa 4.76 pair, because a lower pKa resists added acid more effectively
The pKa 9.25 pair, because the target pH lies on the alkaline side of neutral
The pKa 3.75 pair, because the strongest weak acid provides the most capacity

rationales.whyCorrect: From pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]), a buffer holds appreciable amounts of both members only when the target pH is within roughly 1 unit of its pKa; there the ratio stays between about 1:10 and 10:1 and capacity is greatest. A pKa of 7.21 is only 0.19 unit from 7.4, requiring a near-equimolar mixture. The pKa 4.76 and 3.75 pairs would exist almost entirely as conjugate base at pH 7.4, and the pKa 9.25 pair almost entirely as the protonated acid, leaving little of the partner species to absorb an insult in either direction.
rationales.eli10: A buffer works because both partners are present in usable amounts; whichever one runs out first sets the limit. The pKa is the pH at which the two are equal, and each pH unit away from it tilts the mixture tenfold toward one side. Two units away the minority species is only about 1 percent of the pair, so the buffer is nearly exhausted before it starts. Matching the pKa to the target pH keeps both partners stocked.

questions.stem: In a model of extracellular fluid, the bicarbonate-to-dissolved-CO2 ratio falls from 20:1 to 10:1 while the pKa remains 6.1. What would happen to the pH?

options.text: It rises from about 7.4 to about 7.7
It stays near 7.4 because the pKa did not change
It falls from about 7.4 to about 7.1
It falls from about 7.4 to about 6.4

rationales.whyCorrect: Using pH = pKa + log([HCO3-]/[CO2]), the 20:1 ratio gives 6.1 + 1.3 = 7.4, while the 10:1 ratio gives 6.1 + 1 = 7.1. Halving the ratio lowers pH by log 2, about 0.3 unit, not a full unit, because the relationship is logarithmic. Option D would require a 2:1 ratio and option A would require the ratio to increase rather than fall.
rationales.eli10: In the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation only the ratio of the two buffer members, not their absolute amounts, sets the pH once the pKa is fixed. Because the ratio enters as a logarithm, cutting it in half subtracts log 2, which is about 0.3 unit. That is why a pH of 7.1 can arise either from losing bicarbonate or from retaining CO2: both change the same ratio, and 0.3 unit is already a large clinical move.

questions.stem:
Calculate the molar solubility of AgCl in pure water at 25 °C.
Ksp(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10^-10.

rationales.whyCorrect: AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag+(aq) + Cl^-(aq). Ksp = [Ag+][Cl^-] = s^2. s = sqrt(Ksp) = sqrt(1.8 × 10^-10) = 1.34 × 10^-5 → 1.3 × 10^-5 M (2 sig figs). Option A (9.0 × 10^-6) comes from s = Ksp/2, incorrectly halving Ksp. Option C (1.8 × 10^-5) uses s = Ksp^(1/2) with a rounding error or drops sig figs. Option D (3.6 × 10^-5) uses s = 2 × sqrt(Ksp).
rationales.eli10: When AgCl dissolves, each formula unit produces exactly one Ag+ and one Cl^-. So if s moles dissolve per liter, both ion concentrations equal s. Ksp = s × s = s^2. Take the square root: s = about 1.3 × 10^-5 M. That means only 0.000013 moles dissolve in a liter — about two grains of salt's worth. Most of the solid stays at the bottom.
rationales.highYield: For a 1:1 salt (AB), molar solubility s = sqrt(Ksp). For a 2:1 salt (A2B), s = (Ksp/4)^(1/3). The relationship depends on stoichiometry.

questions.sourceSnapshotMarkdown:
### Q02-04 Molar solubility from Ksp

Calculate the molar solubility of AgCl in pure water at 25 °C.
Ksp(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10^-10.

- **A.** 9.0 × 10^-6 M
- **B.** 1.3 × 10^-5 M
- **C.** 1.8 × 10^-5 M
- **D.** 3.6 × 10^-5 M

**Correct Answer:** **B.** 1.3 × 10^-5 M

**Why This Is Correct:** AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag+(aq) + Cl^-(aq). Ksp = [Ag+][Cl^-] = s^2. s = sqrt(Ksp) = sqrt(1.8 × 10^-10) = 1.34 × 10^-5 → 1.3 × 10^-5 M (2 sig figs). Option A (9.0 × 10^-6) comes from s = Ksp/2, incorrectly halving Ksp. Option C (1.8 × 10^-5) uses s = Ksp^(1/2) with a rounding error or drops sig figs. Option D (3.6 × 10^-5) uses s = 2 × sqrt(Ksp).

> **High-Yield:** For a 1:1 salt (AB), molar solubility s = sqrt(Ksp). For a 2:1 salt (A2B), s = (Ksp/4)^(1/3). The relationship depends on stoichiometry.

**ELI-10:** When AgCl dissolves, each formula unit produces exactly one Ag+ and one Cl^-. So if s moles dissolve per liter, both ion concentrations equal s. Ksp = s × s = s^2. Take the square root: s = about 1.3 × 10^-5 M. That means only 0.000013 moles dissolve in a liter — about two grains of salt's worth. Most of the solid stays at the bottom.

questions.stem:
Calculate the molar solubility of AgCl in 0.10 M NaCl at 25 °C.
Ksp(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10^-10.

rationales.whyCorrect: AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag+(aq) + Cl^-(aq). NaCl provides 0.10 M Cl^- as a common ion. Let [Ag+] = s, then [Cl^-] = 0.10 + s ≈ 0.10 M (s is negligible). Ksp = [Ag+][Cl^-] = s × 0.10 = 1.8 × 10^-10. s = 1.8 × 10^-10 / 0.10 = 1.8 × 10^-9 M. The solubility drops from 1.3 × 10^-5 M (pure water) to 1.8 × 10^-9 M — a ~7000-fold decrease. Option A is the solubility in pure water. Option B reports Ksp itself. Option D is off by a factor of 10.
rationales.eli10: Adding NaCl to a saturated AgCl solution is like adding more people to an already crowded elevator. AgCl dissolves by releasing Ag+ and Cl^-. If Cl^- is already abundant from NaCl, the dissolving reaction backs off — fewer Ag+ ions can be released before the product [Ag+][Cl^-] hits the Ksp limit. The solubility plummets from 1.3 × 10^-5 M to just 1.8 × 10^-9 M.
rationales.highYield: A common ion suppresses solubility. s = Ksp / [common ion] for 1:1 salts. The more common ion present, the less solid dissolves.

questions.sourceSnapshotMarkdown:
### Q02-06 Common ion effect on solubility

Calculate the molar solubility of AgCl in 0.10 M NaCl at 25 °C.
Ksp(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10^-10.

- **A.** 1.3 × 10^-5 M
- **B.** 1.8 × 10^-10 M
- **C.** 1.8 × 10^-9 M
- **D.** 1.8 × 10^-8 M

**Correct Answer:** **C.** 1.8 × 10^-9 M

**Why This Is Correct:** AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag+(aq) + Cl^-(aq). NaCl provides 0.10 M Cl^- as a common ion. Let [Ag+] = s, then [Cl^-] = 0.10 + s ≈ 0.10 M (s is negligible). Ksp = [Ag+][Cl^-] = s × 0.10 = 1.8 × 10^-10. s = 1.8 × 10^-10 / 0.10 = 1.8 × 10^-9 M. The solubility drops from 1.3 × 10^-5 M (pure water) to 1.8 × 10^-9 M — a ~7000-fold decrease. Option A is the solubility in pure water. Option B reports Ksp itself. Option D is off by a factor of 10.

> **High-Yield:** A common ion suppresses solubility. s = Ksp / [common ion] for 1:1 salts. The more common ion present, the less solid dissolves.

**ELI-10:** Adding NaCl to a saturated AgCl solution is like adding more people to an already crowded elevator. AgCl dissolves by releasing Ag+ and Cl^-. If Cl^- is already abundant from NaCl, the dissolving reaction backs off — fewer Ag+ ions can be released before the product [Ag+][Cl^-] hits the Ksp limit. The solubility plummets from 1.3 × 10^-5 M to just 1.8 × 10^-9 M.

questions.stem: The second law of thermodynamics states that for any spontaneous process:

rationales.whyCorrect: The second law: total entropy of the universe increases for any spontaneous process. ΔS_universe = ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings > 0. The system's entropy can decrease as long as the surroundings' entropy increases more. Option A is common but wrong — system entropy can decrease. Option C relates to enthalpy, not the second law. Option D is true at constant T and P but is a consequence, not the second law itself.
rationales.eli10: The second law is why your room gets messier — the universe's total messiness always increases. You can clean your room (decrease system entropy), but you sweat and heat the air while doing it (increase surroundings entropy), and the total mess still goes up. The universe always wins the entropy game — local order costs global disorder.
rationales.highYield: Second law: ΔS_universe > 0 for spontaneous processes. ΔS_system may decrease if ΔS_surroundings increases more.

### Q04-03 Second law of thermodynamics

The second law of thermodynamics states that for any spontaneous process:

- **A.** ΔS_system > 0
- **B.** ΔS_universe > 0
- **C.** ΔH_system < 0
- **D.** ΔG_system < 0

**Correct Answer:** **B.** ΔS_universe > 0

**Why This Is Correct:** The second law: total entropy of the universe increases for any spontaneous process. ΔS_universe = ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings > 0. The system's entropy can decrease as long as the surroundings' entropy increases more. Option A is common but wrong — system entropy can decrease. Option C relates to enthalpy, not the second law. Option D is true at constant T and P but is a consequence, not the second law itself.

You can clean your room (decrease system entropy), but you sweat and heat the air while doing it (increase surroundings entropy), and the total mess still goes up. The universe always wins the entropy game — local order costs global disorder.

questions.stem: When a reaction is at equilibrium, which of the following is true?

rationales.whyCorrect: At equilibrium, ΔG = 0 (no net driving force in either direction). ΔG° is NOT zero at equilibrium — ΔG° = -RT ln K, which is zero only when K = 1. Option A confuses ΔG° with ΔG. Option C requires K = 1 (rare). Option D is a true relationship at equilibrium (ΔG = ΔH - TΔS = 0 → ΔH = TΔS) but is a consequence, not the defining condition.
rationales.eli10: ΔG and ΔG° are like your current bank balance vs your starting balance. At equilibrium, your net change (ΔG) is zero — you have arrived at the balance point. But your starting balance relative to the equilibrium point (ΔG°) can be anything — it depends on where you started. They are different numbers that agree only in the special case where the starting point is already at equilibrium (K = 1).
rationales.highYield: At equilibrium: ΔG = 0, Q = K. ΔG° ≠ 0 unless K = 1. ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q.

questions.stem: The third law of thermodynamics states that:

options.text: Energy is conserved in all processes
The entropy of a perfect crystal at 0 K is zero
The entropy of the universe always increases

rationales.whyCorrect: The third law provides an absolute zero point for entropy: a perfect crystalline solid at absolute zero has exactly one microstate, so S = 0. This allows calculation of absolute entropies (S° values). Option A is the first law. Option C is the second law. Option D is the definition of Gibbs free energy.
rationales.eli10: The third law gives entropy an absolute starting line, like defining sea level as zero altitude. At absolute zero, a perfect crystal has exactly one arrangement — everything is frozen perfectly in place. This is the one point in the universe with zero entropy. From there, every substance gets a positive entropy score based on how many ways its molecules can arrange themselves at 25 °C.
rationales.highYield: Third law: S = 0 for a perfect crystal at 0 K. Enables absolute entropy values. ΔS° = ΣS°(products) - ΣS°(reactants).

### Q04-06 Third law of thermodynamics

The third law of thermodynamics states that:

- **A.** Energy is conserved in all processes
- **B.** The entropy of a perfect crystal at 0 K is zero
- **C.** The entropy of the universe always increases
- **D.** ΔG = ΔH - TΔS

**Correct Answer:** **B.** The entropy of a perfect crystal at 0 K is zero

**Why This Is Correct:** The third law provides an absolute zero point for entropy: a perfect crystalline solid at absolute zero has exactly one microstate, so S = 0. This allows calculation of absolute entropies (S° values). Option A is the first law. Option C is the second law. Option D is the definition of Gibbs free energy.

> **High-Yield:** Third law: S = 0 for a perfect crystal at 0 K. Enables absolute entropy values. ΔS° = ΣS°(products) - ΣS°(reactants).

**ELI-10:** The third law gives entropy an absolute starting line, like defining sea level as zero altitude. At absolute zero, a perfect crystal has exactly one arrangement — everything is frozen perfectly in place. This is the one point in the universe with zero entropy. questions.stem: For a reaction with ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0, increasing temperature:

options.text: Makes the reaction more spontaneous (ΔG more negative)
Makes the reaction less spontaneous (ΔG more positive)
Changes ΔH from positive to negative

rationales.whyCorrect: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS. With ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0, the -TΔS term is negative and its magnitude increases with T. At sufficiently high T, -TΔS dominates +ΔH, making ΔG < 0. Reactions like melting and vaporization (ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0) become spontaneous above a certain T. Option B describes the opposite case.
rationales.eli10: A reaction that absorbs heat but creates disorder is like melting ice — it costs energy (ΔH > 0) but creates freedom (ΔS > 0). At low temperatures, the energy cost wins and ice stays solid. Turn up the heat, and the disorder benefit gets multiplied by temperature, eventually outweighing the energy cost. That is why ice melts at higher temperatures — the entropy of liquid water finally wins.
rationales.highYield: ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0 → spontaneous at high T (TΔS dominates). ΔH < 0, ΔS < 0 → spontaneous at low T.

> **High-Yield:** ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0 → spontaneous at high T (TΔS dominates). ΔH < 0, ΔS < 0 → spontaneous at low T.

**ELI-10:** A reaction that absorbs heat but creates disorder is like melting ice — it costs energy (ΔH > 0) but creates freedom (ΔS > 0). questions.stem: Which has the highest standard molar entropy S° at 25 °C?

rationales.whyCorrect: S° follows: gases have much higher S° than liquids and solids due to translational freedom. CO2 is a gas with three atoms (translational + rotational + vibrational degrees of freedom). Diamond is a highly ordered covalent network solid (low S°). Liquid water has intermediate S°. NaCl is a crystalline solid (low S°).
rationales.eli10: Entropy is like a "freedom score" for molecules. Gases score highest because they zoom around freely with countless positions and speeds. Liquids score medium — molecules can move but stay touching. Solids score lowest — molecules are locked in place. CO2 gas has a high freedom score because it is a three-atom molecule that can fly, spin, and vibrate. Diamond scores near zero because every carbon is rigidly locked in a crystal cage.
rationales.highYield: S° trends: gas >> liquid > solid. More complex molecules have higher S° (more vibrational modes).

questions.stem: A concentration cell is constructed with Cu(s) | Cu2+(0.010 M) || Cu2+(1.0 M) | Cu(s). What is E_cell at 25 °C?

rationales.whyCorrect: For a concentration cell, E°_cell = 0 (same half-reactions). E_cell = (0.05916/n) log(c_cathode/c_anode) = (0.05916/2) log(1.0/0.010) = 0.02958 × log(100) = 0.02958 × 2 = 0.0592 V. Option A assumes no voltage. Option B forgets to convert from ln to log form. Option D uses n = 1.
rationales.eli10: A concentration cell is like two identical water tanks at different heights connected by a pipe — water flows from high to low until they level out. Even though both electrodes are the same (copper), the concentration difference (1.0 M vs 0.010 M) creates a voltage of 0.0592 V. As the cell runs, the concentrated side gets diluted and the dilute side gets more concentrated until they equalize and the voltage drops to zero.
rationales.highYield: Concentration cell: E_cell = (0.05916/n) log(c_high/c_low). Voltage from concentration difference alone.

questions.sourceSnapshotMarkdown:
### Q05-02 Nernst equation concentration cell

A concentration cell is constructed with Cu(s) | Cu2+(0.010 M) || Cu2+(1.0 M) | Cu(s). What is E_cell at 25 °C?

- **A.** 0.000 V
- **B.** 0.0296 V
- **C.** 0.0592 V
- **D.** 0.118 V

**Correct Answer:** **C.** 0.0592 V

**Why This Is Correct:** For a concentration cell, E°_cell = 0 (same half-reactions). E_cell = (0.05916/n) log(c_cathode/c_anode) = (0.05916/2) log(1.0/0.010) = 0.02958 × log(100) = 0.02958 × 2 = 0.0592 V. Option A assumes no voltage. Option B forgets to convert from ln to log form. Option D uses n = 1.

> **High-Yield:** Concentration cell: E_cell = (0.05916/n) log(c_high/c_low). Voltage from concentration difference alone.

**ELI-10:** A concentration cell is like two identical water tanks at different heights connected by a pipe — water flows from high to low until they level out. Even though both electrodes are the same (copper), the concentration difference (1.0 M vs 0.010 M) creates a voltage of 0.0592 V. As the cell runs, the concentrated side gets diluted and the dilute side gets more concentrated until they equalize and the voltage drops to zero.

questions.stem: Using the Nernst equation E = E° - (0.05916/n) log Q, when Q = 0.010, n = 2, and E° = 0.50 V, E_cell equals:

rationales.whyCorrect: log(0.010) = -2.000. E = 0.50 - (0.05916/2)(-2.000) = 0.50 - 0.02958(-2.000) = 0.50 + 0.0592 = 0.5592 V ≈ 0.56 V. The minus sign in the Nernst equation followed by a negative log Q results in ADDITION — cell voltage increases when Q < 1. Option A flips the sign. Option B ignores the Nernst correction. Option D miscalculates.
rationales.eli10: The Nernst equation's minus sign can be tricky. When Q is less than 1 (0.010), log Q is negative (-2). Subtracting a negative means adding — the voltage goes UP from E°. A fresh battery with mostly reactants (small Q) delivers more than its rated voltage. As it discharges and Q grows, the voltage drops. It is like a new battery having a little extra kick right out of the package.
rationales.highYield: Nernst: E = E° - (0.05916/n) log Q. When Q < 1, log Q < 0, so E > E°. Fresh cells with low product/reactant ratios give higher voltage.

Using the Nernst equation E = E° - (0.05916/n) log Q, when Q = 0.010, n = 2, and E° = 0.50 V, E_cell equals:

- **A.** 0.44 V
- **B.** 0.50 V
- **C.** 0.56 V
- **D.** 0.62 V

**Correct Answer:** **C.** 0.56 V

**Why This Is Correct:** log(0.010) = -2.000. E = 0.50 - (0.05916/2)(-2.000) = 0.50 - 0.02958(-2.000) = 0.50 + 0.0592 = 0.5592 V ≈ 0.56 V. The minus sign in the Nernst equation followed by a negative log Q results in ADDITION — cell voltage increases when Q < 1. Option A flips the sign. Option B ignores the Nernst correction. Option D miscalculates.

> **High-Yield:** Nernst: E = E° - (0.05916/n) log Q. When Q < 1, log Q < 0, so E > E°. Fresh cells with low product/reactant ratios give higher voltage.

**ELI-10:** The Nernst equation's minus sign can be tricky. When Q is less than 1 (0.010), log Q is negative (-2). Subtracting a negative means adding — the voltage goes UP from E°. questions.stem: Lipids are defined by their:

options.text: Solubility in nonpolar solvents and insolubility in water

rationales.whyCorrect: Lipids are defined operationally by solubility — they are hydrophobic biomolecules extractable with nonpolar solvents. Unlike carbohydrates, proteins, and nucleic acids (defined by structure), lipids are a functionally diverse group unified by hydrophobic character. Option A is false — lipids have diverse functional groups.
rationales.eli10: Lipids are like the oil in a salad dressing — they hate water and love grease. Unlike other biomolecules that share a common building plan (proteins are all amino acid chains), lipids are grouped only by their water-fearing personality. This is like categorizing things as "things that float" rather than "things made of wood" — a whale and a rubber duck share the category despite being completely different.
rationales.highYield: Lipids are defined by solubility, not by a common functional group. Includes fats, phospholipids, steroids, and waxes.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A reaction mechanism is best described as:

options.text: The overall balanced chemical equation showing reactants and products.
The experimental rate law determined by the method of initial rates.
A sequence of elementary steps that describes how reactant molecules actually become products.
An energy profile diagram showing activation barriers and enthalpy changes.

rationales.whyCorrect: A reaction mechanism is the step-by-step sequence of elementary reactions at the molecular level. The elementary steps must sum to the overall balanced equation. Option A describes the overall stoichiometric equation, not the mechanism. Option B describes the experimental rate law, which is a consequence of the mechanism. Option D describes the reaction coordinate diagram, which illustrates energetics but not the sequence of bond-breaking and bond-forming events.
rationales.eli10: A reaction mechanism is like a cooking recipe. The overall reaction is the finished dish on the menu, but the mechanism is every tiny step — chop the onions, then saute them, then add the tomatoes. Each step is an elementary reaction that must happen in order. You cannot jump straight from raw ingredients to the plated dish. If the recipe predicts a 30-minute cook time (rate law) but the dish actually takes 45 minutes, the recipe needs to be fixed.
rationales.highYield: The mechanism is a hypothesis for the molecular pathway; the rate law predicted by the mechanism must match the experimentally observed rate law.

subjectWideQuestions.sourceSnapshotMarkdown:
### Q01-01 Reaction mechanism definition

A reaction mechanism is best described as:

- **A.** The overall balanced chemical equation showing reactants and products.
- **B.** The experimental rate law determined by the method of initial rates.
- **C.** A sequence of elementary steps that describes how reactant molecules actually become products.
- **D.** An energy profile diagram showing activation barriers and enthalpy changes.

**Correct Answer:** **C.** A sequence of elementary steps that describes how reactant molecules actually become products.

**Why This Is Correct:** A reaction mechanism is the step-by-step sequence of elementary reactions at the molecular level. The elementary steps must sum to the overall balanced equation. Option A describes the overall stoichiometric equation, not the mechanism. Option B describes the experimental rate law, which is a consequence of the mechanism. Option D describes the reaction coordinate diagram, which illustrates energetics but not the sequence of bond-breaking and bond-forming events.

> **High-Yield:** The mechanism is a hypothesis for the molecular pathway; the rate law predicted by the mechanism must match the experimentally observed rate law.

**ELI-10:** A reaction mechanism is like a cooking recipe. The overall reaction is the finished dish on the menu, but the mechanism is every tiny step — chop the onions, then saute them, then add the tomatoes. Each step is an elementary reaction that must happen in order. You cannot jump straight from raw ingredients to the plated dish. If the recipe predicts a 30-minute cook time (rate law) but the dish actually takes 45 minutes, the recipe needs to be fixed.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An elementary step written as A → B + C is classified as:

rationales.whyCorrect: Molecularity counts the number of reactant molecules in an elementary step, not the products. A single reactant molecule A undergoing decomposition to B + C is unimolecular — one molecule acts alone. Option B (bimolecular) would require two reactant molecules colliding, such as A + B → products. Option C (termolecular) requires three simultaneous reactants, which is extremely rare. Option D confuses reaction order with molecularity; zeroth-order is a kinetic order, not a molecularity.
rationales.eli10: Molecularity is like counting how many people start a race. A unimolecular step is a solo sprint — one runner decides to go. A bimolecular step is a relay handoff — two runners must meet and exchange the baton. A termolecular step would be three runners all grabbing the same baton at the exact same instant — possible in theory, but so unlikely that it almost never happens in practice. The number of products does not matter; only the starting runners count.
rationales.highYield: Molecularity counts only reactant molecules in an elementary step: unimolecular (1), bimolecular (2), termolecular (3, rare). For an elementary step, order = molecularity.

An elementary step written as A → B + C is classified as:

- **A.** Unimolecular
- **B.** Bimolecular
- **C.** Termolecular
- **D.** Zeroth-order

**Correct Answer:** **A.** Unimolecular

**Why This Is Correct:** Molecularity counts the number of reactant molecules in an elementary step, not the products. A single reactant molecule A undergoing decomposition to B + C is unimolecular — one molecule acts alone. Option B (bimolecular) would require two reactant molecules colliding, such as A + B → products. Option C (termolecular) requires three simultaneous reactants, which is extremely rare. Option D confuses reaction order with molecularity; zeroth-order is a kinetic order, not a molecularity.

> **High-Yield:** Molecularity counts only reactant molecules in an elementary step: unimolecular (1), bimolecular (2), termolecular (3, rare). For an elementary step, order = molecularity.

**ELI-10:** Molecularity is like counting how many people start a race. A unimolecular step is a solo sprint — one runner decides to go. A bimolecular step is a relay handoff — two runners must meet and exchange the baton. A termolecular step would be three runners all grabbing the same baton at the exact same instant — possible in theory, but so unlikely that it almost never happens in practice. The number of products does not matter; only the starting runners count.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A reaction mechanism has three elementary steps. Step 1 has an activation energy of 15 kJ/mol, step 2 has an activation energy of 85 kJ/mol, and step 3 has an activation energy of 5 kJ/mol. Which step is the rate determining step?

options.text: Step 1, because it is the first step in the sequence.
Step 2, because it has the highest activation energy barrier.
Step 3, because it has the lowest activation energy barrier.
All three steps contribute equally to the overall rate.

rationales.whyCorrect: The rate determining step (RDS) is the step with the largest activation energy — the highest energetic hurdle. Molecules cross this barrier most slowly, creating a bottleneck. Steps 1 and 3 are much faster and do not limit the overall rate, regardless of their position in the mechanism. Option A is wrong because the first step is not automatically the RDS. Option C reverses the logic (the fastest step does not limit the rate). Option D ignores that one step is dramatically slower than the others.
rationales.eli10: Picture three hurdles on a running track. The first hurdle is knee-high (15 kJ/mol — easy), the second is shoulder-high (85 kJ/mol — hard), and the third is ankle-high (5 kJ/mol — trivial). Every runner stumbles at the tall second hurdle, so that hurdle sets the pace for the whole race. It does not matter that it is in the middle or that the last hurdle is easy. The tallest hurdle controls how fast everyone finishes.
rationales.highYield: The rate determining step is the elementary step with the highest activation energy, not necessarily the first step. It controls the overall reaction rate like a traffic bottleneck.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
Consider the mechanism for iodide-catalyzed decomposition of hydrogen peroxide:

```
H2O2(aq) + I^-(aq) → H2O(l) + IO^-(aq)   (slow)
H2O2(aq) + IO^-(aq) → H2O(l) + O2(g) + I^-(aq)   (fast)
```

Which species is the catalyst?

rationales.whyCorrect: I^- is consumed in the slow step and regenerated in the fast step, so it appears as a reactant early and as a product later — it is not consumed overall. This is the defining behavior of a catalyst. IO^- is an intermediate: produced in step 1, consumed in step 2, and absent from the overall reaction (2 H2O2 → 2 H2O + O2). H2O2 is a reactant. H2O is a product.
rationales.eli10: I^- is like a reusable shopping bag. You pick it up at the store entrance (reactant in step 1), fill it with groceries, then empty it at your car and bring it back for the next trip (regenerated in step 2). The bag is not consumed — you end with it. IO^- is like the receipt that gets printed during checkout and tossed before you leave — it exists briefly during the process but is gone at the end. Neither the bag nor the receipt appears on your final grocery list (the overall equation).
rationales.highYield: Catalyst: consumed in an early step, regenerated in a later step, net unchanged. Intermediate: produced in one step and consumed in a later step, never present at start or finish.

### Q01-04 Intermediate and catalyst identification

Consider the mechanism for iodide-catalyzed decomposition of hydrogen peroxide:

```
H2O2(aq) + I^-(aq) → H2O(l) + IO^-(aq)   (slow)
H2O2(aq) + IO^-(aq) → H2O(l) + O2(g) + I^-(aq)   (fast)
```

Which species is the catalyst?

- **A.** H2O2
- **B.** H2O
- **C.** IO^-
- **D.** I^-

**Correct Answer:** **D.** I^-

**Why This Is Correct:** I^- is consumed in the slow step and regenerated in the fast step, so it appears as a reactant early and as a product later — it is not consumed overall. This is the defining behavior of a catalyst. IO^- is an intermediate: produced in step 1, consumed in step 2, and absent from the overall reaction (2 H2O2 → 2 H2O + O2). H2O2 is a reactant. H2O is a product.

> **High-Yield:** Catalyst: consumed in an early step, regenerated in a later step, net unchanged. Intermediate: produced in one step and consumed in a later step, never present at start or finish.

**ELI-10:** I^- is like a reusable shopping bag. You pick it up at the store entrance (reactant in step 1), fill it with groceries, then empty it at your car and bring it back for the next trip (regenerated in step 2). The bag is not consumed — you end with it. IO^- is like the receipt that gets printed during checkout and tossed before you leave — it exists briefly during the process but is gone at the end. Neither the bag nor the receipt appears on your final grocery list (the overall equation).

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
The mechanism for 2 NO(g) + 2 H2(g) → N2(g) + 2 H2O(g) is:

```
Step 1: 2 NO(g) + H2(g) → N2O(g) + H2O(g)   k1 = 2.5 × 10^-3 M^-2 s^-1 (slow)
Step 2: N2O(g) + H2(g) → N2(g) + H2O(g)     (fast)
```

Calculate the initial rate when [NO] = 0.15 M and [H2] = 0.20 M.

rationales.whyCorrect: The slow step is rate determining, so the rate law matches the rate law of step 1: Rate = k1[NO]^2[H2]. Substituting: Rate = (2.5 × 10^-3 M^-2 s^-1)(0.15 M)^2(0.20 M) = (2.5 × 10^-3)(0.0225)(0.20) = (2.5 × 10^-3)(4.5 × 10^-3) = 1.125 × 10^-5 M/s. With 2 significant figures: 1.1 × 10^-5 M/s. Option A uses first order in NO (forgot to square): k1[NO][H2] = 7.5 × 10^-5 M/s. Option B omits [H2] entirely: k1[NO]^2 = 5.6 × 10^-5 M/s. Option D reports the rate constant k1 itself as the rate, ignoring all concentration terms.
rationales.eli10: The slow step is like the one slow cashier at a grocery store. No matter how fast the bagger works, the line moves at the cashier's speed. ### Q01-05 Rate from a mechanism with a slow first step

The mechanism for 2 NO(g) + 2 H2(g) → N2(g) + 2 H2O(g) is:

```
Step 1: 2 NO(g) + H2(g) → N2O(g) + H2O(g)   k1 = 2.5 × 10^-3 M^-2 s^-1 (slow)
Step 2: N2O(g) + H2(g) → N2(g) + H2O(g)     (fast)
```

Calculate the initial rate when [NO] = 0.15 M and [H2] = 0.20 M.

- **A.** 7.5 × 10^-5 M/s
- **B.** 5.6 × 10^-5 M/s
- **C.** 1.1 × 10^-5 M/s
- **D.** 2.5 × 10^-3 M/s

Substituting: Rate = (2.5 × 10^-3 M^-2 s^-1)(0.15 M)^2(0.20 M) = (2.5 × 10^-3)(0.0225)(0.20) = (2.5 × 10^-3)(4.5 × 10^-3) = 1.125 × 10^-5 M/s. With 2 significant figures: 1.1 × 10^-5 M/s. Option A uses first order in NO (forgot to square): k1[NO][H2] = 7.5 × 10^-5 M/s. Option B omits [H2] entirely: k1[NO]^2 = 5.6 × 10^-5 M/s. Option D reports the rate constant k1 itself as the rate, ignoring all concentration terms.

The rate law comes from counting how the cashier processes customers — in this case, the cashier needs two NO molecules and one H2 molecule. subjectWideQuestions.stem: For the mechanism A ⇌ B (k1 = 4.0 s^-1, k-1 = 2.0 s^-1) followed by B → C (k2 = 6.0 s^-1), apply the steady-state approximation to B. If [A] = 0.20 M, what is [B] at steady state?

rationales.whyCorrect: Steady state on B means d[B]/dt = k1[A] - k-1[B] - k2[B] = 0. Rearranging: k1[A] = (k-1 + k2)[B], so [B]ss = k1[A] / (k-1 + k2) = (4.0 s^-1)(0.20 M) / (2.0 s^-1 + 6.0 s^-1) = 0.80 M/s / 8.0 s^-1 = 0.10 M. Option B forgets k2 in the denominator: k1[A]/k-1 = 0.40 M. Option C inverts the ratio: (k-1 + k2)/(k1[A]) ≈ 40 M^-1 (units wrong). Option D omits the division step and reports just k1[A] = 0.80 M.
rationales.eli10: The steady-state approximation is like a busy coffee shop during the morning rush. Customers (A) enter, wait in line (B), then get their coffee and leave (C). Even though specific people come and go, the number of people in line stays roughly constant. You can find that number by setting the arrival rate equal to the departure rate. Here, 0.80 M/s of B are made from A, and B leaves through two exits at a combined rate of 8.0 per second, leaving a steady crowd of 0.10 M.
rationales.highYield: Steady-state approximation: d[intermediate]/dt = 0, so rate of formation = rate of consumption. Solve for the intermediate concentration algebraically.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An enzyme-catalyzed reaction follows Michaelis-Menten kinetics with Vmax = 8.0 × 10^-5 M/s and Km = 4.0 × 10^-3 M. Calculate the initial rate v0 when [S] = 2.0 × 10^-3 M.

rationales.whyCorrect: The Michaelis-Menten equation: v0 = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]). Substituting: v0 = (8.0 × 10^-5 M/s)(2.0 × 10^-3 M) / (4.0 × 10^-3 M + 2.0 × 10^-3 M) = (1.60 × 10^-7 M^2/s^2) / (6.0 × 10^-3 M) = 2.667 × 10^-5 M/s ≈ 2.7 × 10^-5 M/s (2 sig figs). The substrate concentration is less than Km, so v0 < Vmax/2. Option A is Vmax/2 (would be correct only if [S] = Km). Option B is Vmax itself — the saturated rate. Option C results from multiplying Vmax × [S] without dividing by the denominator.
rationales.eli10: The enzyme is like a ticket booth at a movie theater. Vmax (8.0 × 10^-5 M/s) is how fast tickets sell when the line is so long the booth never pauses. Km (4.0 × 10^-3 M) is the crowd size at which the booth runs at exactly half speed. Here, the crowd (2.0 × 10^-3 M) is smaller than Km, so the booth is not at full tilt — it runs at about one-third of max speed. When [S] is well below Km, doubling the crowd roughly doubles the speed.
rationales.highYield: Michaelis-Menten: v0 = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]). When [S] = Km, v0 = Vmax/2. When [S] << Km, v0 ≈ (Vmax/Km)[S] (first order). When [S] >> Km, v0 ≈ Vmax (zero order).

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes homogeneous from heterogeneous catalysis?

options.text: Homogeneous catalysts are always solids; heterogeneous catalysts are always gases.
A homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants; a heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase.
Homogeneous catalysts cannot be recovered after the reaction; heterogeneous catalysts are always consumed.
Heterogeneous catalysts lower the activation energy more than homogeneous catalysts in every reaction.

rationales.whyCorrect: The defining distinction is phase: homogeneous catalysts share a phase with reactants (e.g., an aqueous acid catalyzing an aqueous reaction), while heterogeneous catalysts occupy a different phase (e.g., a solid platinum surface with gaseous reactants). Option A reverses the typical physical states. Option C is wrong — both catalyst types can be recovered, and heterogeneous catalysts are not consumed. Option D is false — the degree of rate enhancement depends on the specific reaction, not the catalyst type.
rationales.eli10: Homogeneous catalysis is like a swimming instructor who jumps into the pool with you — same phase, working alongside. Heterogeneous catalysis is like a climbing wall — the wall is solid, you are not, and you grab holds (active sites) to make your move. Both help you complete the climb faster by giving you an easier route, but the wall stays put for the next climber while the instructor needs to get out and dry off. Catalytic converters use solid platinum that gas molecules briefly stick to, react on, and leave.
rationales.highYield: Homogeneous = same phase; heterogeneous = different phase (usually solid catalyst with liquid or gas reactants). Heterogeneous catalysts are easier to separate and reuse.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A reaction has an uncatalyzed activation energy of 80 kJ/mol. A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with an activation energy of 30 kJ/mol. Assuming the pre-exponential factor A is unchanged, by what factor does the catalyst increase the rate at 298 K? Use R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).

rationales.whyCorrect: The Arrhenius equation: k = A exp(-Ea/RT). The ratio is k_cat / k_uncat = exp[-(Ea_cat - Ea_uncat)/RT] = exp[(80 - 30) × 10^3 J/mol / (8.314 J/(mol·K) × 298 K)] = exp(50 × 10^3 / 2477.6) = exp(20.18) = 5.8 × 10^8. The 50 kJ/mol reduction in Ea produces a rate enhancement of nearly six hundred million. Option A results from a unit mismatch — using kJ with R in J gives exp(0.020) ≈ 1. Option D substitutes only Ea_cat (30 kJ/mol) instead of the difference ΔEa.
rationales.eli10: A catalyst is like carving a tunnel through a mountain instead of climbing over the peak. The uncatalyzed route climbs to 80 kJ/mol — a steep haul. The catalyzed tunnel goes through at only 30 kJ/mol — much easier. The fraction of molecules with enough energy to make it follows an exponential rule, so shaving off 50 kJ/mol at room temperature lets about 600 million times more molecules through per second. This is why a pinch of enzyme can process an enormous amount of substrate.
rationales.highYield: k_cat/k_uncat = exp(ΔEa/RT). A 50 kJ/mol drop in Ea at 298 K gives ~10^9 rate enhancement. Always convert Ea to J when R is in J/(mol·K).

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In Michaelis-Menten kinetics, which statement about Km is correct?

options.text: A smaller Km indicates tighter binding between the enzyme and its substrate.
Km equals the substrate concentration at which the enzyme operates at Vmax.
Km is the turnover number of the enzyme, measured in s^-1.
Km is independent of the specific enzyme-substrate pair and is constant for all enzymes.

rationales.whyCorrect: Km is the substrate concentration at which v0 = Vmax/2. A low Km means the enzyme reaches half its maximum rate at very low substrate concentrations, reflecting high affinity (tight binding) between enzyme and substrate. Option B is wrong — Km corresponds to Vmax/2, not Vmax. Option C confuses Km with kcat (the turnover number). Option D is false: Km values vary enormously between different enzyme-substrate pairs.
rationales.eli10: Km is like how picky a friend is about food. A friend with low Km loves a specific food so much they are satisfied with just a tiny taste — the enzyme grabs its substrate tightly even when there is barely any around. A friend with high Km needs a huge plateful before they are halfway happy — the enzyme binds loosely and needs lots of substrate. Km measures the concentration that half-satisfies the enzyme, and a smaller number means stronger attraction between the enzyme and its target.
rationales.highYield: Km = [S] at half Vmax. Low Km = high substrate affinity. Km is an intrinsic property of each enzyme-substrate pair, not a universal constant.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A catalyst increases the rate of a chemical reaction by:

options.text: Increasing the equilibrium constant so more products form.
Increasing the kinetic energy of the reactant molecules.
Increasing the concentration of reactants at the transition state.
Providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.

rationales.whyCorrect: A catalyst works by offering a different mechanism with a lower activation energy barrier, increasing the fraction of molecules that can surmount the barrier. It does not change the equilibrium constant (option A) — a catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally. It does not raise the temperature or kinetic energy (option B). It does not change reactant concentrations (option C). A catalyst is not consumed and leaves the thermodynamics unchanged.
rationales.eli10: A catalyst is not a cheerleader that makes molecules more energetic, and it is not a magician that changes the final outcome. It is more like a mountain guide who knows a secret pass through a lower part of the ridge. The starting point and destination are the same, and the guide takes no shortcuts on the map — both the hike out and the hike back use the same easier pass. The guide (catalyst) emerges from the hike unchanged, ready to lead the next group.
rationales.highYield: Catalysts lower Ea by providing an alternative pathway. They do not change ΔH, ΔG, or K_eq. They accelerate both forward and reverse reactions equally.

The mechanism for 2 A + B → D is:

```
Step 1: A + B ⇌ C      K = 4.0 × 10^2 M^-1  (fast equilibrium)
Step 2: C → D          k2 = 0.50 s^-1        (slow)
```

Calculate the initial rate when [A] = 0.050 M and [B] = 0.030 M.

rationales.whyCorrect: Step 2 is rate determining: Rate = k2[C]. From the fast pre-equilibrium in step 1: K = [C] / ([A][B]), so [C] = K[A][B]. Substituting: Rate = k2 K [A][B] = (0.50 s^-1)(4.0 × 10^2 M^-1)(0.050 M)(0.030 M) = (2.0 × 10^2 M^-1 s^-1)(1.5 × 10^-3 M^2) = 0.30 M/s. Option A inadvertently doubles one concentration. Option C omits K and uses only k2[A][B] = 7.5 × 10^-4 M/s. Option D reports k2K without multiplying by [A][B].
rationales.eli10: This mechanism is like a two-stage entry to a concert. First, people pair up (A + B ⇌ C) in a fast, reversible meetup outside — lots of pairs form and break apart quickly. Then, pairs enter through a slow ticket-check door (C → D). The overall rate depends on how many pairs exist outside (K[A][B]) times how fast the door processes them (k2). The fast step outside sets up the crowd, and the slow door controls the entry speed. Multiply the crowd size by the door speed to get the total entry rate.
rationales.highYield: When a fast equilibrium precedes the RDS, substitute the equilibrium expression into the RDS rate law to eliminate the intermediate: Rate = k_RDS × K_eq × [reactants].


- **A.** 0.60 M/s
- **B.** 0.30 M/s

- **D.** 2.0 × 10^2 M/s

Substituting: Rate = k2 K [A][B] = (0.50 s^-1)(4.0 × 10^2 M^-1)(0.050 M)(0.030 M) = (2.0 × 10^2 M^-1 s^-1)(1.5 × 10^-3 M^2) = 0.30 M/s. Option A inadvertently doubles one concentration. Option C omits K and uses only k2[A][B] = 7.5 × 10^-4 M/s. Option D reports k2K without multiplying by [A][B].

Then, pairs enter through a slow ticket-check door (C → D). The overall rate depends on how many pairs exist outside (K[A][B]) times how fast the door processes them (k2). > **Common Mistake:** Students often write the rate law from the overall balanced equation (rate = k[A]^2[B]) instead of deriving it from the mechanism. subjectWideQuestions.stem:
For a triprotic acid H3A, which relationship between successive Ka values is
correct?

options.text: Ka1 = Ka2 = Ka3 because all three protons are equivalent
Ka1 >> Ka2 >> Ka3 because each successive proton is harder to remove
Ka1 << Ka2 << Ka3 because removing protons makes the anion more reactive
Ka1 > Ka2 but Ka2 < Ka3 because the dianion is unstable

rationales.whyCorrect: Removing H+ from a neutral molecule (H3A) is easiest because the resulting anion (H2A^-) has a -1 charge that stabilizes the remaining O-H bonds. Removing H+ from H2A^- is harder because the proton must overcome attraction to a -1 anion. Removing H+ from HA^2- is hardest because the proton must escape a -2 anion. Typically Ka1 / Ka2 ≈ 10^4 to 10^6. Option A ignores electrostatic effects. Option C reverses the trend. Option D invents a nonexistent pattern.
rationales.eli10: Picture peeling stickers off a surface. The first sticker comes off easily because nothing is holding it back. The second sticker is harder because the surface is now sticky with residue. The third is even tougher. Protons on a polyprotic acid work the same way — each one removed makes the molecule more negatively charged, which holds the remaining protons tighter. That is why Ka1 is biggest and Ka3 is smallest.
rationales.highYield: For any polyprotic acid, Ka1 >> Ka2 >> Ka3. The first proton is always easiest to lose; successive Ka values drop by factors of 10^3 to 10^6.

The third is even tougher. Protons on a polyprotic acid work the same way — each one removed makes the molecule more negatively charged, which holds the remaining protons tighter. That is why Ka1 is biggest and Ka3 is smallest.

Calculate the pH of 0.10 M H2CO3 at 25 °C.
Ka1 = 4.3 × 10^-7, Ka2 = 5.6 × 10^-11.

rationales.whyCorrect: For a polyprotic acid with Ka1 >> Ka2, the first dissociation dominates the [H+]. subjectWideQuestions.stem:
AgCl has Ksp = 1.8 × 10^-10. Ag2CrO4 has Ksp = 1.1 × 10^-12.
Which salt has the higher molar solubility in pure water?

options.text: AgCl, because its Ksp is larger
The molar solubilities are equal because both contain Ag+
Cannot be determined without temperature data
Ag2CrO4, because its 1:2 stoichiometry produces more ions per formula unit

rationales.whyCorrect: AgCl (1:1): s = sqrt(1.8 × 10^-10) = 1.3 × 10^-5 M. Ag2CrO4 (2:1): Ksp = [Ag+]^2 [CrO4^2-] = (2s)^2 (s) = 4s^3. s = (Ksp/4)^(1/3) = (1.1 × 10^-12 / 4)^(1/3) = (2.75 × 10^-13)^(1/3) = 6.5 × 10^-5 M. Ag2CrO4 is about 5× more soluble despite a Ksp that is ~100× smaller. Ksp values cannot be directly compared when stoichiometries differ. Option A makes this common error. Option B is factually wrong. Option C is wrong — Ksp at 25 °C is sufficient.
rationales.eli10: Comparing Ksp values directly is like comparing salaries without knowing the currency. AgCl's Ksp looks bigger (10^-10 vs 10^-12), but Ag2CrO4 releases three ions per formula unit instead of two. That cubed relationship in the math gives Ag2CrO4 a higher molar solubility. Always convert Ksp to actual molar solubility before deciding which salt dissolves more.
rationales.highYield: Never compare Ksp values directly when stoichiometries differ. Always calculate molar solubility s from Ksp, then compare.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
Calculate the molar solubility of Zn(OH)2 in a buffer at pH 7.00 at 25 °C.
Ksp(Zn(OH)2) = 3.0 × 10^-16.

rationales.whyCorrect: Zn(OH)2(s) ⇌ Zn2+(aq) + 2OH^-(aq). At pH 7.00: pOH = 14.00 - 7.00 = 7.00, [OH^-] = 1.0 × 10^-7 M. The buffer fixes [OH^-]. Ksp = [Zn2+][OH^-]^2. [Zn2+] = s = Ksp / [OH^-]^2 = 3.0 × 10^-16 / (1.0 × 10^-7)^2 = 3.0 × 10^-16 / 1.0 × 10^-14 = 0.030 M. Option B (4.2 × 10^-6) is the solubility in pure water, where [OH^-] comes only from dissolution. Option C (3.0 × 10^-9) forgets to square [OH^-]. Option D reports Ksp as the answer.
rationales.eli10: Zn(OH)2 dissolving is like trying to pour water into a cup that already has water in it — the more that dissolves, the harder it gets to dissolve more because the OH^- it produces crowds out further dissolution. In pure water, Zn(OH)2 must supply its own OH^-, and once a tiny amount dissolves (4.2 × 10^-6 M), the [OH^-] rises enough to shut things down. But in a buffer at pH 7, the [OH^-] is locked at a fixed low level of 10^-7 M by the buffer — the salt can keep dissolving without raising [OH^-], so solubility jumps to 0.030 M. At even lower pH, H+ gobbles up OH^-, and even more solid dissolves.
rationales.highYield: Lowering pH (making solution more acidic) increases solubility of hydroxide and basic salts by consuming OH^-. The pH controls [OH^-], which is then substituted into Ksp to find s.
