AgNO3 (0.010 mol) is dissolved in 1.00 L of 1.0 M NH3. Ag+ reacts:
Ag+ + 2NH3 ⇌ [Ag(NH3)2]+, Kf = 1.7 × 10^7.
Calculate [Ag+] at equilibrium.

rationales.whyCorrect: Kf is large and NH3 is in excess, so nearly all Ag+ is complexed. [Ag(NH3)2+] ≈ 0.010 M. NH3 remaining = 1.0 - 2(0.010) = 0.98 M. Kf = [Ag(NH3)2+] / ([Ag+][NH3]^2). [Ag+] = [Ag(NH3)2+] / (Kf × [NH3]^2) = 0.010 / (1.7 × 10^7 × (0.98)^2) = 0.010 / (1.7 × 10^7 × 0.960) = 0.010 / (1.63 × 10^7) = 6.1 × 10^-10 M. Option A assumes no complexation. Option B reports Kd = 1/Kf. Option C uses initial [NH3] = 1.0 M and forgets the squared term.
rationales.eli10: NH3 molecules grab Ag+ ions like magnetic hands. With a million-fold excess of NH3 and a very strong grip (Kf = 17 million), nearly every Ag+ gets snatched. Only about 6 out of every 10 billion Ag+ ions remain free-floating. Think of it as a giant claw machine — with so many claws and such a strong grip, almost no prizes are left ungrabbed.
rationales.highYield: With large Kf and excess ligand, find free metal by [M] = [ML_n] / (Kf × [L]^n) after subtracting complexed ligand from initial.

A solution contains 0.010 M Cl^- and 0.010 M I^-. Solid AgNO3 is added slowly.
Ksp(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10^-10, Ksp(AgI) = 8.5 × 10^-17.
Which precipitates first?

options.text: AgCl, because Cl^- is a smaller anion
AgI, because it requires a lower [Ag+] to begin precipitating
AgCl, because its Ksp is larger

rationales.whyCorrect: Precipitation begins when Q = Ksp. For AgCl: [Ag+] = 1.8 × 10^-10 / 0.010 = 1.8 × 10^-8 M. For AgI: [Ag+] = 8.5 × 10^-17 / 0.010 = 8.5 × 10^-15 M. AgI needs ~2000× less Ag+ to start precipitating, so AgI appears first as AgNO3 is added. Option A is irrelevant — ion size does not determine precipitation order. Option C ignores the different Ksp values. Option D has the logic backward — larger Ksp means more soluble, so AgCl precipitates later.
rationales.eli10: Imagine two buckets — one with a tiny pinhole (AgI, very low Ksp) and one with a bigger hole (AgCl). As you pour in Ag+ like water, the pinhole bucket overflows first because it fills up with far less water. AgI needs only 8.5 × 10^-15 M Ag+ to start forming solid, while AgCl needs 1.8 × 10^-8 M. Iodide grabs silver ions and crashes out of solution long before chloride even notices the silver is there.
rationales.highYield: The salt with the smallest [Ag+] threshold (Ksp / [anion]) precipitates first. For equal anion concentrations, the salt with the smaller Ksp precipitates first.

0.010 mol CuSO4 is dissolved in 1.00 L of 0.50 M NH3.
Cu2+ + 4NH3 ⇌ [Cu(NH3)4]2+, Kf = 5.0 × 10^13.
Calculate [Cu2+] at equilibrium.

rationales.whyCorrect: Kf is enormous and NH3 is in excess. Nearly all Cu2+ complexes: [Cu(NH3)4^2+] ≈ 0.010 M. NH3 consumed = 4 × 0.010 = 0.040 mol, so [NH3] remaining = 0.50 - 0.040 = 0.46 M. Kf = [Cu(NH3)4^2+] / ([Cu2+][NH3]^4). [Cu2+] = 0.010 / (5.0 × 10^13 × (0.46)^4). 0.46^4 = 0.045. [Cu2+] = 0.010 / (5.0 × 10^13 × 0.045) = 0.010 / (2.2 × 10^12) = 4.5 × 10^-15 M. Option A reports Kd = 1/Kf. Option B ignores complexation. Option D is off by a factor of ~50.
rationales.eli10: Cu2+ is surrounded by four NH3 arms in a square grip. With Kf = 50 trillion and plenty of NH3, the grip is nearly unbreakable. Out of every 0.010 M of copper added, almost every ion gets grabbed. Only about 5 copper ions out of every quadrillion remain free. The NH3 leftover is 0.46 M — still plenty for the next batch. This is why deep blue [Cu(NH3)4]2+ forms instantly when you add ammonia to copper solution.
rationales.highYield: For complexes with large Kf and excess ligand, [M] = [ML_n] / (Kf × [L]^n). Remember to subtract the ligand consumed by complexation: n × [ML_n].

At what pH does Fe(OH)3 just begin to precipitate from a 0.010 M Fe3+ solution?
Ksp(Fe(OH)3) = 4 × 10^-38.

rationales.whyCorrect: Fe(OH)3(s) ⇌ Fe3+(aq) + 3OH^-(aq). Ksp = [Fe3+][OH^-]^3. Precipitation begins when [OH^-]^3 = Ksp / [Fe3+] = 4 × 10^-38 / 0.010 = 4 × 10^-36. [OH^-] = (4 × 10^-36)^(1/3) = 1.59 × 10^-12 M. pOH = -log(1.59 × 10^-12) = 11.80. pH = 14.00 - 11.80 = 2.20. Option A multiplies instead of dividing by [Fe3+]. Option B uses [OH^-] = Ksp^(1/3), forgetting [Fe3+]. Option C reports pOH (11.80) instead of pH — a common error of forgetting to convert.
rationales.eli10: Fe(OH)3 is so insoluble that it crashes out even in very acidic solution. With only 0.010 M Fe3+ present, rust starts forming at pH 2.20 — about as acidic as lemon juice. That is why iron-rich acidic mine drainage forms orange-red sludge the moment it hits a stream and the pH rises even slightly. The Ksp is mind-bogglingly small (4 × 10^-38), so almost any OH^- triggers precipitation.
rationales.highYield: For hydroxide salts, precipitation pH = 14 - (-log((Ksp/[M^n+])^(1/n))). Lower Ksp or higher [M^n+] shifts precipitation to lower pH.

At what pH does Fe(OH)3 just begin to precipitate from a 0.010 M Fe3+ solution?
Ksp(Fe(OH)3) = 4 × 10^-38.

- **A.** 0.87
- **B.** 1.53
- **C.** 11.80
- **D.** 2.20

**Correct Answer:** **D.** 2.20

**Why This Is Correct:** Fe(OH)3(s) ⇌ Fe3+(aq) + 3OH^-(aq). Ksp = [Fe3+][OH^-]^3. Precipitation begins when [OH^-]^3 = Ksp / [Fe3+] = 4 × 10^-38 / 0.010 = 4 × 10^-36. [OH^-] = (4 × 10^-36)^(1/3) = 1.59 × 10^-12 M. pOH = -log(1.59 × 10^-12) = 11.80. pH = 14.00 - 11.80 = 2.20. Option A multiplies instead of dividing by [Fe3+]. Option B uses [OH^-] = Ksp^(1/3), forgetting [Fe3+]. Option C reports pOH (11.80) instead of pH — a common error of forgetting to convert.

> **High-Yield:** For hydroxide salts, precipitation pH = 14 - (-log((Ksp/[M^n+])^(1/n))). Lower Ksp or higher [M^n+] shifts precipitation to lower pH.

**ELI-10:** Fe(OH)3 is so insoluble that it crashes out even in very acidic solution. With only 0.010 M Fe3+ present, rust starts forming at pH 2.20 — about as acidic as lemon juice. That is why iron-rich acidic mine drainage forms orange-red sludge the moment it hits a stream and the pH rises even slightly. The Ksp is mind-bogglingly small (4 × 10^-38), so almost any OH^- triggers precipitation.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which of the following aqueous mixtures produces a **buffer** solution?

rationales.whyCorrect: A buffer requires a weak acid and its conjugate base in significant concentrations. Option D contains H2PO4^- (weak acid) and HPO4^2- (its conjugate base) — the classic phosphate buffer system. Option A has a strong acid (HCl), which cannot form a buffer. Option B contains two salts with no weak acid/conjugate-base pair. Option C is a weak acid plus exactly one equivalent of strong base, resulting in complete neutralization to NaCH3COO with no weak acid remaining.
rationales.eli10: A buffer is like a chemical sponge — it soaks up added acid or base to keep pH steady. To be a sponge, you need both the weak acid (the sponge material) and its conjugate base (water already in the sponge). Option D has H2PO4^- and HPO4^2- — the acid and base forms of phosphate — so it works. Option A is like trying to soak up water with a rock (strong acid HCl); it cannot do the job.
rationales.highYield: A buffer is a mixture of a weak acid and its conjugate base (or weak base and conjugate acid) in appreciable concentrations. Strong acids or bases dilute but do not buffer.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the pH of a buffer solution containing 0.35 M CH3COOH and 0.25 M NaCH3COO? (pKa of CH3COOH = 4.74)

rationales.whyCorrect: The **Henderson-Hasselbalch equation** is pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]). Here [A-] = [CH3COO-] = 0.25 M and [HA] = [CH3COOH] = 0.35 M. pH = 4.74 + log(0.25/0.35) = 4.74 + log(0.714) = 4.74 + (-0.146) = 4.59. Option B assumes equal concentrations (pH = pKa). Option C adds instead of subtracting log term. Option D uses inverted ratio [HA]/[A-].
rationales.eli10: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation is like a see-saw centered at the pKa. When there is more acid form (0.35 M) than base form (0.25 M), the pH tips below the pKa — giving 4.59 instead of 4.74. If the two concentrations were equal, the see-saw would balance exactly at pKa. The log term tells you how far off-center you are.
rationales.highYield: pH = pKa + log([conjugate base]/[acid]). When [A-] < [HA], the log term is negative and pH < pKa.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which of the following does **NOT** increase the **buffer capacity** of a buffer solution?

options.text: Increasing the total concentration of both buffer components
Increasing the total volume of the buffer solution while maintaining the same concentrations
Increasing the temperature of the buffer solution

rationales.whyCorrect: Buffer capacity — the amount of strong acid or base a buffer can absorb with minimal pH change — depends on the total number of moles of buffer components present. Higher concentrations (A) and larger volumes (C) both increase total moles, increasing capacity. A ratio near 1 (B) maximizes capacity for a given total concentration. Temperature (D) alters the pKa slightly by shifting Ka but does not directly increase the number of buffer molecules available to neutralize added acid or base.
rationales.eli10: Buffer capacity is like how many buckets of acid or base your chemical sponge can soak up before it is overwhelmed. A bigger sponge (higher concentration) or more sponges (bigger volume) means more capacity. A balanced sponge (equal acid and base forms) is ready for either direction. Heating the sponge does not make it bigger — it just changes how tightly it holds the water, without adding capacity.
rationales.highYield: Buffer capacity is proportional to total buffer concentration. Maximum capacity occurs when [A-]/[HA] ≈ 1 (pH = pKa). Temperature shifts pKa but does not increase capacity.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A buffer solution has a measured pH of 4.30. The weak acid in the buffer has a pKa of 4.74. What is the ratio [A-]/[HA] in this buffer?

rationales.whyCorrect: Rearranging the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: log([A-]/[HA]) = pH - pKa = 4.30 - 4.74 = -0.44. Taking the antilog: [A-]/[HA] = 10^-0.44 = 0.36. Since pH < pKa, the ratio is less than 1 — the acid form predominates. Option B is the inverted ratio ([HA]/[A-] = 2.75). Option C mistakenly uses the raw log value (0.44) as the ratio. Option D assumes equal concentrations.
rationales.eli10: Think of pKa as the tipping point — a pH lower than pKa means the solution is more acidic than the acid's natural strength, so the acid form (HA) keeps its proton and outnumbers the base form 3-to-1. To find the exact ratio, subtract pKa from pH and use the "10-to-the-power-of" button on your calculator. The negative exponent (10^-0.44) gives a number smaller than 1, confirming the acid form dominates.
rationales.highYield: When pH < pKa, [A-]/[HA] < 1 (acid form dominates). When pH > pKa, [A-]/[HA] > 1 (base form dominates). When pH = pKa, [A-]/[HA] = 1.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How many grams of solid NaCH3COO (molar mass = 82.0 g/mol) must be added to 250.0 mL of 0.300 M CH3COOH to produce a buffer with pH equal to the pKa of CH3COOH? (pKa = 4.74, assume negligible volume change upon addition of the solid)

rationales.whyCorrect: When pH = pKa, the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation gives log([A-]/[HA]) = 0, so [A-] = [HA] = 0.300 M. Moles of NaCH3COO needed = 0.300 mol/L × 0.2500 L = 0.0750 mol. Mass = 0.0750 mol × 82.0 g/mol = 6.15 g. Option A doubles the mass (would give [A-] = 0.600 M). Option C halves the mass. Option D quadruples the mass by using a 1.00 L volume assumption.
rationales.eli10: Making a buffer at exactly the pKa is the easiest recipe — equal amounts of acid and base forms. Here you already have the acid (0.300 M CH3COOH in 250 mL), so you need the same number of moles of its conjugate base. That is 0.0750 moles of sodium acetate, which weighs 6.15 grams — about a teaspoon of a fine white powder. Dissolve it in the acid solution and the pH lands right on 4.74.
rationales.highYield: When preparing a buffer with pH = pKa, the conjugate base and acid concentrations must be equal. Calculate moles from concentration × volume, then convert to mass.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the pH at the **equivalence point** when 40.0 mL of 0.100 M CH3COOH is titrated with 0.100 M NaOH? (Ka of CH3COOH = 1.8 × 10^-5)

rationales.whyCorrect: At the equivalence point, all CH3COOH has been converted to CH3COO-. Moles CH3COOH = 0.100 M × 0.0400 L = 0.00400 mol. Volume of NaOH added = 0.00400 mol / 0.100 M = 0.0400 L. Total volume = 0.0800 L. [CH3COO-] = 0.00400 mol / 0.0800 L = 0.0500 M. The acetate ion hydrolyzes: CH3COO- + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + OH-. Kb = Kw/Ka = 1.0×10^-14 / 1.8×10^-5 = 5.56×10^-10. [OH-] = sqrt(Kb × [CH3COO-]) = sqrt(5.56×10^-10 × 0.0500) = sqrt(2.78×10^-11) = 5.27×10^-6 M. pOH = -log(5.27×10^-6) = 5.28. pH = 14.00 - 5.28 = 8.72. Option A would be correct for a strong acid–strong base titration. Option B is the pOH value. Option D uses incorrect arithmetic.
rationales.eli10: At the equivalence point, all the vinegar molecules (acetic acid) have been turned into acetate ions by the NaOH. Acetate is a weak base — it steals protons from water, leaving OH- behind, which makes the solution basic (pH 8.72). It is like turning every sour molecule into a slightly soapy one. That is why the equivalence pH is above 7 even though you started with an acid.
rationales.highYield: The equivalence point of a weak acid–strong base titration is basic (pH > 7) because the conjugate base hydrolyzes water to produce OH-. pH = 14 - pOH; [OH-] = sqrt(Kb × [conjugate base]).

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During the titration of a weak monoprotic acid with a strong base, which statement is true at the **half-equivalence point**?

options.text: pH = pKa of the weak acid
The moles of added base equal the initial moles of weak acid

rationales.whyCorrect: At the half-equivalence point, exactly half of the weak acid has been converted to its conjugate base, so [HA] = [A-]. The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation gives pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]) = pKa + log(1) = pKa. Option A is true only for a strong acid–strong base titration. Option C describes a neutral solution (pH = 7), not the half-equivalence point. Option D describes the full equivalence point, not the half-equivalence point.
rationales.eli10: The half-equivalence point is the halfway mark of the titration — like reaching the midpoint of a race. At this spot, exactly half the acid molecules have given up their protons, so the solution is a perfect 50-50 mix of HA and A-. When the two are equal, the Henderson-Hasselbalch log term becomes zero, and pH locks onto the pKa. This makes the half-equivalence point the easiest way to measure an unknown acid's pKa in the lab.
rationales.highYield: At the half-equivalence point of a weak acid titration: [HA] = [A-] and pH = pKa. This is the most buffered region of the titration curve.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A 1.00-L buffer solution contains 0.400 M NH3 and 0.300 M NH4Cl. What is the pH after adding 0.100 mol of NaOH? (pKa of NH4+ = 9.26, assume negligible volume change)

rationales.whyCorrect: NaOH reacts with the acid component (NH4+): NH4+ + OH- → NH3 + H2O. New [NH4+] = 0.300 - 0.100 = 0.200 M. New [NH3] = 0.400 + 0.100 = 0.500 M. Apply Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([base]/[acid]) = 9.26 + log(0.500/0.200) = 9.26 + log(2.50) = 9.26 + 0.398 = 9.66. Option A incorrectly subtracts the log term. Option B uses the initial buffer pH: 9.26 + log(0.400/0.300) = 9.38. Option C is the pKa itself, ignoring the concentration ratio.
rationales.eli10: Adding NaOH to an ammonia buffer is like throwing a base-seeking sponge into the mix — the OH- grabs protons from NH4+, converting it to NH3. So NH4+ drops from 0.300 M to 0.200 M and NH3 rises from 0.400 M to 0.500 M. With more base form than acid form, the pH climbs from its starting value up to 9.66. The buffer softens the blow, but the pH still shifts in the direction of the added substance.
rationales.highYield: When strong base is added to a buffer, it reacts with the acid component (HA or BH+). Recalculate [A-] and [HA], then reapply Henderson-Hasselbalch. Strong acid reacts with the base component.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which indicator is most appropriate for detecting the equivalence point when CH3COOH (pKa = 4.74) is titrated with NaOH?

rationales.whyCorrect: The equivalence point of a weak acid–strong base titration is basic (pH ≈ 8.72; see Q03-06). The ideal **indicator** has a pKa near the equivalence-point pH, with its color-change range straddling the steep portion of the titration curve. Phenolphthalein (8.2–10.0) covers the equivalence pH of 8.72. Methyl orange (B) is suitable for strong acid–strong base titrations. Bromothymol blue (C) changes too early for this titration. Thymol blue (D) is far too acidic.
rationales.eli10: Choosing an indicator is like picking a finish-line camera — you want it to flash exactly when the race ends (the equivalence point). Acetic acid titrated with NaOH finishes at pH 8.72, so phenolphthalein, which turns pink between pH 8.2 and 10.0, gives you a clean signal right on time. Methyl orange changes color way too early (pH 3–4), like declaring a marathon winner at mile 3.
rationales.highYield: Match the indicator's pKa to the equivalence-point pH. Weak acid + strong base → phenolphthalein. Strong acid + strong base → bromothymol blue or methyl orange. Weak base + strong acid → methyl orange or methyl red.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Phosphoric acid (H3PO4) is a triprotic acid with pKa1 = 2.12, pKa2 = 7.21, and pKa3 = 12.32. Which phosphorus-containing species predominates in an aqueous solution at pH = 4.50?

rationales.whyCorrect: For polyprotic acids, the dominant species in solution is determined by comparing the solution pH to the successive pKa values. At pH values between pKa1 (2.12) and pKa2 (7.21), the intermediate species H2PO4^- is the major form. At pH = 4.50, the solution is above pKa1 (most H3PO4 has lost its first proton) but below pKa2 (most H2PO4^- has not yet lost its second proton). Option A (H3PO4) dominates only below pH 2.12. Option C (HPO4^2-) dominates between pH 7.21 and 12.32. Option D (PO4^3-) dominates above pH 12.32.
rationales.eli10: Think of a polyprotic acid as a person wearing three hats. At very low pH (below 2.12), H3PO4 wears all three hats (three protons). As pH rises past the first pKa (2.12), one hat comes off — H2PO4^- dominates. At pH 4.50, which is above pKa1 but below pKa2, the molecule has lost exactly one hat. The second hat stays on until pH passes 7.21. By pH above 12.32, all three hats are gone and PO4^3- is bare.
rationales.highYield: In polyprotic systems: pH < pKa1 → fully protonated; between pKa1 and pKa2 → intermediate species; between pKa2 and pKa3 → next intermediate; pH > pKa3 → fully deprotonated.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A 0.100 M solution of the diprotic acid H2A (Ka1 = 1.0 × 10^-3, Ka2 = 1.0 × 10^-7) is titrated with NaOH. What is the approximate pH at the first equivalence point?

rationales.whyCorrect: At the first equivalence point, the predominant species is HA-, an amphoteric species that can act as both an acid and a base. For a diprotic acid where Ka1 and Ka2 are well separated (by at least a factor of 10^4), the pH at the first equivalence point is approximately the average of the two pKa values: pH ≈ (pKa1 + pKa2)/2 = (3.00 + 7.00)/2 = 5.00. This formula works because HA- undergoes both hydrolysis (as a base: HA- + H2O ⇌ H2A + OH-) and dissociation (as an acid: HA- + H2O ⇌ A^2- + H3O+) to comparable extents. Option A is pKa1 alone. Option C is neutral pH. Option D is pKa2 alone.
rationales.eli10: The first equivalence point of a diprotic acid is like reaching the bottom of a staircase landing — you have removed exactly one proton from every molecule, and the solution contains only HA-. This species is a chemical fence-sitter: it can donate its remaining proton (acting as an acid) or snatch a proton from water (acting as a base). The pH lands right in the middle of the two pKa values — at 5.00, halfway between 3.00 and 7.00.
rationales.highYield: For a diprotic acid with well-separated Ka values, pH at the first equivalence point ≈ (pKa1 + pKa2)/2. At the second equivalence point, treat A^2- as a monobasic weak base.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: 25.0 mL of 0.100 M CH3COOH is titrated with 0.100 M NaOH. What is the pH after 10.0 mL of NaOH has been added? (pKa of CH3COOH = 4.74)

rationales.whyCorrect: Before the equivalence point, the solution is a buffer. Moles CH3COOH initially = 0.100 M × 0.0250 L = 0.00250 mol. Moles NaOH added = 0.100 M × 0.0100 L = 0.00100 mol. The added OH- converts CH3COOH to CH3COO-: moles CH3COOH remaining = 0.00250 - 0.00100 = 0.00150 mol; moles CH3COO- formed = 0.00100 mol. Since both species are in the same total volume, the ratio [A-]/[HA] = 0.00100/0.00150 = 0.667. pH = pKa + log(0.667) = 4.74 + (-0.176) = 4.56. Option A would be correct if exactly 12.5 mL were added (half-equivalence). Option B uses the inverted ratio. Option C uses wrong arithmetic.
rationales.eli10: Adding NaOH to acetic acid is like slowly converting sour molecules (HA) to their salty cousins (A-). After adding 10.0 mL of NaOH — but before the full 25.0 mL needed to finish — you have created a buffer with 0.00100 moles of acetate and 0.00150 moles of remaining acetic acid. Because there is still more acid than base form (ratio 0.667), the pH (4.56) sits just below the pKa (4.74). The moles ratio is all you need; the volume is the same for both, so it cancels out.
rationales.highYield: During the buffer region of a weak acid–strong base titration (before equivalence), pH = pKa + log(moles base added / moles acid remaining). No need to compute concentrations — the volume cancels in the ratio.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A reaction has ΔH = -50 kJ and ΔS = -120 J/K at 298 K. Which statement is correct?

rationales.whyCorrect: ΔH < 0 (favorable), ΔS < 0 (unfavorable). ΔG = ΔH - TΔS. At low T, the -TΔS term is small, so ΔH dominates and ΔG < 0 (spontaneous). At high T, -TΔS becomes large positive, making ΔG > 0 (nonspontaneous). Crossover: T = ΔH/ΔS = -50000/(-120) = 417 K. Option A would require ΔS > 0. Option C would require ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0. Option D would require both unfavorable.
rationales.eli10: Gibbs free energy is like a financial decision with two factors: heat (ΔH) and disorder (ΔS). This reaction releases heat (good, -50 kJ) but creates order (bad, -120 J/K). At low temperatures, the heat benefit wins and the reaction is spontaneous — like saving money being more important than neatness. At high temperatures, the order penalty gets multiplied and outweighs the heat benefit — like a boss who penalizes neatness harshly in hot weather.
rationales.highYield: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS. Four sign combinations determine T dependence of spontaneity.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Calculate ΔG° for a reaction with K = 2.5 × 10^4 at 298 K. R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).

rationales.whyCorrect: ΔG° = -RT ln K = -(8.314 J/(mol·K))(298 K) ln(2.5×10^4) = -(2478)(10.13) = -25100 J = -25.1 kJ. K > 1, so ΔG° < 0 (products favored). Option B uses log instead of ln (ln 2.5×10^4 = 10.13; log = 4.40, giving ~-10.9 kJ). Option C and D have wrong signs.
rationales.eli10: The free energy-equilibrium connection is like a spring. A large K (2.5×10^4) means the reaction is strongly product-favored, which shows up as a negative ΔG° (-25.1 kJ) — the spring is compressed and ready to push toward products. Every 5.7 kJ of negative free energy at room temperature roughly corresponds to a tenfold preference for products.
rationales.highYield: ΔG° = -RT ln K. K > 1 → ΔG° < 0. Every ~5.7 kJ/mol at 298 K ≈ factor of 10 in K.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which process has the largest positive ΔS?

rationales.whyCorrect: Entropy increases most dramatically in vaporization (liquid → gas). Gas molecules have far more positional freedom and energy distribution than liquids. ΔS_vap for water is large and positive. Option A is freezing — entropy decreases. Option C decreases the number of gas molecules (3 → 0), decreasing entropy. Option D has ΔS ≈ 0.
rationales.eli10: Entropy is like the number of ways molecules can arrange themselves. A gas is like a room full of bouncing superballs — countless positions and speeds. A liquid is like a crowded dance floor — molecules can move but stay close. A solid is like soldiers standing at attention — nearly fixed positions. Going from liquid to gas is the biggest entropy jump, like releasing the superballs from a box into the room.
rationales.highYield: ΔS > 0: solid → liquid → gas; Δn_gas > 0; dissolving; heating. S°(gas) >> S°(liquid) > S°(solid).

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Calculate ΔG° for N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g) given: ΔH° = -92.2 kJ, ΔS° = -198.8 J/K at 298 K.

rationales.whyCorrect: ΔG° = ΔH° - TΔS° = -92200 J - (298 K)(-198.8 J/K) = -92200 + 59252 = -32948 J ≈ -33.0 kJ. Despite the unfavorable entropy (ΔS < 0), the favorable enthalpy dominates at 298 K. Option B ignores the entropy term. Option C adds the entropy term incorrectly. Option D flips the sign.

At room temperature, the entropy penalty costs about 59 kJ, reducing the net free energy to -33 kJ — still spontaneous but weaker than the enthalpy alone suggests. The TΔS term is like a temperature-dependent tax on orderliness.
rationales.highYield: ΔG° = ΔH° - TΔS°. Convert units: ΔH in J to match ΔS (J/K). TΔS term can be positive or negative.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A reaction has ΔG° = +25 kJ (nonspontaneous). It can be driven by coupling with ATP hydrolysis (ΔG° = -30.5 kJ). The coupled reaction is:

options.text: Nonspontaneous because the unfavorable reaction dominates
Nonspontaneous because coupling requires a common intermediate

rationales.whyCorrect: ΔG°_total = ΔG°_1 + ΔG°_2 = +25 + (-30.5) = -5.5 kJ. Since ΔG°_total < 0, the coupled reaction is spontaneous — provided the reactions share a common intermediate (e.g., phosphorylation by ATP). Option A ignores the favorable ATP contribution. Option C incorrectly adds magnitudes. Option D is partially correct that coupling requires an intermediate but wrong about spontaneity.
rationales.eli10: Coupled reactions are like a seesaw with a heavy kid and a light kid. The unfavorable reaction (+25 kJ) is the light kid trying to go up. ATP hydrolysis (-30.5 kJ) is the heavy kid pushing down hard. The net result (-5.5 kJ) tips the seesaw toward spontaneity. Your body uses this trick constantly — ATP's energetic push powers everything from muscle contraction to protein synthesis.
rationales.highYield: ΔG°_total = ΣΔG°_i. Unfavorable reactions can be driven by coupling with a more favorable reaction sharing an intermediate.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What does ΔG represent for a process at constant T and P?

options.text: The entropy change of the surroundings

rationales.whyCorrect: ΔG = maximum useful (non-expansion) work obtainable from a spontaneous process at constant T and P. For a galvanic cell: ΔG = -nFE (maximum electrical work). For a biological process: ΔG is the maximum work available for biosynthesis. Option A describes ΔH. Option B describes ΔU. Option D is -ΔH/T.
rationales.eli10: Gibbs free energy is the "useful work" bank account of a reaction. Heat (ΔH) is like total revenue, but entropy losses (TΔS) are like operating costs. ΔG is the net profit — the maximum useful work you can extract after paying the entropy tax. In a battery, this profit shows up as electrical work (voltage × charge). In your body, it is the energy available to build proteins and contract muscles.
rationales.highYield: ΔG = w_max (non-PV) at constant T and P. ΔG = -nFE_cell for electrochemical work.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How many grams of copper (M = 63.55 g/mol) are deposited when a current of 5.00 A passes through CuSO4(aq) for 30.0 minutes? Cu2+ + 2e^- → Cu(s)

rationales.whyCorrect: Charge = I × t = 5.00 A × (30.0 × 60) s = 9000 C. moles e^- = 9000 C / 96485 C/mol = 0.09328 mol. Cu2+ needs 2 e^-: moles Cu = 0.09328/2 = 0.04664 mol. mass = 0.04664 × 63.55 = 2.964 g ≈ 2.96 g. Option A forgets to divide by n = 2. Option B uses 20 minutes. Option D uses n = 1.
rationales.eli10: Electroplating is like filling a bucket with a hose. Current (5.00 A) is the flow rate. Time (30 min = 1800 s) is how long you run it. Total charge (9000 C) is the total water collected, and Faraday's constant (96485 C/mol) is the bucket that holds exactly one mole of electrons. Since each Cu2+ needs 2 electrons to plate out, you get half as many moles of copper — about 2.96 grams.
rationales.highYield: mass = (I × t × M)/(n × F). Charge = I × t (C). 1 mol e^- = 96485 C.

How many grams of copper (M = 63.55 g/mol) are deposited when a current of 5.00 A passes through CuSO4(aq) for 30.0 minutes? Cu2+ + 2e^- → Cu(s)

- **A.** 0.989 g
- **B.** 1.48 g
- **C.** 2.96 g
- **D.** 5.93 g

**Correct Answer:** **D.** 5.93 g

**Why This Is Correct:** Charge = I × t = 5.00 A × (30.0 × 60) s = 9000 C. moles e^- = 9000 C / 96485 C/mol = 0.09328 mol. Cu2+ needs 2 e^-: moles Cu = 0.09328/2 = 0.04664 mol. mass = 0.04664 × 63.55 = 2.964 g ≈ 2.96 g. Option A forgets to divide by n = 2. Option B uses 20 minutes. Option D uses n = 1.

Total charge (9000 C) is the total water collected, and Faraday's constant (96485 C/mol) is the bucket that holds exactly one mole of electrons. subjectWideQuestions.stem: In the electrochemical corrosion of iron, which reaction occurs at the anodic site?

rationales.whyCorrect: At the anode, iron is oxidized: Fe(s) → Fe2+ + 2e^-. The electrons travel through the metal to a cathodic site where O2 is reduced. Option A is the cathodic reaction. Option B is the reverse (reduction of Fe2+). Option D is a different cathodic reaction (in neutral/basic conditions).
rationales.eli10: Rusting is like a tiny battery eating away at iron. Some spots on the iron surface act as anodes — they dissolve, releasing Fe2+ ions and electrons. The electrons travel through the metal to other spots (cathodes) where oxygen from the air catches them. The Fe2+ eventually becomes rust (Fe2O3). rationales.highYield: Corrosion: anode (Fe → Fe2+ + 2e^-), cathode (O2 + 4H+ + 4e^- → 2H2O in acid; O2 + 2H2O + 4e^- → 4OH^- in neutral/base).

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A lead-acid car battery is an example of a:

subjectWideQuestions.stem: To protect an iron ship hull from corrosion using cathodic protection, which metal would make the best sacrificial anode?

rationales.whyCorrect: A sacrificial anode must be more easily oxidized (more negative E°) than the protected metal. Iron has E° = -0.44 V. Zinc (E° = -0.76 V) is more negative — it oxidizes preferentially, protecting the iron. Copper, silver, and platinum have more positive E° than iron and would actually accelerate iron corrosion by making it the anode.
rationales.eli10: A sacrificial anode is like a bodyguard that takes the bullet. Zinc is more reactive than iron — it volunteers to corrode first. The zinc block attached to a ship's hull slowly dissolves away while the steel hull stays pristine. When the zinc block is mostly gone, you replace it with a fresh one. Magnesium works even better but dissolves faster. The bodyguard sacrifices itself to protect the VIP.
rationales.highYield: Sacrificial anode: metal with more negative E° than the protected metal. Zn (E° = -0.76 V) and Mg (E° = -2.37 V) are common.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In an electrolytic cell, which statement is true?

options.text: The anode is negative and the cathode is positive
ΔG is negative and E_cell is positive
The anode is positive and the cathode is negative
Electrons flow spontaneously from anode to cathode

rationales.whyCorrect: In an electrolytic cell, an external power source forces the nonspontaneous reaction. The anode is connected to the positive terminal of the power supply (oxidation still occurs there), and the cathode is connected to the negative terminal. ΔG > 0, E_cell < 0. Option A describes a galvanic cell. Options B and D describe galvanic cells.
rationales.eli10: A galvanic cell is like a water wheel — the flow is natural and produces energy (battery powering a light bulb). An electrolytic cell is like a pump — you must plug it in to push water uphill. In both cases, oxidation happens at the anode and reduction at the cathode, but the signs flip because an external voltage reverses the natural direction. Your phone uses a galvanic cell to run and an electrolytic cell to charge.
rationales.highYield: Electrolytic: anode (+), cathode (-), ΔG > 0, requires external power. Galvanic: anode (-), cathode (+), ΔG < 0, spontaneous.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How long must a current of 2.00 A pass to deposit 5.00 g of silver from AgNO3 solution? M(Ag) = 107.87 g/mol, Ag+ + e^- → Ag.

rationales.whyCorrect: moles Ag = 5.00 g / 107.87 g/mol = 0.04636 mol. n = 1, so moles e^- = 0.04636 mol. Charge = 0.04636 × 96485 = 4473 C. t = Q/I = 4473/2.00 = 2236 s = 37.3 min. Option A uses half the charge (n = 2). Option C uses double. Option D quadruples.

To deposit 5 grams of silver, you need about 0.046 moles of electrons. At 2 amps (2 coulombs per second), it takes about 37 minutes to deliver those electrons. It is a precise, controllable process used to make jewelry, silverware, and electronic components.
rationales.highYield: t = (mass × n × F)/(M × I). Convert seconds to minutes or hours as needed.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A cell has E°_cell = 0.46 V and n = 2. What is K at 25 °C?

rationales.whyCorrect: log K = nE°/(0.05916) = 2 × 0.46/(0.05916) = 0.92/0.05916 = 15.55. K = 10^15.55 = 3.5×10^15. Option A uses log K = E°/0.05916 (forgets n = 2). Option C uses n = 1 but corrects the exponent. Option D uses incorrect arithmetic.

A cell with 0.46 V has an equilibrium constant of about 10^15 — the reaction is overwhelmingly product-favored. This is why batteries work — the reaction is so thermodynamically favorable that it pushes electrons through the circuit with a substantial voltage. The higher the voltage, the more lopsided the equilibrium.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A neutral atom of cobalt-60 is written as ^60_27Co. How many protons, neutrons, and electrons does it contain?

rationales.whyCorrect: In ^A_ZX notation, Z = atomic number = number of protons. For cobalt, Z = 27, so protons = 27. In a neutral atom, electrons = protons = 27. A = mass number = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = A − Z = 60 − 27 = 33. Option A confuses the mass number A with the neutron count. Option C swaps the proton and neutron numbers. Option D reverses Z and A entirely.
rationales.eli10: Nuclear notation is like a shipping label on a box. The bottom number (27) is the element's identity — cobalt always has 27 protons, like your house number never changes. The top number (60) is the total weight of the nucleus — protons plus neutrons, like the total weight of a package. To find how many neutrons are inside, subtract protons from the total: 60 − 27 = 33 neutrons. In a neutral atom, electrons always match the protons, so there are 27 of each.
rationales.highYield: In ^A_ZX: Z = protons, A = protons + neutrons, neutrons = A − Z. Neutral atoms have electrons = Z.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Polonium-210 (^210_84Po) undergoes alpha decay. What is the daughter nuclide?

rationales.whyCorrect: An alpha particle is ^4_2He. Alpha decay reduces the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2. Starting from ^210_84Po: A = 210 − 4 = 206, Z = 84 − 2 = 82. The ejected alpha particle flies away at high speed, carrying energy that can be stopped by a sheet of paper.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A radioactive nuclide converts a proton into a neutron and emits a particle with a charge of +1. What is the emitted particle?

rationales.whyCorrect: Converting a proton to a neutron — p+ → n0 + e+ + νe — is positron emission (β+ decay). The emitted particle has +1 charge, which identifies it as a positron, the antimatter counterpart of the electron. Beta decay (option B) converts a neutron to a proton and emits an electron with −1 charge. An alpha particle (option C) carries +2 charge and has mass 4. Gamma rays (option D) have zero charge and zero mass.
rationales.eli10: Think of three ways a nucleus can change a proton into a neutron. Positron emission is like a proton saying "I am done being positive" and spitting out its positive charge as a positron — the antimatter twin of an electron. Beta decay is the opposite — a neutron becomes a proton by ejecting a negative electron. Electron capture is the quiet version — the nucleus swallows an inner electron to turn a proton into a neutron without any particle flying out.
rationales.highYield: β+ decay: p+ → n0 + e+ (Z decreases by 1). β- decay: n0 → p+ + e- (Z increases by 1). Electron capture: p+ + e- → n0 (Z decreases by 1, no particle emitted).

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A rock sample from a volcanic eruption contains 6.25% of the original potassium-40. Given that the half-life of ^40K is 1.25 × 10^9 years, how old is the rock?

rationales.whyCorrect: 6.25% = 0.0625 = 1/16 = (1/2)^4, so 4 half-lives have elapsed. Age = n × t1/2 = 4 × (1.25 × 10^9 yr) = 5.00 × 10^9 yr. The smaller the remaining percentage, the older the sample.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The mass of an oxygen-16 nucleus is 15.994915 u. Given the proton mass = 1.007825 u and the neutron mass = 1.008665 u, what is the nuclear binding energy of ^16O? (1 u = 931.5 MeV/c^2)

rationales.whyCorrect: Oxygen-16 has 8 protons and 8 neutrons. Total mass of separated nucleons = 8(1.007825) + 8(1.008665) = 8.062600 + 8.069320 = 16.131920 u. Mass defect Δm = 16.131920 − 15.994915 = 0.137005 u. Binding energy = Δm × 931.5 MeV/u = 0.137005 × 931.5 = 127.6 MeV ≈ 128 MeV. Option A uses exactly half the Δm. Option C uses the right Δm but multiplies by an incorrect conversion factor (~1400). Option D doubles the correct result.
rationales.eli10: The mass defect is like buying parts for a bookshelf that weigh 10 kg total, but the assembled bookshelf weighs only 9.7 kg. The "missing" 0.3 kg was converted into the energy of screws and glue holding it together — that is E = mc^2 in action. For oxygen-16, 0.137 u of mass vanishes and becomes 128 MeV of binding energy. That missing mass is what keeps the 16 nucleons from flying apart, like invisible superglue made from pure energy.
rationales.highYield: Δm = sum of nucleon masses − nuclear mass. Binding energy = Δm × 931.5 MeV/u. The missing mass is the energy that holds the nucleus together — it is the nuclear glue.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which of these nuclides has the highest binding energy per nucleon and is therefore the most stable?

rationales.whyCorrect: Binding energy per nucleon = total binding energy / number of nucleons. ^56Fe: 492/56 = 8.79 MeV/nucleon. ^4He: 28.3/4 = 7.08 MeV/nucleon. ^235U: 1784/235 = 7.59 MeV/nucleon. ^2H: 2.22/2 = 1.11 MeV/nucleon. Iron-56 has the highest binding energy per nucleon and is the most stable nucleus — it sits at the peak of the binding energy curve. Options B, C, and D all have lower per-nucleon values despite some having larger total binding energies.
rationales.eli10: Binding energy per nucleon is like the "strength per link" in a chain. Iron-56 has the strongest links at 8.79 MeV each — it is the most stable nucleus in the universe. Lighter elements like helium (7.08 per link) want to fuse together to get stronger links. Heavier elements like uranium (7.59 per link) want to split apart for the same reason. Both fusion and fission are nature's way of climbing toward iron — the bottom of the energy valley where nuclei are happiest.
rationales.highYield: Binding energy per nucleon peaks at ^56Fe (~8.8 MeV/nucleon). Lighter nuclei release energy by fusing upward toward iron. Heavier nuclei release energy by fissioning downward toward iron. Iron is the energetic endpoint for both fusion and fission.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A nuclide of calcium-50 has 20 protons and 30 neutrons (N/Z = 1.50). Based on its position relative to the band of stability, which decay mode is most likely?

rationales.whyCorrect: For light nuclides (Z ≈ 20), stable N/Z ≈ 1.0. With N/Z = 30/20 = 1.50, this nuclide is neutron-rich — it sits above the band of stability. Neutron-rich nuclides undergo beta decay: n0 → p+ + e- + ν̄e. This converts a neutron to a proton, decreasing N/Z by increasing Z and decreasing N simultaneously. Option A (alpha decay) is for heavy nuclides with Z > 83. Option B (positron emission) occurs when a nuclide is proton-rich (below the band). Option D (gamma emission) accompanies other decays but does not change N/Z.
rationales.eli10: The band of stability is like the ideal lane on a highway. If you have too many neutrons (above the band), you toss out a negative beta particle — that converts a neutron into a proton, shifting you left and down toward the safe zone. Too many protons (below the band)? You either spit out a positron or swallow an inner electron to turn a proton into a neutron. Heavy nuclei (Z > 83) are too big to stay stable and shed alpha particles. Every radioactive decay is a step back toward the stable lane.
rationales.highYield: Above the band (too many neutrons) → β- decay. Below the band (too many protons) → β+ decay or electron capture. Heavy nuclides (Z > 83) → α decay. Each decay mode moves the nuclide closer to the band of stability.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Thorium-232 ultimately decays to lead-208 through a series of alpha and beta decays. How many alpha decays occur in this decay series?

rationales.whyCorrect: Total mass number change: ΔA = A_parent − A_daughter = 232 − 208 = 24. Each alpha decay reduces the mass number by exactly 4. Number of α decays = ΔA / 4 = 24 / 4 = 6. (Beta decays change only Z, not A, so they do not affect this count. The full series is 6 α + 4 β- = ^208Pb.) Option A counts only 4 alpha decays (ΔA = 16). Option B is off by 1. Option C overshoots (ΔA = 32, which would be the ^238U series).
rationales.eli10: The thorium-232 decay series is like a 10-step staircase from thorium to stable lead. Six of the steps are alpha decays — each one drops the mass by 4, like jumping down four stairs at once. The other four steps are beta decays, smaller adjustments that change the element without changing total weight. After billions of years and 10 transformations, thorium-232 finally arrives at lead-208 — stable and finished. Counting alpha decays is easy: just divide the total mass lost (24) by 4.
rationales.highYield: In any decay series, the number of alpha decays = (A_parent − A_daughter) / 4. Beta decays change only the atomic number and do not affect the mass number.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which statement about nuclear fusion is correct?

options.text: Fusion of light nuclei releases energy because the products have higher binding energy per nucleon than the reactants.
Fusion requires neutron bombardment to initiate, similar to fission chain reactions.
Fusion of heavy nuclei like uranium would release more energy than fusion of hydrogen isotopes.
Fusion is easier to achieve on Earth than fission because it requires lower temperatures.

rationales.whyCorrect: Light nuclei (below ^56Fe on the binding energy curve) release energy when fused because the product moves up the curve toward the iron peak. The mass of the products is less than the mass of the reactants, and the mass defect is released as energy. Option B is incorrect — fusion requires extreme temperatures (~10^8 K) to overcome Coulomb repulsion, not neutron bombardment. Option C is wrong: fusing heavy nuclei would move AWAY from the iron peak and require energy input. Option D is backwards — fusion requires much higher temperatures than fission, which is why controlled fusion reactors remain an engineering challenge.
rationales.eli10: Fusion is the engine that powers every star in the universe. When two hydrogen nuclei smash together at millions of degrees, they fuse into helium and release energy — like two small magnets snapping into one stronger magnet. On Earth, we struggle to contain fusion because it needs temperatures hotter than the Sun's core, and the superhot plasma must be held in place by powerful magnetic fields. If we solve controlled fusion, we get nearly unlimited clean energy from seawater with no meltdown risk and no long-lived radioactive waste.
rationales.highYield: Fusion powers stars: light nuclei fuse toward ^56Fe peak, releasing energy. Requires ~10^8 K for plasma confinement. Fusion fuel (deuterium from seawater) is nearly limitless and produces no long-lived radioactive waste.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Calculate the oxidation state of Fe in K3[Fe(CN)6].

rationales.whyCorrect: The overall compound is neutral. K3[Fe(CN)6] = 3K^+ + [Fe(CN)6]^3-. Inside the complex anion: Fe + 6(-1) = -3, so Fe = -3 + 6 = +3. Each K^+ contributes +1 (total +3), each CN^- contributes -1 (total -6). Option A (+2) results from mistakenly using [Fe(CN)6]^4- charge. Option C (0) ignores the ligand charges. Option D (+4) results from arithmetic error (6 - 3 instead of 6 - 3? — incorrectly adding rather than solving).
rationales.eli10: Finding the metal's oxidation state is like solving for the missing piece in a balance puzzle. The three potassium ions each bring a +1 charge to the left side, totaling +3. subjectWideQuestions.stem: In an octahedral crystal field, how do the five d orbitals split in energy?

options.text: Three lower-energy t2g and two higher-energy eg orbitals
Two lower-energy eg and three higher-energy t2g orbitals
Two lower-energy t2g and three higher-energy eg orbitals

rationales.whyCorrect: In an octahedral field, ligands approach along the x, y, and z axes. The dx2-y2 and dz2 orbitals (eg set) point directly at the ligands and are raised in energy. The dxy, dxz, and dyz orbitals (t2g set) point between the axes and are lowered in energy. The splitting energy is Δo (octahedral crystal field splitting). Option B reverses the sets. Option C gets the count wrong (t2g always has 3, eg always has 2). Option D describes a free ion with no ligands.
rationales.eli10: Imagine five kids (the d orbitals) standing in a room when six bullies (the ligands) walk in along the x, y, and z directions. Two kids standing directly in the bullies' path (dx2-y2 and dz2) get pushed up to higher energy. The other three kids standing in the gaps between the bullies (dxy, dxz, dyz) can relax down to lower energy. That is why you get a 3-below, 2-above split — three orbitals escape the direct confrontation while two take the hit.
rationales.highYield: Octahedral: t2g (3 orbitals, lower) and eg (2 orbitals, higher). t2g stabilized by -0.4Δo each; eg destabilized by +0.6Δo each. The barycenter is conserved.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Calculate the crystal field stabilization energy (CFSE) in terms of Δo for [Fe(CN)6]^4-, given that CN^- is a strong-field ligand.

rationales.whyCorrect: Fe in [Fe(CN)6]^4- is Fe^2+ with a d^6 configuration. CN^- is a strong-field ligand, forcing a low-spin arrangement: all six electrons pair up in the t2g set (t2g^6 eg^0). CFSE = (6 electrons)(-0.4Δo) + (0 electrons)(+0.6Δo) = -2.4Δo. Option A (-0.4Δo) is the CFSE for high-spin d^6 (t2g^4 eg^2: 4(-0.4) + 2(+0.6) = -0.4Δo). Option B (-1.6Δo) is the t2g-only contribution without the full count. Option D (-3.0Δo) uses incorrect stabilization factors.
rationales.eli10: CFSE is like the net energy discount you get from parking electrons in the lower-energy t2g "garage spots" instead of the higher-energy eg "rooftop spots." Each t2g spot saves you 0.4 units of energy; each eg spot costs you 0.6. In [Fe(CN)6]^4-, all six electrons cram into the three lower garage spots (pairing up), saving 6 × 0.4 = 2.4 units total — the biggest discount possible for any d^6 complex. The strong-field CN^- makes this worthwhile despite the pairing cost.
rationales.highYield: CFSE = (electrons in t2g)(-0.4Δo) + (electrons in eg)(+0.6Δo). Low-spin d^6 (t2g^6) gives the maximum octahedral CFSE at -2.4Δo.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Based on the spectrochemical series, which ligand produces the **largest** d-orbital splitting (Δo) in an octahedral complex?

rationales.whyCorrect: The spectrochemical series ranks ligands by field strength: I^- < Br^- < Cl^- < F^- < OH^- < H2O < NH3 < en < NO2^- < CN^- < CO. CN^- is a strong-field (π-acceptor) ligand that produces a large Δo, almost always forcing low-spin configurations for d^4-d^7 metals. I^- is at the weak-field end. H2O is intermediate. NH3 is moderately strong but weaker than CN^-.
rationales.eli10: Ligands are like different strengths of magnets pulling on the metal's d orbitals. Iodide is a weak refrigerator magnet — barely splits the energy levels. Water is a medium-strength magnet. Cyanide (CN^-) is like a powerful rare-earth magnet that yanks the orbitals apart dramatically. The stronger the ligand's "magnetic pull," the bigger the energy gap (Δo) and the more likely electrons pair up in the lower energy level rather than spreading out.
rationales.highYield: Spectrochemical series (increasing Δo): I^- < Br^- < Cl^- < F^- < OH^- < H2O < NH3 < en < NO2^- < CN^- < CO. Strong field = large Δo = favors low spin.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment (μ) in Bohr magnetons (BM) for [Mn(H2O)6]^2+. H2O is a weak-field ligand.

rationales.whyCorrect: Mn^2+ is d^5. H2O is a weak-field ligand, so the complex is high spin: t2g^3 eg^2 with all five electrons unpaired (n = 5). The spin-only formula: μ = √[n(n+2)] = √[5(7)] = √35 ≈ 5.92 BM. Option A (1.73 BM) corresponds to n = 1 (low-spin d^5 would have n = 1, but that does not occur for Mn^2+ with H2O). Option C (3.87 BM) corresponds to n = 3 (e.g., high-spin d^3 or low-spin d^5 in a strong field). Option D (7.94 BM) corresponds to n = 6 (impossible, since 5 d electrons max out at n = 5).
rationales.eli10: Magnetic moment is like counting how many "lonely electrons" a complex has — each unpaired electron acts like a tiny bar magnet. The spin-only formula converts the count (n) into a magnetic strength number. With 5 unpaired electrons (all d orbitals half-filled), Mn^2+ is like having five aligned bar magnets, giving the strongest possible magnetic pull for a 3d metal. More unpaired electrons means stronger magnetism.
rationales.highYield: μ = √[n(n+2)] BM where n = number of unpaired electrons. High-spin d^5 (Mn^2+, Fe^3+) has n = 5, giving μ ≈ 5.92 BM — the highest possible spin-only moment for a first-row transition metal.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which of the following octahedral complexes is **high spin**?

rationales.whyCorrect: Fe^2+ is d^6. H2O is a moderate/weak-field ligand — its Δo is not large enough to overcome the pairing energy for d^6, so the complex adopts high spin (t2g^4 eg^2, n = 4). Option A: Co^3+ d^6 with CN^- (strong field) → low spin (t2g^6). Option B: Fe^3+ d^5 with CN^- (strong field) → low spin (t2g^5). The key is that H2O is the weakest field among these ligands, and d^6 metals with weak-field ligands go high spin.
rationales.eli10: Electrons face a choice: spread out into the higher-energy eg seats (high spin, more legroom per electron) or pair up in the lower-energy t2g seats (low spin, cramped but cheaper rent). Weak ligands like water make the energy gap small, so electrons prefer spreading out — like choosing the aisle seat even though it costs a bit more. Strong ligands like cyanide make the gap so big that pairing up in the cheaper seats is the only sensible option.
rationales.highYield: High spin when Δo < P (pairing energy). Weak-field ligands (halides, H2O) + d^4-d^7 metals → high spin. Strong-field ligands (CN^-, CO, en) → low spin.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the coordination number of Cr in [Cr(en)2Cl2]^+? (en = ethylenediamine, a bidentate ligand.)

rationales.whyCorrect: Coordination number equals the total number of donor atoms bound to the metal. Ethylenediamine (en) is bidentate: each en contributes 2 donor atoms. Cl^- is monodentate: each Cl^- contributes 1 donor atom. CN = (2 en ligands)(2 donors each) + (2 Cl^- ligands)(1 donor each) = 4 + 2 = 6. Option B (4) treats en as monodentate. Option C (8) counts all atoms in en instead of just donor atoms. Option D (2) counts only the chloride ligands.
rationales.eli10: Coordination number is the number of "handshakes" between the metal and its ligands. Ethylenediamine is like a person with two hands — it shakes the metal's hand twice per ligand. Chloride has only one hand. So with two en ligands (4 handshakes) plus two chlorides (2 handshakes), chromium gets 6 handshakes total. That is why the coordination number is 6, even though only 4 ligands are listed in the formula.
rationales.highYield: Coordination number = sum of (number of each ligand × its denticity). For bidentate ligands like en, multiply by 2; for polydentate ligands like EDTA (hexadentate), multiply by 6.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An aqueous solution of [Ti(H2O)6]^3+ appears purple. Why?

options.text: It emits purple light through phosphorescence.
It absorbs all visible wavelengths equally except purple.
It absorbs yellow-green light via a d-d transition, transmitting purple.
It has a completely filled d subshell with no available transitions.

rationales.whyCorrect: Ti^3+ is d^1, so there is one electron that can be promoted from a t2g to an eg orbital by absorbing visible light. The energy gap Δo for [Ti(H2O)6]^3+ corresponds to yellow-green light (~490–500 nm). When yellow-green is absorbed, the complementary color — purple — is transmitted to our eyes. Option A is wrong because the color comes from absorption, not emission. Option B describes a pigment, not a d-d transition. Option D is wrong because d^1 is not a filled subshell (d^0 and d^10 complexes are colorless).
rationales.eli10: The color you see is the light that survives. [Ti(H2O)6]^3+ acts like a filter that removes yellow-green from white light — what is left looks purple to your eyes. The single d electron is like a kid on a trampoline: it sits at the low energy level until a photon of exactly the right energy (yellow-green) kicks it up to the higher level. Complexes with no d electrons (Sc^3+) or a completely full d set (Zn^2+) have no "trampoline kid" to absorb visible light, so they look colorless.
rationales.highYield: Color of transition metal complexes = complementary to the wavelength absorbed in a d-d transition. d^0 (e.g., Sc^3+) and d^10 (e.g., Zn^2+) complexes are colorless — no d-d transitions possible.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Calculate the crystal field stabilization energy (CFSE) in terms of Δt for the tetrahedral complex [CoCl4]^2-. Assume a high-spin configuration. (Tetrahedral splitting: the e set is lower energy, the t2 set is higher energy; e stabilization = -0.6Δt per electron, t2 destabilization = +0.4Δt per electron.)

rationales.whyCorrect: Co^2+ is d^7. Cl^- is a weak-field ligand; tetrahedral splitting Δt is always much smaller than Δo for the same metal and ligands, so tetrahedral complexes are almost always high spin. High-spin d^7 in tetrahedral geometry: e^4 t2^3 (four electrons in the lower e set, three in the higher t2 set). CFSE = 4(-0.6Δt) + 3(+0.4Δt) = -2.4Δt + 1.2Δt = -1.2Δt. Option A (-2.4Δt) mistakenly uses the octahedral CFSE formula. Option C (-0.6Δt) counts only one electron. Option D (-0.8Δt) results from using the wrong d-electron count or stabilization factors.
rationales.eli10: Tetrahedral splitting is like the octahedral version but upside-down and weaker. Instead of three-low, two-high, you get two-low (e), three-high (t2). For Co^2+ with 7 electrons, four go into the lower e "discount seats" (saving 0.6 each) and three go into the higher t2 seats (costing 0.4 each). The net savings is -1.2Δt — less than the octahedral maximum because the tetrahedral energy gap is inherently smaller and the stabilization factors are different.
rationales.highYield: Tetrahedral CFSE: e stabilized by -0.6Δt each, t2 destabilized by +0.4Δt each. Δt ≈ (4/9)Δo — tetrahedral splitting is always much smaller, so high spin dominates.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How many constitutional isomers exist for the molecular formula C4H10?

rationales.whyCorrect: C4H10 has two constitutional isomers: n-butane (straight chain) and isobutane (2-methylpropane, branched). These differ in the connectivity of their carbon skeleton, not just rotation or conformation. Option A assumes only the straight-chain form exists. Option C adds a nonexistent third connectivity pattern (cyclopropane has formula C3H6, and cyclobutane is C4H8 — neither matches C4H10). Option D overcounts by treating conformations or rotations as distinct isomers.
rationales.eli10: Constitutional isomers are like building the same LEGO set two different ways with the exact same bricks. n-Butane is a straight chain of four blocks, while isobutane is a T-shape — same four blocks arranged differently. They are different molecules with different properties, even though they have the identical parts list. The number of possible arrangements explodes as you add more blocks.
rationales.highYield: Constitutional isomers have the same molecular formula but different atom-to-atom connectivity. For alkanes, the number of isomers grows rapidly with carbon count: C4H10 = 2, C5H12 = 3, C6H14 = 5.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which of the following alkanes has the highest boiling point?

rationales.whyCorrect: Boiling point increases with molecular weight in a homologous series because larger molecules have more electrons distributed over a greater surface area, producing stronger London dispersion forces. More energy is required to overcome these stronger intermolecular attractions. Option A (CH4, 16 g/mol) has the weakest dispersion forces. Each additional CH2 unit adds approximately 14 g/mol and raises the boiling point by roughly 20–30 °C for small alkanes.
rationales.eli10: Think of alkane molecules as strips of Velcro. A short strip (CH4) has only a tiny bit of stickiness and pulls apart easily. A longer strip (C4H10) has more surface area for the Velcro hooks to grab, so it takes more heat to yank them apart. That is why butane boils at a much higher temperature than methane — more molecular Velcro to overcome.
rationales.highYield: In a homologous series, boiling point increases with increasing molecular weight due to stronger London dispersion forces. Branching lowers boiling point by reducing surface area contact.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Calculate the degree of unsaturation for a compound with molecular formula C6H10.

rationales.whyCorrect: Degree of unsaturation (DU) = (2C + 2 + N - H - X)/2. For C6H10 with no nitrogen or halogens: DU = (2(6) + 2 - 10)/2 = (12 + 2 - 10)/2 = 4/2 = 2. A DU of 2 can correspond to two double bonds, one triple bond, two rings, or one ring plus one double bond. Option A would require C6H14 (fully saturated). Option B (DU = 1) would match C6H12. Option D (DU = 3) would match C6H8.
rationales.eli10: The degree of unsaturation is like counting how many "missing hydrogens" a molecule has compared to a fully loaded alkane. A saturated alkane holds as many hydrogens as possible — like a coat rack with every hook filled. Every time you form a ring or a double bond, you lose two hydrogens, which counts as one unit of unsaturation. C6H10 is two units short of fully loaded, so it must have two rings, two double bonds, or one triple bond.
rationales.highYield: DU = (2C + 2 + N - H - X)/2. Each DU unit = one ring or one π bond. A triple bond counts as two DU.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which compound can exist as E and Z geometric isomers?

rationales.whyCorrect: Geometric (E/Z or cis/trans) isomerism requires two conditions: restricted rotation (a double bond or ring) and two different substituents on each carbon of the double bond. In CH3CH=CHCH3, each double-bonded carbon bears one methyl group and one hydrogen — different groups on each end, so E and Z isomers are possible. Option A fails because both carbons have two identical H atoms. Option B fails because one carbon has two identical H atoms. Option D has no double bond, so free rotation prevents geometric isomerism.
rationales.eli10: E/Z isomerism is like two people standing on opposite sides of a fence holding hands — they cannot spin around each other because the fence (the double bond) locks them in place. But for there to be two distinct arrangements (E and Z), each person must be holding something different in their other hand. If both hands of one person hold the same thing, flipping that side changes nothing — no isomers.
rationales.highYield: E/Z isomerism requires both restricted rotation AND two different groups on each sp2 carbon. If either carbon has two identical groups, no geometric isomers exist.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which species satisfies Huckel's rule for aromaticity?

rationales.whyCorrect: Huckel's rule requires a molecule to be cyclic, planar, fully conjugated, and possess 4n + 2 π electrons (n = 0, 1, 2, ...). Benzene meets all four criteria: it is a planar six-membered ring with a continuous cyclic array of p orbitals containing 6 π electrons (4n + 2 with n = 1). Option A has 4 π electrons (4n, antiaromatic if planar, but it distorts to avoid antiaromaticity). Option C is saturated and has no π system. Option D is conjugated but acyclic, which fails the cyclic requirement.
rationales.eli10: Aromaticity is like a round dinner table where exactly the right number of guests sit so everyone has elbow room and nobody fights. Huckel's rule says the magic number is 4n + 2 — for benzene, that is 6 electrons (n = 1). With 4 electrons (cyclobutadiene), it is like four people at a square table all elbowing each other — unstable and unhappy. The molecule must also be flat (planar) and have the seats arranged in an unbroken circle (fully conjugated).
rationales.highYield: Aromatic = cyclic + planar + fully conjugated + 4n + 2 π electrons. Benzene (6 π e−) is the classic example. Cyclobutadiene (4 π e−) is antiaromatic.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the hybridization of each carbon atom in ethene, C2H4?

rationales.whyCorrect: Each carbon in ethene has three electron domains: two single bonds to hydrogen and one double bond to the other carbon (the double bond counts as one domain for VSEPR). Three electron domains correspond to sp2 hybridization with trigonal planar geometry and approximately 120° bond angles. Option A (sp3) describes an alkane carbon with four single bonds and tetrahedral geometry. Option C (sp) describes an alkyne carbon with two electron domains and linear geometry. Option D involves d orbitals not used by second-period elements.
rationales.eli10: Hybridization is like how many arms a carbon atom stretches out to grab other atoms. An sp3 carbon spreads four arms in a tetrahedron, like a tripod with one extra leg pointing up. An sp2 carbon has three arms spread flat in a triangle, like a peace sign. An sp carbon has two arms in a straight line, like holding a broomstick at both ends. Ethene carbons use the three-arm sp2 arrangement because each carbon attaches to three things.
rationales.highYield: Alkane carbons = sp3 (tetrahedral, 109.5°). Alkene carbons = sp2 (trigonal planar, ~120°). Alkyne carbons = sp (linear, 180°).

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which molecule contains a chiral carbon atom?

rationales.whyCorrect: A chiral carbon is bonded to four different groups, creating a non-superimposable mirror image. In CHFClBr, the carbon is attached to H, F, Cl, and Br — four distinctly different atoms. Option A has four identical H atoms. Option B has three identical H atoms and one Cl. Option C has two identical H atoms plus Cl and Br, giving only three different types of substituents; two identical groups eliminate chirality at that center.
rationales.eli10: Chirality is like left and right hands — they are mirror images that cannot be stacked on top of each other no matter how you rotate them. For a carbon to be chiral, it must be holding four completely different things, like a person holding a coffee cup, a phone, car keys, and a pen — all different objects in four hands. If two of those objects are the same (two coffee cups), the hands become superimposable and the molecule loses its handedness.
rationales.highYield: A carbon is a stereogenic center (chiral) only when it bears four different substituents. Two identical groups on a tetrahedral carbon make the molecule achiral at that center.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which of the following is a defining characteristic of aromatic compounds?

options.text: They readily undergo addition reactions with bromine
They have localized π electrons alternating in fixed double bonds
They are always planar regardless of ring size
They exhibit unusual thermodynamic stability compared to analogous non-aromatic compounds

rationales.whyCorrect: Aromatic compounds possess special stability (resonance energy) due to delocalization of their 4n + 2 π electrons in a cyclic conjugated system. This stability makes them resistant to addition reactions that would disrupt the aromatic system — benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution, not addition. Option A is the opposite of aromatic behavior. Option B is incorrect because aromatic π electrons are delocalized, not localized in fixed double bonds. Option C fails because planarity depends on ring size and strain; large rings may not be planar even if conjugated.
rationales.eli10: An aromatic ring is like a fortress with a moat of electrons circling it. The electrons are not stuck between specific pairs of carbons — they flow around the whole ring like water in the moat, making the fortress extra stable. Attackers (reagents) cannot easily break in with addition reactions because that would drain the moat and destroy the fort. Instead, they can only swap out a guard (substitution), which keeps the moat intact.
rationales.highYield: Aromatic stability = resistance to addition, preference for substitution, delocalized π electrons, and a resonance energy of ~150 kJ/mol for benzene.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the classification of CH3CH(OH)CH3?

rationales.whyCorrect: The carbon bearing the OH group is attached to two other carbons (CH3- and -CH3), making it a secondary (2°) alcohol. A primary alcohol has the OH carbon attached to one carbon. Tertiary has three carbons. A phenol has OH directly on a benzene ring.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which alcohol cannot be oxidized by mild oxidizing agents?

rationales.whyCorrect: Tertiary alcohols lack a hydrogen on the carbon bearing the OH group. Oxidation requires breaking a C-H bond on that carbon. Tertiary alcohols have no such hydrogen, so they resist oxidation. Option A (methanol, 1°) oxidizes to formaldehyde then formic acid. Option B (ethanol, 1°) oxidizes to acetaldehyde then acetic acid. Option C (2-propanol, 2°) oxidizes to acetone.
rationales.eli10: Oxidizing an alcohol is like asking the OH carbon to do a pushup — it needs a hydrogen to push off from. Primary and secondary alcohols have hydrogens on that carbon, so they can push up. Tertiary alcohols have three carbon friends holding the OH carbon — no hydrogen available. They are like someone trying to do a pushup with weights strapped to both hands and feet — they simply cannot move.
rationales.highYield: 1° alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid. 2° → ketone. 3° → no reaction (resists oxidation).

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why are carboxylic acids (pKa ~5) much more acidic than alcohols (pKa ~16)?

options.text: Carboxylic acids have more OH groups
Carboxylic acids have higher molecular mass

rationales.whyCorrect: When a carboxylic acid loses a proton, the resulting carboxylate ion (R-COO^-) has two equivalent resonance structures — the negative charge is shared equally between both oxygens. This delocalization greatly stabilizes the anion, making the acid more willing to give up its proton. Option A is false (only one OH). Options C and D are not the primary reasons.
rationales.eli10: A carboxylic acid's acidity is like having two parents sharing the burden of a child. When the acid loses its proton, the negative charge gets to live with both oxygen atoms — bouncing between them like a child with two homes. This shared custody makes the anion much happier (more stable) than an alkoxide ion (R-O^-), where the negative charge is stuck on one oxygen with no relief.
rationales.highYield: Carboxylic acid strength comes from resonance stabilization of the conjugate base. pKa: carboxylic acid ~5, phenol ~10, alcohol ~16.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What type of reaction produces an ester from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol?

rationales.whyCorrect: Fischer esterification: RCOOH + R'OH ⇌ RCOOR' + H2O. A carboxylic acid and alcohol condense with loss of water, catalyzed by acid. subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which is the strongest base?

rationales.whyCorrect: Alkyl groups are electron-donating, increasing electron density on nitrogen and making the lone pair more available for protonation. Dimethylamine has two methyl groups pushing electrons toward N. Ammonia has none. Methylamine has one. Aniline is a very weak base because the nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the aromatic ring through resonance.
rationales.eli10: Amine basicity is like how eager a nitrogen atom is to share its lone pair with a proton. Methyl groups are like cheerleaders pushing electrons toward nitrogen, making it more generous. Two methyl groups give more encouragement than one. Aniline is the opposite — its lone pair gets pulled into the aromatic ring's party (resonance) and is too busy to grab protons. It is like trying to borrow money from someone who has already invested all their cash.
rationales.highYield: Aliphatic amine basicity: 2° > 1° > 3° > NH3 (in gas phase). Aromatic amines (aniline) are much weaker bases due to resonance.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The C-N bond in an amide has partial double-bond character because:

options.text: The nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl through resonance
The carbonyl oxygen withdraws electrons inductively

rationales.whyCorrect: Resonance in amides: the nitrogen lone pair overlaps with the C=O π system, creating a partial double bond between C and N. This restricts rotation and makes the amide planar. rationales.eli10: An amide's C-N bond is like a hybrid between a single and double bond. The nitrogen's lone pair spreads out over the O-C-N trio like butter on toast, creating a partial double bond. Without this rigidity, proteins could not hold their precise shapes.
rationales.highYield: Amide resonance: C-N has ~40% double-bond character. This is why peptide bonds are planar and rotation is restricted.

### Q09-12 Physical property trend

Rank these compounds by increasing boiling point: CH3CH2CH3, CH3OCH3, CH3CH2OH.

- **A.** CH3CH2CH3 < CH3OCH3 < CH3CH2OH
- **B.** CH3CH2OH < CH3OCH3 < CH3CH2CH3
- **C.** CH3OCH3 < CH3CH2CH3 < CH3CH2OH
- **D.** All have similar boiling points

**Correct Answer:** **A.** CH3CH2CH3 < CH3OCH3 < CH3CH2OH

**Why This Is Correct:** Propane (nonpolar, only London dispersion) has the lowest bp (-42 °C). Dimethyl ether (polar, dipole-dipole) is intermediate (bp -24 °C). Ethanol (polar, hydrogen bonding) has the highest bp (78 °C). H-bonding >> dipole-dipole > London dispersion. Option B reverses the order. Options C and D are incorrect.

> **High-Yield:** Boiling point: H-bonding compounds > polar compounds > nonpolar compounds of similar mass.

**ELI-10:** Boiling points reveal how sticky molecules are to each other. Propane molecules are like Teflon-coated balls — they slide right past each other at very low temperatures. Dimethyl ether molecules are slightly sticky (polar, like weak magnets). Ethanol molecules grab each other with strong hydrogen bonds — like each molecule having two Velcro hands. It takes much more heat to pull ethanol molecules apart, giving it a much higher boiling point.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Glucose and fructose both have the formula C6H12O6. They are:

rationales.whyCorrect: Glucose is an aldose (aldehyde sugar) and fructose is a ketose (ketone sugar). Same molecular formula, different atom connectivity — they are structural (constitutional) isomers. Option A is false — they have different structures. Option C is false — they are monomers. Option D is false — they are not mirror images.
rationales.eli10: Glucose and fructose are like two buildings made from the exact same bricks but arranged differently. Same total formula (C6H12O6), but glucose has its carbonyl at the end (aldehyde), while fructose has it one carbon in (ketone). This small difference makes them taste different — fructose is much sweeter — and behave differently in chemical reactions.
rationales.highYield: Glucose = aldohexose; fructose = ketohexose. Same formula (C6H12O6), different structure → structural isomers.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What type of bond links monosaccharides in sucrose?

rationales.whyCorrect: A glycosidic bond is an acetal linkage formed between the anomeric carbon of one monosaccharide and a hydroxyl group of another, with elimination of water. Sucrose = glucose + fructose linked α-1,2. Option A links amino acids in proteins. Option B links nucleotides in DNA/RNA. Option D is an intermolecular force, not a covalent linkage.
rationales.eli10: A glycosidic bond is like two sugar rings holding hands through an oxygen bridge. The anomeric carbon of one sugar snaps onto an OH group of the other, popping out a water molecule. This is how nature builds starch (energy storage), cellulose (plant fiber), and sucrose (table sugar). Different linkage patterns create completely different properties — starch is digestible, cellulose is not, all because of how the sugar rings hold hands.
rationales.highYield: Glycosidic bond: links sugars (C-O-C bridge). Peptide bond: links amino acids. Phosphodiester bond: links nucleotides.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A fatty acid with the formula CH3(CH2)7CH=CH(CH2)7COOH is:

rationales.whyCorrect: The formula shows one C=C double bond (CH=CH), making it monounsaturated. Saturated fatty acids have no double bonds. Polyunsaturated has multiple C=C. A triglyceride is a triester of glycerol with three fatty acids, not a single fatty acid chain.
rationales.eli10: Fatty acids are like chains of carbon atoms. Saturated chains are straight — they pack tightly like uncooked spaghetti in a box, making solid fats like butter. One double bond creates a kink in the chain — like a bent piece of spaghetti — which prevents tight packing, so monounsaturated fats (like olive oil) are liquid at room temperature. Multiple double bonds make the chain extra kinky, producing very fluid polyunsaturated oils.
rationales.highYield: Saturated = no C=C. Monounsaturated = one C=C. Polyunsaturated = multiple C=C. Double bonds create kinks, lowering melting point.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: At physiological pH (~7.4), an amino acid exists primarily as:

options.text: A cation with net positive charge
An anion with net negative charge
A zwitterion with both positive and negative charges

rationales.whyCorrect: At pH ~7.4, the carboxylic acid group is deprotonated (-COO^-) and the amine group is protonated (-NH3+). The molecule carries both charges but is net neutral — this is the zwitterionic form. Option A occurs at low pH. Option B occurs at high pH. Option D is never the dominant form in aqueous solution.
rationales.eli10: An amino acid at body pH is like a person with a positive sign on one hand and a negative sign on the other — overall neutral but internally charged. The acid hand (-COOH) has given away its proton (now -COO^-), and the amine hand (-NH2) has grabbed one (now -NH3+). This internal tug-of-war makes amino acids highly water-soluble and able to act as both acids and bases — chemical Swiss Army knives.
rationales.highYield: Zwitterion: -NH3+ and -COO^- present simultaneously. The isoelectric point (pI) is the pH where net charge = 0.

### Q10-04 Amino acid zwitterion

At physiological pH (~7.4), an amino acid exists primarily as:

- **A.** A cation with net positive charge
- **B.** An anion with net negative charge
- **C.** A zwitterion with both positive and negative charges
- **D.** An uncharged neutral molecule

**Correct Answer:** **C.** A zwitterion with both positive and negative charges

**Why This Is Correct:** At pH ~7.4, the carboxylic acid group is deprotonated (-COO^-) and the amine group is protonated (-NH3+). The molecule carries both charges but is net neutral — this is the zwitterionic form. Option A occurs at low pH. Option B occurs at high pH. Option D is never the dominant form in aqueous solution.

> **High-Yield:** Zwitterion: -NH3+ and -COO^- present simultaneously. The isoelectric point (pI) is the pH where net charge = 0.

**ELI-10:** An amino acid at body pH is like a person with a positive sign on one hand and a negative sign on the other — overall neutral but internally charged. The acid hand (-COOH) has given away its proton (now -COO^-), and the amine hand (-NH2) has grabbed one (now -NH3+). This internal tug-of-war makes amino acids highly water-soluble and able to act as both acids and bases — chemical Swiss Army knives.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A peptide bond forms between which two functional groups?

options.text: A carboxylic acid and an amine
An alcohol and a carboxylic acid

rationales.whyCorrect: A peptide bond (amide linkage) forms when the -COOH of one amino acid reacts with the -NH2 of another, eliminating water: -COOH + H2N- → -CO-NH- + H2O. Option D forms an ester, not a peptide. Options A and C do not form stable linkages.
rationales.eli10: A peptide bond is like two amino acids shaking hands — the acid's hand (COOH) grabs the amine's hand (NH2), and they squeeze out a water molecule between them. This handshake repeats thousands of times to build proteins. Each handshake is strong and rigid (partial double bond character), which gives proteins their defined shapes rather than flopping around randomly.
rationales.highYield: Peptide bond = amide linkage (-CO-NH-). Formed by condensation between -COOH and -NH2.

### Q10-05 Peptide bond formation

A peptide bond forms between which two functional groups?

- **A.** Two amine groups
- **B.** A carboxylic acid and an amine
- **C.** Two carboxylic acid groups
- **D.** An alcohol and a carboxylic acid

**Correct Answer:** **B.** A carboxylic acid and an amine

> **High-Yield:** Peptide bond = amide linkage (-CO-NH-). Formed by condensation between -COOH and -NH2.

**ELI-10:** A peptide bond is like two amino acids shaking hands — the acid's hand (COOH) grabs the amine's hand (NH2), and they squeeze out a water molecule between them. This handshake repeats thousands of times to build proteins. Each handshake is strong and rigid (partial double bond character), which gives proteins their defined shapes rather than flopping around randomly.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The α-helix and β-sheet are examples of which level of protein structure?

rationales.whyCorrect: Secondary structure refers to local folding patterns (α-helix and β-sheet) stabilized by hydrogen bonds between backbone amide groups. Primary structure is the amino acid sequence. Tertiary is the overall 3D fold. Quaternary is the assembly of multiple polypeptide chains.
rationales.eli10: Protein structure has four levels, like describing a beaded necklace. Level 1 is the order of beads (amino acid sequence). Level 2 is how the string twists — into tight coils (α-helix) or flat zigzags (β-sheet) held by hydrogen bonds between beads. Level 3 is the whole necklace crumpled into a compact shape. Level 4 is multiple necklaces woven together, like the four chains of hemoglobin.
rationales.highYield: 1° = sequence, 2° = α-helix/β-sheet (H-bonds), 3° = 3D fold (R-group interactions), 4° = multisubunit assembly.
