subjectWideQuestions.stem: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine through:

rationales.whyCorrect: A-T base pairing involves two hydrogen bonds; G-C involves three. The specificity of pairing (A only with T, G only with C) ensures faithful DNA replication. Option A is too few. Option C describes G-C pairing. Option D is incorrect — the two strands are held by H-bonds, not covalent bonds.
rationales.eli10: DNA base pairing is like a puzzle where A and T are a two-finger handshake, while G and C have a stronger three-finger grip. This is why DNA with lots of G-C pairs is harder to unzip — it takes more heat to break those extra hydrogen bonds. The handshake specificity (A only shakes T's hand, G only shakes C's) is what makes DNA replication so accurate.
rationales.highYield: A-T: 2 H-bonds. G-C: 3 H-bonds. More G-C content = higher DNA melting temperature (more H-bonds to break).

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The sugar in DNA differs from the sugar in RNA by:

options.text: Lacking an OH group at the 2' position (deoxy)
Being a ketose instead of an aldose

rationales.whyCorrect: DNA contains 2'-deoxyribose (H at 2' instead of OH). RNA contains ribose (OH at 2'). This single difference makes DNA more chemically stable (less susceptible to hydrolysis), which is critical for long-term genetic storage. Option A is false. Options C and D are incorrect.
rationales.eli10: DNA and RNA differ by a single oxygen atom at the 2' position of the sugar — DNA is "deoxy" (missing an O). It is like DNA wearing a protective helmet (H instead of OH), making it less likely to get chemically "hit" and break. RNA's exposed OH makes it more reactive and shorter-lived — perfect for temporary messages, while DNA is the permanent archive.
rationales.highYield: DNA = deoxyribose (H at 2'). RNA = ribose (OH at 2'). The missing OH makes DNA more stable.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Phospholipids spontaneously form bilayers in water because:

options.text: They are amphipathic — hydrophilic heads face water, hydrophobic tails avoid water
They form covalent bonds with water molecules

rationales.whyCorrect: Phospholipids have a polar (charged) head and two nonpolar fatty acid tails. In water, the tails cluster together away from water while heads face outward — this is the thermodynamically favored arrangement and the basis of all cell membranes. Options A and B are false. Option D is incorrect.
rationales.eli10: Phospholipids are like matches with a water-loving head and two water-hating tails. Throw thousands of them into water, and they automatically arrange into a double layer — tails tucked inside away from water, heads facing out. This is exactly how every cell membrane in your body is built. It happens spontaneously, like oil droplets forming in water, because the tails desperately want to escape the water.
rationales.highYield: Phospholipid bilayer: heads out (hydrophilic), tails in (hydrophobic). Driven by the hydrophobic effect, not covalent bonding.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Cooking an egg white causes the proteins to denature. This primarily disrupts:

options.text: The non-covalent interactions maintaining higher-order structure

rationales.whyCorrect: Denaturation disrupts hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, ionic bonds, and disulfide bridges (if reduced) that maintain secondary, tertiary, and quaternary structure. The primary structure (peptide bonds) remains intact. Option A is false — the sequence is unchanged. Option C is false — peptide bonds are not broken by heat alone.
rationales.eli10: Cooking an egg is like unraveling a carefully folded origami sculpture. The paper (amino acid chain) is still the same, but all the intricate folds (secondary and tertiary structure) come undone. The peptide bonds holding the chain together survive — you would need much harsher conditions to break those. The white goes from clear and runny to white and solid because the unraveled chains tangle together randomly like spaghetti.
rationales.highYield: Denaturation: loss of 2°/3°/4° structure without breaking peptide bonds. Caused by heat, pH extremes, organic solvents, heavy metals.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A nucleotide consists of:

rationales.whyCorrect: A nucleotide (monomer of nucleic acids) has three components: a nitrogenous base (A, G, C, T, or U), a 5-carbon sugar (ribose or deoxyribose), and one or more phosphate groups. Option A describes a modified amino acid. Option C describes a phospholipid. Option D is incomplete.
rationales.eli10: A nucleotide is like a three-piece puzzle: a flat information tag (the base, like A, T, G, or C), a sugar connector, and a phosphate linker. The bases carry the genetic code, the sugars form the backbone handrail, and the phosphates link everything together like zip ties. ATP is a special nucleotide that carries three phosphates like a loaded spring — snap one off and energy is released to power cellular work.
rationales.highYield: Nucleotide = base + sugar + phosphate. Nucleoside = base + sugar (no phosphate). ATP is a nucleotide with three phosphates.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which alkali metal reacts most vigorously with water?

rationales.whyCorrect: Alkali metal reactivity increases down the group as atomic radius increases and ionization energy decreases. The valence electron is held more loosely and is more easily lost. Cs, at the bottom of Group 1, is the most reactive — it explodes on contact with water. Li, Na, and K are progressively less reactive.
rationales.eli10: Alkali metals are like people who desperately want to get rid of their one extra dollar (electron). As you go down the group, the dollar gets farther from the body (larger atom), making it easier to hand off. Cesium at the bottom practically throws its electron at water, creating an explosion. Lithium at the top holds on tighter and reacts more calmly.
rationales.highYield: Group 1 reactivity: Cs > Rb > K > Na > Li. Larger atom → lower IE → higher reactivity.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which noble gas is known to form stable compounds with fluorine?

rationales.whyCorrect: Xenon's large size and relatively low ionization energy allow highly electronegative fluorine to pull electrons away, forming compounds like XeF2, XeF4, and XeF6. He, Ne, and Ar have no known neutral compounds — their ionization energies are too high and their atoms are too small.
rationales.eli10: Noble gases were long thought to be complete hermits, refusing all social contact. Xenon, the biggest and most easygoing of the stable noble gases, was the first to be coaxed into a compound. Fluorine, the most aggressive element, can grab xenon's electrons because xenon's outer electrons are far from the nucleus and held loosely enough to be tugged away.
rationales.highYield: Xenon forms compounds with highly electronegative elements (F, O). Heavier noble gases are more reactive due to lower IE and larger size.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which oxide is amphoteric?

rationales.whyCorrect: Al2O3 reacts with both acids and bases: with acid (Al2O3 + 6HCl → 2AlCl3 + 3H2O) and with base (Al2O3 + 2NaOH + 3H2O → 2Na[Al(OH)4]). Na2O is basic. MgO is basic. SO3 is acidic.
rationales.eli10: Aluminum oxide is a fence-sitter — it reacts with both acids and bases like a bilingual person who can talk to either side. Metal oxides (like sodium oxide) are basic — they party with acids. Nonmetal oxides (like sulfur trioxide) are acidic — they party with bases. Aluminum oxide is the rare molecule that goes to both parties and fits in equally well.
rationales.highYield: Metal oxides → basic. Nonmetal oxides → acidic. Metalloid/amphoteric metal oxides (Al2O3, ZnO, SnO) → amphoteric.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which halogen is the strongest oxidizing agent?

rationales.whyCorrect: Fluorine is the most electronegative element and the strongest oxidizing agent. Halogen oxidizing power decreases down the group: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2. Fluorine's small size and high electronegativity make it extremely eager to gain an electron.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Lithium shows chemical similarities to which Group 2 element?

rationales.whyCorrect: Li and Mg exhibit a diagonal relationship due to similar charge-to-size ratios (ionic potential). Both form nitrides (Li3N, Mg3N2), have similar solubilities of carbonates and phosphates, and form organometallic compounds. Be is similar to Al. Other diagonal pairs: Be-Al, B-Si.
rationales.eli10: Diagonal relationships are like unlikely friendships across the periodic table. Lithium (Group 1) acts more like magnesium (Group 2) than like sodium (its own group). It is like a short basketball player who relates better to tall soccer players than to other short basketball players. The reason: Li+ and Mg2+ have similar charge density — Li is small with a +1 charge, Mg is bigger with a +2 charge, and the ratio ends up being about the same.
rationales.highYield: Diagonal relationships: Li-Mg, Be-Al, B-Si. Result from similar charge density (charge/radius ratio).

subjectWideQuestions.stem: CO2 dissolves in water to form:

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The chlor-alkali process produces which three products?

rationales.whyCorrect: Electrolysis of aqueous NaCl: anode (2Cl^- → Cl2 + 2e^-), cathode (2H2O + 2e^- → H2 + 2OH^-). Overall: 2NaCl + 2H2O → Cl2 + H2 + 2NaOH. All three products are industrially valuable.
rationales.eli10: The chlor-alkali process is like splitting salt water with electricity into three valuable products. It is one of the most important industrial electrochemical processes.
rationales.highYield: Chlor-alkali: 2NaCl + 2H2O → Cl2 (anode) + H2 (cathode) + 2NaOH. Drives the production of PVC, paper, and water treatment.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the maximum oxidation state of sulfur?

rationales.whyCorrect: Sulfur is in Group 16 with 6 valence electrons. Its maximum oxidation state is +6 (as in H2SO4, SF6). The maximum oxidation state for main-group elements equals the group number. Option D (+8) is impossible for sulfur. Options A and B are lower oxidation states that sulfur can adopt.
rationales.eli10: The maximum oxidation state is like the most money an atom can spend. Sulfur (Group 16) can give away up to 6 electrons — it empties its entire outer wallet. That is +6, as in sulfuric acid (H2SO4) where sulfur has given all 6 valence electrons to oxygen. Sulfur can also be stingier — +4 in SO2 or -2 in H2S where it gains electrons instead.
rationales.highYield: Max oxidation state = group number for main-group elements. S (+6), Cl (+7), N (+5), C (+4).

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Hydrogen is placed in Group 1 but is not considered an alkali metal because:

options.text: It is a nonmetal that shares electrons rather than losing them
It is a liquid at room temperature
It has a higher atomic mass than lithium

rationales.whyCorrect: Although hydrogen has one valence electron like alkali metals, it behaves as a nonmetal — it shares electrons in covalent bonds (H2, CH4, H2O) rather than losing its electron to form H+ in condensed phases. H+ exists only as a bare proton, unlike M+ alkali cations. Options A, C, and D are factually incorrect.
rationales.eli10: Hydrogen is the periodic table's maverick — it sits in Group 1 because it has one electron, but it acts nothing like lithium or sodium. Instead of giving its electron away like metals do, hydrogen shares it, forming partnerships with almost every other nonmetal. It is like the only vegetarian at a table of meat-eaters — same number of dinner guests (electrons), completely different diet (bonding behavior).
rationales.highYield: Hydrogen is unique: can form H+ (acid), H^- (hydride), or covalent bonds. Placed in Group 1 for electronic configuration but chemically distinct.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Sodium oxide (Na2O) dissolves in water to form:

rationales.whyCorrect: Na2O(s) + H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq). Metal oxides are basic anhydrides — they react with water to form metal hydroxides (bases). This is the opposite of nonmetal oxides, which form acids.
rationales.eli10: Sodium oxide in water is like dropping an alkaline tablet into a glass — it dissolves and makes the solution basic. Metal oxides are the chemical opposite of nonmetal oxides: one makes bases, the other makes acids. This is why the oxides across a period go from strongly basic (Na2O) to amphoteric (Al2O3) to strongly acidic (SO3, Cl2O7) — a smooth transition reflecting the metallic-to-nonmetallic character.
rationales.highYield: Na2O + H2O → 2NaOH (basic). SO3 + H2O → H2SO4 (acidic). Metal oxide → base; nonmetal oxide → acid.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which element exhibits the widest range of oxidation states?

rationales.whyCorrect: Manganese exhibits oxidation states from +2 to +7: MnO (Mn2+), Mn2O3 (Mn3+), MnO2 (Mn4+), K2MnO4 (Mn6+), KMnO4 (Mn7+). This is the widest range among first-row transition metals. Fe shows +2 and +3 (and rarely +6). Cu shows +1 and +2. Zn shows only +2 (d^10 configuration).
rationales.eli10: Manganese is like a performer who can wear seven different hats — it can lose anywhere from 2 to 7 electrons, each giving it a different color and personality. Mn2+ is pale pink, MnO2 is brown-black, MnO4^- (permanganate) is deep purple. No other transition metal has this many costume changes. The secret is manganese's half-filled 3d^5 arrangement, which makes losing different numbers of electrons energetically feasible.
rationales.highYield: Mn has the widest oxidation state range (+2 to +7) due to its 3d^5 4s^2 configuration that allows progressive loss of d electrons.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which of the following is NOT considered a transition metal by the IUPAC definition?

rationales.whyCorrect: IUPAC defines a transition metal as an element whose atom has a partially filled d subshell, or which can give rise to cations with an incomplete d subshell. Zn has configuration [Ar] 3d^10 — completely filled d orbitals — and only forms Zn2+ (still d^10). Fe (3d^6), Cu (3d^10 4s^1, but Cu2+ is 3d^9), and Co (3d^7) all have or can form incomplete d subshells.
rationales.eli10: Zinc is like someone who bought a ticket to the transition metal party but sits in the corner with a full dance card. It has a complete set of d electrons (d^10) and refuses to give any up beyond its two s electrons. No colorful compounds, no multiple oxidation states, no catalytic magic. True transition metals like iron and copper have partially empty d orbitals — like having empty seats at the table for new guests (electrons) to arrive or leave.
rationales.highYield: Zn, Cd, Hg are d-block but NOT transition metals — they have full d^10 in all common oxidation states. No colored compounds, no variable oxidation states.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The intense purple color of KMnO4 is due to:

rationales.whyCorrect: In MnO4^-, Mn is in the +7 oxidation state (d^0 — no d electrons). Therefore d-d transitions are impossible. The color arises from ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT): an electron from an oxygen p orbital is excited into an empty manganese d orbital. Most intensely colored high-oxidation-state compounds (CrO4^2- yellow, MnO4^- purple) owe their color to charge transfer.
rationales.eli10: Permanganate's stunning purple comes from electrons jumping from oxygen to manganese — like oxygen throwing electrons up to manganese's empty d-orbital balcony. It is not the usual d-d transition (electron gymnastics within the d orbitals) because manganese has zero d electrons to play with in the +7 state. Charge transfer is like an electron commuting from one atom to another rather than just changing seats within the same atom.
rationales.highYield: d-d transitions require partially filled d orbitals. With d^0 or d^10, color (if any) comes from charge transfer.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Stainless steel contains a minimum of approximately what percentage of chromium?

rationales.whyCorrect: Stainless steel requires at least 10.5% Cr by mass. Options A and B are too low to form a continuous protective layer. Option D is too high — typical stainless is 10.5–20% Cr.
rationales.eli10: Stainless steel is like iron wearing an invisible chrome shield. The chromium atoms at the surface react with oxygen to form an incredibly thin, transparent layer of chromium oxide — like a force field only a few atoms thick. If you scratch it, it instantly re-forms. That is why stainless steel does not rust like regular steel — the chrome shield never sleeps.
rationales.highYield: Stainless steel: Fe + Cr (≥10.5%) + Ni (optional). Cr forms a protective Cr2O3 passive layer.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The lanthanide contraction explains why:

options.text: Hafnium has nearly the same atomic radius as zirconium

rationales.whyCorrect: The lanthanide contraction is the steady decrease in atomic/ionic radii across the 4f series (La to Lu) due to poor shielding by 4f electrons. This causes the 5d transition metals (Hf, Ta, etc.) to be nearly the same size as their 4d counterparts (Zr, Nb, etc.). This makes Zr/Hf separation extremely difficult.
rationales.eli10: The lanthanide contraction is like a belt slowly tightening across 14 elements. Even though you add electrons as you cross the lanthanide row, those 4f electrons are terrible at blocking the increasing nuclear pull, so the atoms get squeezed smaller and smaller. By the time you reach hafnium (in the next row), it is almost exactly the same size as zirconium above it — like a taller person who is also thinner, wearing the same size clothes.
rationales.highYield: Lanthanide contraction: 4f electrons shield poorly → steady radius decrease → 5d metals similar in size to 4d metals above them.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Cisplatin, Pt(NH3)2Cl2, is used as:

rationales.whyCorrect: Cisplatin is a square-planar Pt(II) complex that cross-links DNA, preventing cancer cell division. It is one of the most successful metal-based drugs. The cis configuration is essential — the trans isomer is inactive. Option A is the Haber catalyst (Fe). Options C and D are incorrect.
rationales.eli10: Cisplatin is the chemical equivalent of handcuffs for DNA. It enters cancer cells, loses its chloride "leaving groups," and grabs onto two spots on the DNA strand — like a metal clip snapping shut. This prevents the DNA from being copied, so the cancer cell cannot divide and dies. It must be the cis version (both NH3 on the same side) — the trans version is like trying to handcuff someone with your hands on opposite sides of your body.
rationales.highYield: Cisplatin (cis-[Pt(NH3)2Cl2]): square planar Pt(II). Binds to DNA, cross-links strands, inhibits replication. The trans isomer is inactive.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why are many transition metal compounds paramagnetic?

options.text: They have completely filled d orbitals

rationales.whyCorrect: Paramagnetism requires unpaired electrons. Partially filled d orbitals in transition metal compounds often leave unpaired electrons, which align with an external magnetic field. Compounds with all electrons paired (d^0, low-spin d^6, d^10) are diamagnetic.
rationales.eli10: Paramagnetism is like having tiny compass needles inside a material. Each unpaired electron acts as a microscopic magnet. When enough of them align, the whole compound is attracted to a big magnet. Transition metal compounds often have unpaired d electrons — like iron in hemoglobin or the manganese in permanganate — making them magnetic. Fully paired compounds (like Zn2+ with d^10) are diamagnetic and ignore magnets completely.
rationales.highYield: Paramagnetic = unpaired electrons (attracted to magnet). Diamagnetic = all paired (weakly repelled). Hund's rule maximizes unpaired electrons in high-spin complexes.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Brass is an alloy of copper with:

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Fe2+ compounds are typically pale green while Fe3+ compounds are yellow-brown because:

options.text: The different d-electron counts produce different d-d transition energies

rationales.whyCorrect: Fe2+ is d^6, Fe3+ is d^5. Different d^n configurations have different energy level schemes, absorbing different wavelengths of light. The complementary transmitted color differs. Fe2+(aq) absorbs in the red and appears green; Fe3+(aq) absorbs in the blue and appears yellow-brown.
rationales.eli10: The color difference between Fe2+ (pale green) and Fe3+ (rusty brown) is like two musicians playing different notes on the same instrument. Both are iron, but one has lost 2 electrons, the other 3. The remaining d electrons absorb different colors of light because the energy gaps between their d-orbital levels are different. It is the same reason green plants and red flowers absorb different light — the electron arrangements differ.
rationales.highYield: d^n configuration determines d-d splitting pattern and thus color. Same metal, different oxidation state = different color.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In the extraction of iron from Fe2O3 in a blast furnace, the reducing agent is:

rationales.whyCorrect: In the blast furnace, coke (C) is oxidized to CO, which then reduces Fe2O3: Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2. CO is the actual reducing agent that strips oxygen from the iron ore. CaCO3 (limestone) is a flux that removes silica impurities as slag. SiO2 is an impurity.
rationales.eli10: Making iron from rust is like using carbon monoxide as a chemical crowbar to pry oxygen atoms off the iron. Coke (coal baked without air) burns partially to CO gas, which rises through the furnace and grabs oxygen from the iron ore, turning it into CO2 and leaving behind molten iron. The limestone acts like a sponge, soaking up sandy impurities to form slag that floats on the liquid iron and can be skimmed off.
rationales.highYield: Blast furnace: C + O2 → CO2; CO2 + C → 2CO; Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2. CO does the reduction, not C directly.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which cubic unit cell has atoms at all 8 corners and one atom at the center?

rationales.whyCorrect: BCC has atoms at 8 corners (each 1/8 contributes to the cell = 1) plus one full atom at the center = 2 atoms total per unit cell. Simple cubic has only corners (1 atom/cell). FCC has corners plus face centers (4 atoms/cell). HCP is not cubic.
rationales.eli10: Unit cells are like the smallest Lego block that repeats to build the whole crystal. Simple cubic is a cube with atoms only at the corners — like dice with dots only on the corners. BCC has one bonus atom in the middle — like a die with a dot in the exact center. FCC has atoms at corners AND in the center of every face — the most efficiently packed cube, like oranges stacked at a grocery store.
rationales.highYield: Simple cubic: 1 atom/cell, 52% PE. BCC: 2 atoms/cell, 68% PE. FCC: 4 atoms/cell, 74% PE. HCP also 74% PE.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the packing efficiency of a face-centered cubic structure?

rationales.whyCorrect: FCC and HCP are the closest-packed structures with 74% of volume occupied by spheres. The remaining 26% is interstitial void space. Simple cubic is 52%. BCC is 68%. 100% is impossible for equal spheres.
rationales.eli10: Packing efficiency is like how tightly you can pack oranges in a box. No matter how cleverly you arrange them, 26% of the box is always empty space — gaps between the round oranges. FCC and HCP (74% full) are mathematically proven to be the best possible packing of equal spheres. It is like the Kepler conjecture — grocery store stacking is optimal.
rationales.highYield: FCC = HCP = 74%. These are the maximum packing efficiencies for equal spheres — mathematically proven.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In a metallic conductor, electrical conductivity is possible because:

options.text: The valence band and conduction band are separated by a large gap
The valence band and conduction band overlap or the conduction band is partially filled
Electrons are localized on individual atoms
There are no electrons in the conduction band

rationales.whyCorrect: In metals, there is no band gap — the valence and conduction bands overlap, allowing electrons to move freely under an applied electric field. In semiconductors, a small gap (~1 eV) allows thermal excitation. In insulators, a large gap (>5 eV) prevents conduction.
rationales.eli10: Band theory is like a parking garage. In metals, the top occupied floor spills directly into the next building — electrons can drive freely between them (conduct electricity). In semiconductors, there is a small gap between floors — only energetic electrons can jump across. In insulators, the gap is enormous — no electron can make the leap. Silicon's small gap makes it perfect for computer chips; diamond's huge gap makes it just a pretty insulator.
rationales.highYield: Conductors: bands overlap or partially filled. Semiconductors: small gap (~1 eV). Insulators: large gap (~5+ eV).

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Silicon doped with phosphorus produces an n-type semiconductor because:

options.text: Phosphorus has one more valence electron than silicon, providing extra electrons

rationales.whyCorrect: Si has 4 valence electrons; P has 5. When P substitutes for Si in the lattice, the extra electron occupies a donor level just below the conduction band and is easily excited — n-type (negative charge carriers). Option A describes p-type doping (e.g., B in Si with only 3 valence electrons).
rationales.eli10: Doping silicon is like adding a few special atoms to a plain cookie recipe. Phosphorus brings 5 electrons instead of silicon's 4 — the extra electron is like a free chocolate chip that pops out easily and moves around. That is n-type ("n" for negative charge carriers). Boron brings only 3 electrons, leaving a hole where an electron should be — like a missing chocolate chip that neighboring electrons rush to fill. That is p-type ("p" for positive holes).
rationales.highYield: n-type: dopant with extra valence e- (P, As in Si). p-type: dopant with fewer valence e- (B, Ga in Si).

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Polyethylene is classified as an addition polymer because:

options.text: It is formed by eliminating a small molecule
The monomer contains a C=C bond and no small molecule is eliminated
It is formed from two different monomers

rationales.whyCorrect: Addition polymerization: monomers with C=C double bonds (ethylene, CH2=CH2) add to a growing chain without eliminating any atoms. rationales.eli10: Addition polymerization is like linking paperclips — each new clip just snaps onto the end of the chain without losing anything. Polyethylene is just thousands of ethylene molecules linked in a long chain with exactly the same atoms. Condensation polymerization is like linking two different puzzle pieces — each connection kicks out a water molecule as waste. Nylon is a condensation polymer; plastic bags are addition polymers.
rationales.highYield: Addition: monomer has C=C, no byproduct. Condensation: two functional groups react, small molecule eliminated.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which statement about thermoplastics is true?

options.text: They soften when heated and can be reshaped

rationales.whyCorrect: Thermoplastics (polyethylene, polystyrene, PVC) consist of linear or branched chains with no cross-linking. Weak intermolecular forces allow chains to slide when heated, so they melt and can be remolded. Thermosets (epoxy, vulcanized rubber) have covalent cross-links and decompose before melting.
rationales.eli10: Thermoplastics are like spaghetti — heat them and the noodles slide apart (melt), cool them and they lock in a new shape. You can reheat and reshape spaghetti endlessly. Thermosets are like a waffle — once the batter is cooked and cross-linked, you can never turn it back into batter. Reheating just burns it. That is why plastic bottles (thermoplastic) are recyclable but epoxy glue (thermoset) is permanent.
rationales.highYield: Thermoplastic: no cross-links, melts on heating, recyclable. Thermoset: cross-linked, decomposes on heating, not remoldable.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Ionic solids are typically brittle because:

options.text: They have strong covalent bonds throughout
Displacing a layer aligns like charges, causing repulsion and fracture
They have free electrons that weaken the structure

rationales.whyCorrect: In an ionic crystal, cations and anions alternate. If you strike it and displace one layer, like charges become adjacent (+ next to + and - next to -), and the electrostatic repulsion shatters the crystal. Metals are malleable because the electron sea allows atoms to slide without breaking bonds.
rationales.eli10: An ionic crystal is like a perfectly alternating checkerboard of positive and negative pieces. Hit it hard and one row shifts — suddenly two positive pieces sit next to each other. They repel violently and the whole board shatters. A metal is like a board where all pieces float in a pool of electrons — you can push rows around and they just slide without any same-type pieces touching.
rationales.highYield: Ionic solids are brittle — like charges repel when layers shift. Metals are malleable — electron sea allows atoms to slide.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon but have vastly different properties because:

options.text: Diamond is sp2 hybridized; graphite is sp3
They are allotropes with different bonding arrangements (sp3 vs sp2)

rationales.whyCorrect: Diamond is sp3 hybridized — each carbon bonded tetrahedrally to 4 others, forming a rigid 3D covalent network (hardest natural substance). Graphite is sp2 hybridized — carbons form hexagonal sheets with delocalized electrons between layers, allowing layers to slide (soft, conductive). Same element, different bonding → different properties.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: As temperature increases, the conductivity of a semiconductor:

options.text: Increases (more electrons excited across the band gap)

rationales.whyCorrect: In semiconductors, thermal energy excites electrons from the valence band to the conduction band, creating electron-hole pairs. rationales.eli10: Heating a semiconductor is like turning up the energy at a party — more people (electrons) get excited enough to jump from the seated area (valence band) to the dance floor (conduction band). rationales.highYield: Semiconductor: conductivity increases with T (more carriers). Metal: conductivity decreases with T (more scattering).

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An elastomer (like rubber) can stretch and return to its original shape because:

options.text: It has extensive cross-linking like a thermoset
It has light cross-linking that prevents permanent chain slippage while allowing extension
The polymer chains are rigid rods

rationales.whyCorrect: Elastomers have occasional cross-links between polymer chains. These links prevent chains from sliding past each other permanently (thermoplastic behavior) but are sparse enough to allow large extensions. When released, entropy drives the chains back to their coiled state. Thermosets have extensive cross-linking (rigid); thermoplastics have none.
rationales.eli10: Rubber is like a net made of loose springs. The cross-links are knots that prevent the springs from completely separating, but there are only a few knots, so the net can stretch way out. When you let go, the springs coil back up. Vulcanized rubber (Charles Goodyear's discovery) adds just enough sulfur cross-links to give bounce without making the material rigid like hard plastic.
rationales.highYield: Elastomer: light cross-linking → stretches and recovers. Thermoset: heavy cross-linking → rigid. Thermoplastic: no cross-links → permanent deformation.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Ceramics are typically:

options.text: Hard, brittle, and resistant to high temperatures

rationales.whyCorrect: Ceramics (e.g., Al2O3, SiC, porcelain) are ionic or covalent network compounds. Strong directional bonds make them hard and high-melting but also brittle. They are electrical and thermal insulators. Option A describes metals. Options C and D describe some polymers.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Ground-level (tropospheric) ozone is considered:

A pollutant that causes respiratory problems

A natural component of clean air at high concentrations

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which is NOT a significant greenhouse gas?

rationales.whyCorrect: N2 has no dipole moment and cannot absorb infrared radiation — it is transparent to IR. CO2, CH4, and H2O all absorb IR due to their vibrational modes (CO2 bending, CH4 and H2O stretching/bending). N2 and O2 together make up 99% of the atmosphere but are not greenhouse gases.
rationales.eli10: Greenhouse gases are like heat-trapping blankets. CO2, methane, and water vapor can absorb the Earth's outgoing heat radiation because their bonds can vibrate in ways that create a temporary electric imbalance. Nitrogen and oxygen — despite making up 99% of the air — are symmetric molecules that are invisible to infrared radiation. They are like clear glass windows that let heat pass right through.
rationales.highYield: Greenhouse gases must be IR-active (dipole moment change during vibration). N2 and O2 (homonuclear diatomics) are IR-inactive.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: CFCs deplete stratospheric ozone because:

options.text: UV light breaks CFC bonds, releasing chlorine atoms that catalyze O3 destruction
They absorb UV that would otherwise form ozone
They react with N2 to form NOx

rationales.whyCorrect: CFCs are stable in the troposphere but photolyze in the stratosphere: CCl2F2 + UV → Cl + CClF2. The Cl atom catalyzes: Cl + O3 → ClO + O2; ClO + O → Cl + O2. Net: O3 + O → 2O2. One Cl atom can destroy ~100,000 O3 molecules before being deactivated.
rationales.eli10: CFCs are like molecular time bombs. They float harmlessly for years until they drift up to the stratosphere, where UV light snaps them open, releasing chlorine atoms. Each chlorine atom becomes a serial ozone killer — it destroys one ozone molecule, gets regenerated, and attacks again, up to 100,000 times. It is like a single vandal with a key that keeps letting them back into the building after each act of destruction.
rationales.highYield: Cl atom is a catalyst for O3 destruction: Cl + O3 → ClO + O2; ClO + O → Cl + O2. Net: O3 + O → 2O2.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Unpolluted rain has a pH of approximately 5.6 because:

rationales.whyCorrect: Atmospheric CO2 (~0.04%) dissolves in rainwater: CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3^-. This equilibrium gives clean rain a pH of ~5.6. Acid rain is defined as rain with pH below 5.6, caused by anthropogenic SO2 and NOx. Option A is false — pure water is pH 7.00.
rationales.eli10: Even the cleanest rain is slightly acidic — like water with a tiny squeeze of invisible lemon. The "lemon" is carbon dioxide from the air, which dissolves into raindrops and forms weak carbonic acid. This is natural and harmless at pH 5.6. Acid rain (from power plant SO2 and car NOx) drops the pH below 5, making the rain as acidic as vinegar or lemon juice, which can kill fish and erode stone buildings.
rationales.highYield: Clean rain pH ≈ 5.6 (CO2 + H2O → H2CO3). Acid rain: pH < 5.6 from H2SO4 (SO2) and HNO3 (NOx).

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which two primary pollutants react in sunlight to form photochemical smog?

rationales.whyCorrect: Photochemical smog forms when NOx (from vehicle exhaust) and VOCs (from gasoline, solvents) react in sunlight: NO2 + UV → NO + O; O + O2 → O3 (ground-level); VOCs produce peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN) and aldehydes. rationales.eli10: Photochemical smog is like a chemical soup cooked by sunlight. Car exhaust provides the main ingredients — nitrogen oxides and unburned fuel vapors. Sunlight is the stove, and the cooking produces ozone, eye-stinging PAN, and lung-irritating aldehydes. The brown haze over cities on hot sunny days is this soup, with NO2 giving it the dirty-brown color. This is why "ozone action days" warn people to stay indoors.
rationales.highYield: Photochemical smog = NOx + VOCs + sunlight → O3 + PAN + aldehydes. Brown color from NO2.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Temporary hard water contains which ions that can be removed by boiling?

rationales.whyCorrect: Temporary hardness is caused by Ca(HCO3)2 and Mg(HCO3)2. Boiling precipitates the carbonates: Ca(HCO3)2 → CaCO3(s) + H2O + CO2 (the scale in kettles). Permanent hardness (CaSO4, MgCl2) cannot be removed by boiling and requires ion exchange or chemical softening.
rationales.eli10: Temporary hard water is like water with dissolved invisible chalk. When you boil it, the chalk reappears as solid white scale in your kettle — the bicarbonate ions break down, releasing CO2 and leaving behind solid calcium carbonate. Permanent hardness is like dissolved gypsum that boiling cannot remove — you need a water softener that swaps the troublesome calcium for sodium.
rationales.highYield: Temporary hardness: Ca(HCO3)2/Mg(HCO3)2 — removed by boiling. Permanent hardness: CaSO4/MgCl2 — requires ion exchange.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The greenhouse effect warms Earth because:

options.text: Greenhouse gases reflect visible sunlight back to space
Earth's surface absorbs visible light and re-emits IR, which greenhouse gases absorb and re-radiate
Greenhouse gases generate heat through chemical reactions
The ozone hole allows more UV to reach the surface

rationales.whyCorrect: Solar radiation (mostly visible) passes through the atmosphere and warms Earth's surface. The surface re-emits energy as infrared (IR). Greenhouse gas molecules absorb this IR and re-emit it in all directions, including back toward the surface — trapping heat. Without this natural effect, Earth's average T would be -18 °C.
rationales.eli10: The greenhouse effect is like a car parked in the sun. Sunlight shines through the windows (atmosphere), heating the seats (Earth's surface). The hot seats emit infrared radiation, but the windows (greenhouse gases) trap some of it, making the car hotter than outside. Without any greenhouse gases, Earth would be a frozen ice ball. The problem is that adding extra CO2 is like adding extra layers of glass — the car gets dangerously hot.
rationales.highYield: Greenhouse effect: sunlight (visible) in → surface heats → IR out → absorbed by GHGs → re-radiated back. Natural effect is essential; enhanced effect is problematic.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) measures:

options.text: The amount of oxygen dissolved in water
The amount of oxygen consumed by microorganisms decomposing organic matter
The amount of oxygen produced by aquatic plants

rationales.whyCorrect: BOD is a measure of organic pollution. High BOD means lots of organic waste that bacteria will decompose, consuming dissolved oxygen and potentially causing fish kills. Clean water has low BOD; sewage-contaminated water has high BOD.
rationales.eli10: BOD is like measuring how much of a mess bacteria need to clean up. Raw sewage dumped in a river is a huge meal for bacteria — they feast on it and use up all the dissolved oxygen in the process, suffocating fish. A low BOD means the water is clean with little for bacteria to eat. It is like measuring how much food is on the floor of a kitchen — more food means more work for the cleaning crew, consuming more "cleaning oxygen."
rationales.highYield: BOD = oxygen consumed by microbial decomposition of organic matter. High BOD → low DO → fish kills.

options.text: Marble (CaCO3) reacts with acid, dissolving the stone
Acid rain freezes inside cracks and expands
The acid dyes the marble yellow

rationales.whyCorrect: CaCO3(s) + H2SO4(aq) → CaSO4(s) + H2O(l) + CO2(g). Marble and limestone (both CaCO3) are slowly eaten away by acid rain. The gypsum (CaSO4) that forms is more soluble and washes away. This is why ancient marble statues and buildings have eroded features.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The ozone layer is located in which atmospheric layer?

rationales.whyCorrect: The ozone layer resides in the stratosphere (12–50 km altitude), where O3 concentrations peak at ~10 ppm. UV absorption by O3 causes the stratosphere to warm with altitude (temperature inversion), making it stable — which is why pollutants that reach the stratosphere stay there for years.
rationales.eli10: The stratosphere is like Earth's sunscreen shelf — it sits 12 to 50 kilometers up and holds the ozone that blocks UV. Unlike the mixed-up troposphere below (where weather churns everything), the stratosphere is eerily stable — warmer air sits on top of cooler air, so things do not mix vertically. That is why CFCs, once they reach the stratosphere, stay there for decades, slowly eating away at the ozone.
rationales.highYield: Stratosphere = "ozone layer" (12–50 km). Temperature increases with altitude due to UV absorption by O3.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Aluminum sulfate is added during water treatment to:

options.text: Form flocs that trap suspended particles for removal

rationales.whyCorrect: Al2(SO4)3 hydrolyzes to form Al(OH)3, a gelatinous precipitate. The sticky Al(OH)3 flocs trap suspended solids, bacteria, and colloidal particles as they settle — this is coagulation/flocculation. It is a physical removal step before filtration. Disinfection (chlorine) comes later.
rationales.eli10: Aluminum sulfate in water treatment is like adding a snowball starter. It forms fluffy, sticky globs of aluminum hydroxide that roll through the water, picking up dirt, bacteria, and tiny suspended particles like a snowball growing as it rolls downhill. These heavy flocs settle to the bottom of sedimentation tanks, taking the trapped gunk with them. After filtering out the remaining flocs, the water looks crystal clear — but still needs chlorine to kill any remaining germs.
rationales.highYield: Coagulation: Al2(SO4)3 → Al(OH)3(s) — sticky flocs trap particles. Followed by sedimentation, filtration, then disinfection.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Enzymes increase reaction rates by:

options.text: Increasing the temperature of the reaction

rationales.whyCorrect: Enzymes stabilize the transition state, lowering Ea without being consumed. They do NOT change ΔG, K_eq, or the equilibrium position — they only affect kinetics. Option A is false — enzymes do not change thermodynamics. Options C and D are incorrect.
rationales.eli10: An enzyme is like a tunnel through a mountain instead of going over the top. The start and end points are the same (same ΔG and K), but the tunnel (enzyme) makes the journey much faster by lowering the highest point you must climb (activation energy). Without enzymes, most reactions in your body would be impossibly slow — digesting a meal would take years instead of hours.
rationales.highYield: Enzymes lower Ea by stabilizing the transition state. They affect rate, not equilibrium (K stays the same).

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A competitive inhibitor affects enzyme kinetics by:

rationales.whyCorrect: A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and binds to the active site, competing for occupancy. More substrate can overcome the inhibition, so V_max (at infinite [S]) is unchanged. But more substrate is needed to reach half V_max, so K_m increases. Option A describes noncompetitive inhibition.
rationales.eli10: A competitive inhibitor is like a decoy key that fits the same lock but does not open the door. It jams the active site, blocking the real substrate. But if you flood the lock with enough real keys (high substrate concentration), some will get through, and the maximum speed (V_max) stays the same. You just need more substrate to reach it — that is why K_m goes up.
rationales.highYield: Competitive: K_m up, V_max same. Noncompetitive: V_max down, K_m same. Uncompetitive: both down.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: ATP is considered the energy currency of the cell because:

options.text: Hydrolysis of its phosphoanhydride bonds releases energy that drives unfavorable reactions
It is the only molecule that can cross cell membranes
It is the most abundant molecule in cells

rationales.whyCorrect: ATP → ADP + Pi releases ~30.5 kJ/mol under standard conditions (more under cellular conditions). This energy is coupled to drive endergonic processes through phosphorylation — transferring a phosphate group to a reactant. Option A describes DNA. Options C and D are incorrect.
rationales.eli10: ATP is like a rechargeable battery that powers everything in your cells. The last phosphate group is spring-loaded — snap it off and energy bursts out, like a compressed spring releasing. Your body recycles its ATP constantly: you produce and consume roughly your body weight in ATP every day. Each ATP molecule is recharged (ADP → ATP) and discharged (ATP → ADP) thousands of times.
rationales.highYield: ATP hydrolysis: ~30.5 kJ/mol (standard). Coupled to unfavorable reactions through phosphate transfer.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: NAD+ is classified as a:

rationales.whyCorrect: NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) is derived from niacin (vitamin B3). Coenzymes are organic, non-protein molecules that assist enzymes by carrying chemical groups — NAD+ carries hydride (H^-) in redox reactions. Cofactors are typically inorganic (Zn2+, Mg2+, Fe2+). The apoenzyme is the protein alone without its cofactor/coenzyme.
rationales.eli10: NAD+ is like a rechargeable electron taxi. It picks up two electrons and a proton from one reaction (becoming NADH), drives them to another enzyme, and drops them off, then returns empty as NAD+ for another load. It is made from vitamin B3 — which is why you need niacin in your diet. Without it, your electron taxi fleet cannot operate, and your metabolism grinds to a halt.
rationales.highYield: Cofactor = inorganic ion (Zn2+, Mg2+). Coenzyme = organic (NAD+, FAD, CoA, ATP), derived from vitamins.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Catabolism refers to metabolic pathways that:

options.text: Build large molecules from small precursors
Break down large molecules, releasing energy

rationales.whyCorrect: Catabolism = breakdown (energy-releasing, oxidative). Anabolism = synthesis (energy-consuming, reductive). Digestion of food, glycolysis, and fatty acid oxidation are catabolic. Protein synthesis, DNA replication, and glycogen synthesis are anabolic.
rationales.eli10: Catabolism is demolition — your body breaking down the pizza you ate into small pieces (glucose, fatty acids, amino acids) while generating energy (ATP). Anabolism is construction — using those small pieces to build your muscles, enzymes, and cell membranes. You are constantly tearing down and rebuilding yourself, like a city that never stops renovating.
rationales.highYield: Catabolism: breakdown → energy out (ATP, NADH). Anabolism: synthesis → energy in (ATP → ADP, NADPH → NADP+).

subjectWideQuestions.stem: K_m (the Michaelis constant) is:

options.text: The substrate concentration at which the reaction rate is half of V_max
The turnover number of the enzyme

rationales.whyCorrect: K_m = [S] at v = V_max/2. It approximates the enzyme's affinity for substrate — low K_m means high affinity (reaches half V_max at low [S]). K_m is a kinetic parameter, not a binding constant. Option A is V_max. Option C is k_cat.
rationales.eli10: K_m is like measuring how strong a magnet an enzyme is for its substrate. A low K_m means the enzyme grabs its target even at tiny concentrations — like a powerful magnet picking up paperclips from across the room. A high K_m means you need a lot of substrate to get the enzyme working — like a weak magnet that only picks things up when they are practically touching it.
rationales.highYield: K_m = [S] at 1/2 V_max. Low K_m → high affinity. High K_m → low affinity.

subjectWideQuestions.sourceSnapshotMarkdown:

- **A.** The maximum reaction rate
- **B.** The substrate concentration at which the reaction rate is half of V_max

> **High-Yield:** K_m = [S] at 1/2 V_max. Low K_m → high affinity. High K_m → low affinity.

**ELI-10:** K_m is like measuring how strong a magnet an enzyme is for its substrate. A low K_m means the enzyme grabs its target even at tiny concentrations — like a powerful magnet picking up paperclips from across the room. A high K_m means you need a lot of substrate to get the enzyme working — like a weak magnet that only picks things up when they are practically touching it.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Allosteric regulation involves:

options.text: Covalent modification of the active site
Binding of a regulator at a site other than the active site, changing enzyme shape and activity
Competitive binding at the active site

rationales.whyCorrect: Allosteric regulators bind at a site distinct from the active site, inducing a conformational change that alters catalytic activity. This is the basis of feedback inhibition — the end product of a pathway inhibits the first enzyme. Option A describes covalent modification (phosphorylation). Option C describes competitive inhibition.
rationales.eli10: Allosteric regulation is like having a light switch in the hallway that controls the lamp in the bedroom. The regulator binds far from the active site, but its presence twists the enzyme into a different shape — either turning it on or off. This is how your cells avoid wasting energy: when you have enough of product Z, Z binds to the first enzyme in the production line and shuts it down, like a factory stopping when the warehouse is full.
rationales.highYield: Allosteric: regulator binds away from active site, changes shape → changes activity. Can activate or inhibit.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Fatty acid oxidation occurs in the mitochondria while fatty acid synthesis occurs in the cytoplasm because:

options.text: Compartmentalization prevents futile cycling (simultaneous synthesis and degradation)
The enzymes are insoluble in cytoplasm
It is a random evolutionary accident

rationales.whyCorrect: Separating opposing pathways in different organelles prevents them from running simultaneously and wasting energy. If both synthesis and degradation occurred in the same compartment, ATP would be consumed making fatty acids only to be immediately broken down — a futile cycle.
rationales.eli10: Your cells are like a factory with separate rooms for assembly and disassembly. Putting the assembly line (fatty acid synthesis) and the demolition crew (fatty acid oxidation) in the same room would be chaos — they would build and tear down the same molecules simultaneously, wasting energy. Instead, they are in different rooms (organelles), controlled by different signals. It is like keeping the furnace in the basement and the air conditioner on the roof — they should not run at the same time.
rationales.highYield: Organelles separate opposing pathways: FA oxidation (mitochondria) vs FA synthesis (cytoplasm). Prevents futile cycling.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The induced fit model of enzyme action states that:

options.text: The active site is a rigid, pre-shaped pocket
Substrate binding induces a conformational change that optimizes catalysis
The enzyme changes the equilibrium of the reaction
The substrate must be heated to react

rationales.whyCorrect: The induced fit model (Koshland) refines the lock-and-key model: the enzyme is not perfectly complementary to the substrate until binding occurs. The enzyme wraps around the substrate, positioning catalytic groups precisely. This conformational change is essential for catalysis.
rationales.eli10: The induced fit model is like a handshake that tightens. The enzyme's active site starts slightly open, and when the substrate arrives, the enzyme grips tighter, wrapping around the substrate like a glove adjusting to a hand. This grip change positions the catalytic amino acids exactly where they need to be. The old "lock and key" idea was too rigid — enzymes are dynamic, not static.
rationales.highYield: Induced fit: enzyme changes shape upon substrate binding, optimizing catalytic groups. More accurate than rigid lock-and-key.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Insulin promotes:

rationales.whyCorrect: Insulin is released after a meal and signals anabolic processes: glucose uptake into cells, glycogen synthesis (storage), and fat synthesis. Glucagon and epinephrine have the opposite effect — they promote glycogen breakdown and glucose release. This is the fed vs fasting hormonal balance.
rationales.eli10: Insulin is like a "store this now" announcement after a big meal. It knocks on every cell's door saying, "Glucose delivery — open up and store it for later." These two hormones keep your blood sugar in a tight, healthy range.
rationales.highYield: Insulin: fed state → anabolism (glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis). Glucagon: fasting → catabolism (glycogen breakdown, gluconeogenesis).

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Hemoglobin's heme group contains which metal ion cofactor essential for oxygen binding?

rationales.whyCorrect: Heme contains Fe2+ coordinated to four nitrogen atoms of the porphyrin ring. The iron binds O2 reversibly — this is how hemoglobin transports oxygen. Mg2+ is in chlorophyll. Cu2+ is in hemocyanin (some invertebrates). Zn2+ is in carbonic anhydrase and other enzymes.
rationales.eli10: The iron in hemoglobin is like a tiny magnet for oxygen, held in the center of a flat ring called heme. As blood flows through your lungs, each iron grabs an oxygen molecule. In your tissues, the iron lets go, and the oxygen diffuses into your cells. It is a perfect reversible handshake — grab in the lungs, release in the tissues. Carbon monoxide poisoning happens because CO grabs iron 200 times tighter than oxygen and will not let go.
rationales.highYield: Heme: Fe2+ in porphyrin ring, binds O2. Chlorophyll: Mg2+. Vitamin B12: Co2+. Each metal cofactor has a specific role.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In feedback inhibition, the final product of a metabolic pathway:

options.text: Activates the first enzyme of the pathway
Inhibits the first enzyme of the pathway
Becomes the substrate for the next pathway

rationales.whyCorrect: Feedback inhibition is a negative control mechanism: when sufficient product accumulates, it binds to an allosteric site on the first committed enzyme in the pathway, reducing its activity. This prevents overproduction and conserves resources. It is like a thermostat shutting off the furnace when the room is warm enough.
rationales.eli10: Feedback inhibition is like a thermostat for your metabolism. When the room is warm enough (enough product has been made), the thermostat sends a signal to shut off the furnace (inhibit the first enzyme). When the room cools down (product is used up), the furnace turns back on. This elegant system prevents your cells from wasting energy making products they already have enough of — like a factory that stops production when the warehouse is full.

subjectWideQuestions.sourceSnapshotMarkdown:
### Q15-12 Feedback inhibition

In feedback inhibition, the final product of a metabolic pathway:

- **A.** Activates the first enzyme of the pathway
- **B.** Inhibits the first enzyme of the pathway
- **C.** Is excreted from the cell
- **D.** Becomes the substrate for the next pathway

When the room cools down (product is used up), the furnace turns back on. This elegant system prevents your cells from wasting energy making products they already have enough of — like a factory that stops production when the warehouse is full.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In an IR spectrum, a strong peak at approximately 1700 cm^-1 indicates the presence of:

rationales.whyCorrect: C=O stretching appears as a strong, sharp peak at ~1680–1750 cm^-1. O-H is a broad peak at ~3200–3600. C=C is at ~1600–1680. C-H stretches are at ~2850–3000. The carbonyl peak is one of the most distinctive and useful in IR spectroscopy.
rationales.eli10: The carbonyl peak at 1700 is like the bass drum in a rock band — loud, unmistakable, and hard to miss. If your IR spectrum has a strong sharp peak near 1700, you almost certainly have a carbonyl group (aldehyde, ketone, acid, ester, or amide). An OH peak is different — it is broad and rounded, like a foghorn, because OH groups form hydrogen bonds of varying strengths.
rationales.highYield: IR key peaks: C=O ~1700 (sharp, strong), O-H ~3300 (broad), C=C ~1650, C-H ~2900.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In ^1H NMR, a proton with two equivalent neighboring protons will appear as:

rationales.whyCorrect: The n+1 rule: a proton with n equivalent neighbors splits into n+1 peaks. Two neighbors → 2+1 = 3 (triplet). One neighbor → doublet. Three neighbors → quartet. Zero neighbors → singlet. The relative intensities follow Pascal's triangle: triplet = 1:2:1.
rationales.eli10: NMR splitting is like a proton's neighbors raising their hands to vote. Each neighbor can be spin-up or spin-down. With two neighbors, there are three possible vote totals (both up, one up one down, both down), creating a triplet with intensities 1:2:1. It is like two coin flips — you can get HH, HT/TH, or TT. The middle result is twice as likely.
rationales.highYield: n+1 rule: splitting multiplicity = number of equivalent neighboring protons + 1. Intensities follow Pascal's triangle.

- **D.** A quartet (4 peaks)

The middle result is twice as likely.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In mass spectrometry, the peak at the highest m/z value (excluding isotope peaks) represents:

rationales.whyCorrect: The molecular ion peak (M+) corresponds to the intact molecule with one electron removed. Its m/z value gives the molecular mass of the compound. The base peak is the tallest peak (set to 100%). Fragments appear at lower m/z.
rationales.eli10: The molecular ion peak is like weighing the whole intact molecule before it shatters. It is the heaviest piece in the spectrum (the parent ion) and tells you the molecular weight directly. As the molecule flies through the mass spectrometer, most of them break into fragments — those appear as smaller peaks. The tallest peak (base peak) is the most common fragment, like the most common piece after smashing a vase.
rationales.highYield: Molecular ion M+ = highest m/z (intact molecule). Base peak = most intense (100%). Fragments at lower m/z from bond cleavage.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In gas chromatography, components are separated based primarily on differences in:

options.text: Boiling point and polarity (partitioning between mobile and stationary phases)

rationales.whyCorrect: GC separates volatile compounds based on their partitioning between the gaseous mobile phase (carrier gas) and the liquid/solid stationary phase in the column. More volatile (lower bp) compounds spend more time in the gas phase and elute faster. Polar compounds interact more with polar stationary phases.
rationales.eli10: Gas chromatography is like a race through a long, narrow tunnel with sticky walls. The runners (sample molecules) are pushed by a carrier gas wind. Small, light runners that do not stick to the walls race through quickly. Heavy, sticky runners lag behind. Each crosses the finish line at a different time, producing separate peaks on the detector. This is how scientists separate complex mixtures like gasoline into individual components.
rationales.highYield: GC: separation by volatility (bp) and polarity. Mobile phase = inert carrier gas. Stationary phase = liquid coating or solid.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In reverse-phase HPLC, the stationary phase is typically:

rationales.whyCorrect: Reverse-phase HPLC uses a nonpolar stationary phase (C18 chains bonded to silica) and a polar mobile phase (water/acetonitrile or water/methanol). Nonpolar analytes stick to the column and elute later; polar analytes elute early. This is the most common HPLC mode.
rationales.eli10: Reverse-phase HPLC is like a car wash with greasy walls. Polar molecules slide right through without touching the walls — they come out first. Nonpolar molecules get stuck in the grease and take forever to come out. By adjusting the solvent mixture (more acetonitrile = better grease-cutter), you control how fast each compound washes through. This is why it is called "reverse" — it is the opposite of old-style chromatography where polar things stuck to polar columns.
rationales.highYield: Reverse-phase HPLC: nonpolar stationary (C18), polar mobile (H2O/ACN). Nonpolar sticks longer.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In ^1H NMR, protons near electronegative atoms appear at:

options.text: The same shift regardless of environment

rationales.whyCorrect: Electronegative atoms deshield nearby protons — they withdraw electron density, reducing the local magnetic shielding, so the proton experiences a stronger effective magnetic field and resonates at higher frequency (higher δ). The aldehyde proton (R-CHO) at δ 9–10 is a classic example.
rationales.eli10: NMR chemical shift is like real estate — location matters. Protons near electron-grabbing atoms (oxygen, chlorine) live in "electron-poor neighborhoods" and show up at higher ppm (downfield). Protons in electron-rich areas (next to many carbons) are shielded and appear at lower ppm (upfield). An aldehyde proton at δ 10 is in the poorest neighborhood — right next to a carbonyl oxygen that sucks away electrons.
rationales.highYield: Higher δ (downfield) = deshielded = near electronegative atoms or in electron-poor environments. TMS reference = 0 ppm.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In quantitative analysis, a calibration curve is used to:

options.text: Relate instrument response to analyte concentration using standards

rationales.whyCorrect: A calibration curve plots instrument response (absorbance, peak area) vs known concentrations of standards. A linear fit (R^2 > 0.99) allows determination of unknown concentrations by interpolation. This is the foundation of quantitative chemical analysis.
rationales.eli10: A calibration curve is like making a translator between the instrument's language (voltage, absorbance, peak area) and human language (concentration). You measure known standards, draw a line through the points, and then read your unknown sample off that line — like using a ruler to measure distance on a map. If the line is straight (R^2 close to 1), your translator is reliable.
rationales.highYield: Calibration: standards → response curve → interpolate unknown concentration. Must be linear over working range.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The fingerprint region of an IR spectrum (below ~1500 cm^-1) is useful for:

options.text: Confirming the identity of a compound by matching a reference spectrum

rationales.whyCorrect: The fingerprint region (1500–400 cm^-1) contains complex patterns of skeletal vibrations unique to each molecule. No two different compounds (except enantiomers) have identical fingerprint regions. This region is matched against spectral libraries for positive identification. The functional group region (above 1500) identifies what groups are present.
rationales.eli10: The IR fingerprint region is exactly what it sounds like — a unique pattern for each molecule. No two different compounds have the same squiggly pattern of peaks below 1500 cm^-1. Chemists match this pattern against a database of known spectra, just like detectives match fingerprints at a crime scene. The functional group region tells you what kind of person you are looking for; the fingerprint region confirms exactly who it is.
rationales.highYield: Fingerprint region (<1500 cm^-1) = unique to each molecule, like a human fingerprint. Used for compound identification against databases.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In ^1H NMR, integration of peak areas provides:

options.text: The chemical shift of each proton
The relative number of protons giving rise to each signal

rationales.whyCorrect: The area under each NMR peak is proportional to the number of equivalent protons. For ethanol (CH3CH2OH): ratio 3:2:1 for CH3, CH2, and OH protons. Chemical shift tells environment. Splitting tells neighbors. Integration tells how many.
rationales.eli10: NMR integration is like a census for hydrogen atoms. The computer adds up the area under each peak — a bigger area means more protons of that type. In ethanol, the methyl group (3 identical H's) gives a peak three times as large as the single OH proton. The chemist looks at shift (where), splitting (neighbors), and integration (how many) — three clues that together reveal the complete molecular structure.
rationales.highYield: Integration = proton count. Shift = environment. Splitting = neighboring protons (n+1 rule). Three independent pieces of structural information.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The mass spectrum of CH3Cl shows two molecular ion peaks at m/z 50 and 52 in approximately what ratio?

rationales.whyCorrect: Chlorine has two isotopes: ^35Cl (~75%) and ^37Cl (~25%). CH3^35Cl (m/z 50) and CH3^37Cl (m/z 52) appear in approximately 3:1 ratio. This distinctive isotope pattern reveals the presence of chlorine. Bromine gives ~1:1.
rationales.eli10: Chlorine leaves a telltale fingerprint in mass spectra: two peaks two units apart in a 3:1 ratio. It is like a two-toed footprint — you know chlorine was there. This comes from nature's mix of chlorine-35 (about 75% of all chlorine atoms) and chlorine-37 (about 25%). Bromine has its own pattern (1:1 ratio). These isotope signatures are like chemical ID cards.
rationales.highYield: Cl: M:M+2 ≈ 3:1. Br: M:M+2 ≈ 1:1. Isotope patterns identify Cl, Br, S in mass spectra.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The standard addition method is used when:

options.text: The analyte concentration is very high
The sample matrix interferes with the analysis (matrix effects)

rationales.whyCorrect: Standard addition corrects for matrix effects by adding known amounts of analyte directly to the sample. The x-intercept of the standard addition plot gives the original concentration. This is essential for complex samples (blood, seawater, soil extracts) where the matrix affects instrument response differently than pure standards.
rationales.eli10: Standard addition is like figuring out how much salt is already in the soup by adding known pinches of salt and tasting after each one. The soup's complex flavors (the matrix) affect how you perceive saltiness differently than pure salt water. By plotting taste vs added salt and extrapolating backward to "zero taste," you find the original salt content. It is the most reliable method when the sample's background messes with the measurement.
rationales.highYield: Standard addition: spike sample with known analyte amounts → extrapolate to zero response → find original concentration. Corrects for matrix effects.
